2. Residences

Residence is the most basic building type, and also the prototype of other building forms such as ancestral halls and temples. Research on the construction background of a residence, the residence building itself, plus understanding of its residential history and living conditions, is an important way to grasp the natural conditions, social situation and cultural traditions of the region. The information contained in a residence is accumulated through human construction and use. The "people" here is not one person, nor merely several generations of one family, but completed successively by several generations from different families, even different clans. In this long process, "natural conditions, social situation and cultural traditions are changing, and previously formed residences in turn restrict and shape people's construction concepts and usage patterns of residences. This is an endless process of mutual adaptation." At the same time, the building itself is also being quietly changed. This change may leave traces, such as adding a window here, or removing a wall there. In more cases, this change leaves no visible trace, such as a bedroom becoming a small shop selling goods, or an ancestral hall being converted into storage. All these changes stage the residents' own stories.

Residences are like people; they also have birth, old age, illness and death, fat and thin, beautiful and ugly. To understand a nation, one cannot only care about beautiful young people; the same is true for understanding residences. The residences listed below have construction ages spanning over four hundred years from late Ming to before liberation; their architectural quality and preservation condition are not necessarily the best on the old street, but they are representative. The introduction of each residence strives to be based on understanding "the founder's identity and status, family and experience, financial resources and learning," and focuses on the building itself, as well as the development and changes of its usage in the "adaptation process."

Degeng Residence — Early Residential Architecture

Background

Degeng Residence is the oldest surviving building, and is revered as the ancestral house by the Cheng clan of Yanxia Village. The two characters "Degeng" (Obtaining Plowing) commemorate Cheng Quan (1333-1385), the first ancestor of the Cheng clan in Yanxia Village, and the residence he built with a plaque reading "Degeng" in its hall. The original site of this residence was on the east side of the pond in front of Degeng Residence. Degeng Residence was first built by the seventh-generation ancestor Cheng Heng (1474-1548) in the early sixteenth century, but a fire during the Qing Qianlong period (1736-1795) burned down all buildings except the front hall and "Shude Hall." Villagers believe that the front hall survived because it hung the calligraphy of Cheng Wende, Vice Minister of Rites. In the Jiyou year of Qianlong (1789), Degeng Residence was rebuilt and has been preserved to this day.

Environment

Degeng Residence is located within the mouth of Shang Ravine, west of the old street, facing basically south. As the saying goes, "mountains prosper descendants, water prospers wealth"; when Cheng Heng selected the site and built this new residence, for the Cheng family's future prosperity of descendants and wealth, he not only fully considered the surrounding environment, but also artificially made corresponding adjustments to unfavorable factors, giving it the ideal pattern of backing onto mountains and facing water.

Degeng Residence takes Centipede Mountain as its backing mountain; the north wall of the residence almost touches the first small hill at its west end. The ancestral mountain is Lion Mountain, north of Centipede Mountain and taller. The table mountain is Zhu Gong Mountain, over a hundred meters to its south. Zhu Gong Mountain is also called "Front Hill," and is the first small hill of Lizard Mountain. Directly facing Degeng Residence, there was originally a large cypress tree on the mountain, and under the cypress tree there was originally a local protection temple enshrining "Lord Zhu Gong." Regarding the origin of Lord Zhu Gong, according to folk legend, his prototype was Zhu Danxi (1281-1358), a native of Jinhua and a famous physician of the Yuan Dynasty, who after death became one of the main local folk deities.

According to fengshui descriptions, "Jade Belt Encircling the Waist" is a major feature of an "auspicious residence," also called "Belt Water." It refers to a river flowing in a circular, semicircular or arc shape in front of a building. Opposite Degeng Residence, Xiakeng Stream exactly winds along the north foot of Lizard Mountain, but this stream makes two turns in front of a courtyard at the foot of Front Hill, continues west along the courtyard wall, and finally flows into Fangyan Stream outside the ravine mouth, so the "Jade Belt Encircling the Waist" form did not form in front of Degeng Residence. From another angle, fengshui also mentions "one inch lower is water," so a road can also count as "water." The pond in front of Degeng Residence is half-moon shaped, the only arc-shaped pond in the village. Thus, along the road on the south bank of the pond, Degeng Residence forms the "Jade Belt Encircling the Waist" posture.

This half-moon-shaped pond is called Front Pond; according to the "Shiyuan Gong Genealogy," the pond bottom has a "Double Dragons Playing with a Pearl" pattern inlaid with cobblestones. Beside the pond there was originally a pavilion, where Cheng Heng in his later years freely enjoyed himself and entertained guests. Because the pavilion was east of Fangyan Mountain, he also took the name "Dongting Jushi" (East Pavilion Scholar). Between the pond and the building is a spacious courtyard paved with cobblestones. Between the pond/courtyard and the old street, there was originally a garden, with a path through the garden connecting to the old street. It is said that in the garden, besides exotic flowers and rare plants, there were also various shaped ornamental stones called "Jige" by locals. Today, on the former site of the garden, there are several two-story single-courtyard houses; judging from architectural style, they may have been built successively in the early twentieth century due to the rise of the inn industry, as shop-residence combinations. Between Degeng Residence and the old street, there are also over a dozen two-story residences. At the corner, a small inner courtyard is enclosed. It is said some buildings have nearly two hundred years of history. Thus, although Degeng Residence was not built facing the street, from the old street one could at least formerly see the exquisitely carved double-eave gatehouse, plus the pond and pavilions.

Architecture

Degeng Residence is nearly 28 meters wide and about 54 meters deep, including two large courtyards of front hall and rear hall, with 15 wing rooms on each side. Judging from several contemporaneous residences preserved in Dusong Village, this planar layout represents a typical layout form of residences at that time. For this reason, some architectural elements not completely preserved in Degeng Residence can find answers in other similar residences.

The central part of Degeng Residence's front facade is brick-built, with an exquisitely carved double-eave gatehouse, flanked by plain gable walls of the east and west wing rooms. Overall, high and low are well-arranged, with emphasis highlighted. The main structure of the gatehouse was rebuilt in the Jiyou year of Qianlong (1789); the gable walls of the wing rooms on both sides, judging from brick size, quality and laying method, are far later than the gatehouse and were rebuilt in recent decades. The gate lintel has "Degeng Residence" brick-carved in the center, flanked by qilin, with flowers and birds below, and an exquisitely carved "Double Lions Competing for a Ball" on the door plaque. In addition, on both walls there are exquisite brick carvings of auspicious clouds, flowers and birds, carp, fine horses, and figures.

The first courtyard is a nearly square three-sided courtyard, with a three-bay main hall, usually called the Flower Hall. The Flower Hall originally hung the calligraphy of Cheng Wende, Vice Minister of Rites — the "Shude Hall" horizontal plaque and the couplet "When the mansion is first completed the family has celebration; when official ranks are世代显耀 the country shares rest." Villagers believe that precisely because of Cheng Wende's blessing, the Flower Hall survived the Qianlong-era fire. The front of the Flower Hall is entirely these doors, which can be fully opened when needed; the interior space is tall and open. The back usually only has a door in the central bay, with a screen (also called Taishi Wall) at the front and rear gold pillar positions to block the view. Behind the screen is a staircase leading to the two-story stage behind the Flower Hall. Each side of the front courtyard has three wing rooms, plus two rooms on each side of the Flower Hall, totaling five rooms. There are corridors between the wing rooms and the Flower Hall gable walls, leading to the rear courtyard. The rear courtyard is a rectangular courtyard: behind the Flower Hall is a two-story stage, elevated over a pond called Sun-Moon Well; opposite the stage is a three-bay rear hall; each side of the courtyard has ten wing rooms. The rear hall has two floors; the ground-floor central bay is communal, directly open to the courtyard; the side bays, like the wing rooms, are residential spaces. In the central bay, against the back wall, there is a staircase to the second floor. The three bays on the second floor are connected, belonging to clan communal space. On ordinary days, the second floor and ground-floor central bay together are used for weddings and funerals; during performances they are the audience's domain. All wing rooms of Degeng Residence are residential spaces; with the gradual increase of population, most families can only own one bay upstairs and downstairs. Living downstairs, storage upstairs, connected by a ladder between floors; when there are many people, the upstairs also needs to accommodate residents. As the Cheng clan's "old ancestral house," Degeng Residence's property should belong to everyone, but wealthy Cheng descendants over generations all chose to build new houses nearby, so those remaining here are relatively poor Cheng descendants.

Courtyards built in the same period as Degeng Residence all share one feature in planar layout: the rows of rooms enclosing the courtyard are not connected together, but divided into segments by gable walls, with passages between gable walls leading outside. Taking Degeng Residence as an example, between the wing rooms on each side of the Flower Hall, there is an over-one-meter-wide east-west passage, with a door on the outer side leading outside the courtyard. In some old courtyards in Dusong Village, the second floor of the passages also has connecting corridors. There are also passages on both sides of the gable walls of the Flower Hall and rear hall, connecting the spaces before and after the halls. The outer sides of the passages on both sides of the rear hall also have doors leading outside. The reasons may be threefold: first, because the courtyard is too large, dividing with gable walls aims to minimize loss in case of fire; second, for such large courtyards, if built in separate segments, it is technically relatively easier; third, for the many families living together here, having more doors also facilitates entry and exit.

Stage of Life

As the oldest and largest surviving residence in Yanxia Village — Degeng Residence also serves sacrificial functions, and is simultaneously the village's cultural and entertainment center. In the first lunar month, any clan member without a hall in their home will hang portraits of their great-grandparents on the inner gable wall of the Flower Hall, borrowing this place to honor them. The open space in front of the residence is also an important space for the annual dragon lantern festival. The dragon head, dragon tail, plus over a hundred "bridges" of dragon body, are assembled here before setting out. The stage in the rear courtyard performs a "Peace Play" every year on New Year's Eve or in the first lunar month. It is called this because people hope that besides the bustle, the performance can also pray for peace in all four seasons and prosperity of descendants. On ordinary days, when a wealthy family in the village celebrates a birthday, a troupe will perform here for three days and three nights; or well-off families occasionally pay to invite a troupe, as a good deed. Even in the age of television in every home, performing plays remains the village's busiest event after dragon lanterns and temple fairs. The cost of inviting a troupe every New Year's Eve or first lunar month is usually shared by the whole village. During performances, even the backstage of the Flower Hall is used by the troupe as temporary accommodation. Before the performance, villagers mostly bring their own stools. The entire rear courtyard, rear hall central bay and second floor are crowded with men, women and children. Families living in the wing rooms also invite relatives and friends to sit in the corridors or come to their homes to watch. Sometimes, in the rear hall central bay, someone sells snacks like peanuts, smoked tofu, and wontons. In addition, the open space and pond in front of Degeng Residence are also stages where villagers演绎 their daily lives. From morning to night one can see such scenes: women washing clothes and chatting by the pond; children playing and frolicking in the open space; men sitting at the base of walls playing chess and chatting...

Cheng Lizhong Mansion — Large Multi-Courtyard Residence of Mid-Eighteenth Century

Background

Cheng Lizhong (1736-1793), courtesy name Fengshi, hao Yi'an, was the fifteenth-generation ancestor of the Yanxia Cheng clan. Cheng Lizhong's grandfather was Zuoxun Gong, highly respected by villagers and owning a personal ancestral hall; his father was Zuoxun Gong's youngest son, Jingchen, i.e. the ancestor of the Gongchang branch; Cheng Lizhong and his three older brothers were divided into the Fa, Qiang, Gang and Yi branches. Currently Cheng Lizhong has the most descendants on the old street; the genealogy calls this branch "Gongxia Yichang," and they have their own ancestral hall, Shaochang Ancestral Hall. It is said that this three-hall two-courtyard mansion was built by Cheng Lizhong's father-in-law, who sent people to the village to build it before sending his daughter over. This story of "building a flower hall at the rock foot, father-in-law paying the silver" has always been a favorite topic of villagers after meals. Based on Cheng Lizhong's age, the construction date of this residence should be in the mid-eighteenth century.

Environment

Cheng Lizhong Mansion is located south of Xiakeng mouth, at the west foot of Lizard Mountain. Before it was built, village residences were basically all within Xiakeng mouth, in the triangular river valley where Xiakeng Stream and Fangyan Stream meet. This area is high and relatively flat, easy to build on; living here one can both go up the mountain to chop firewood and conveniently tend the fields in Xiakeng, and the inner courtyard can also bathe in morning sunlight. With the continuous increase of population, Cheng descendants had to build new residences elsewhere; Cheng Lizhong Mansion was the first residence built outside Xiakeng mouth.

After leaving Xiakeng mouth, the old street tightly hugs Lizard Mountain, which rises almost from the ground. This section of Lizard Mountain is also called "Front Hill," and also named "Zhu Gong Mountain" after the Zhu Gong Temple on the mountain. Cheng Lizhong Mansion generally faces south; its east and west courtyard walls are perfectly wedged between the north-south old street and Fangyan Stream. The southwest corner of the courtyard also follows the course of Fangyan Stream with a chamfered corner, made into an arc shape.

This courtyard adopts a courtyard-within-courtyard form in planar layout, so its building area is much larger than two Degeng Residences combined. Inside the courtyard walls there are not only the imposing three-courtyard residence for living, but also vegetable plots, gardens, "in-house pond" and "in-house well." Because the old street and Fangyan Stream here have a nearly one-story height difference, the residential part within the courtyard is on the higher east side facing the street, while the pond and vegetable plots are on the lower west side near the water. Viewed from the Fangyan Stream side, the entire building complex sits on a high platform built of giant stones, appearing even more majestic.

Architecture

The main entrance of Cheng Lizhong Mansion is located on the east wall of the courtyard, slightly south, facing the old street. After entering, there is an alley called "Eight-Foot Road," leading straight to another courtyard door on the west wall. Walking on the Eight-Foot Road, on the left is first the open vegetable plot and garden, on the right is the residential courtyard enclosed by gray walls and black tiles. Tight against the west wall of this residential courtyard is a rectangular pond larger than that of an ordinary residence, called "Cheyue Pond"; opposite the pond across the Eight-Foot Road is also a well. Such ponds and wells inside buildings are also called "in-house ponds" and "in-house wells." In that era, in-house ponds and wells were usually synonymous with deep mansions and wealth. The west side of the pond was originally the courtyard wall; now only a two-meter-wide wall base built of stones and rammed earth remains. It is said there was a corridor along the wall, and the space under the corridor could be used both for storage and for raising livestock.

The residential space faces south, originally a three-courtyard residence with three halls and two halls. This complex uses a single-eave gatehouse-style main door as entrance; the brick carvings on the eyebrow eave are still clearly visible. The first courtyard is a three-sided courtyard, with a square mingtang (central courtyard) of similar scale to Degeng Residence's first courtyard. The sparrow brackets (que ti) under the eaves corridor and the second-floor railing style are typical of late Ming-early Qing local residences; on the old street only the contemporaneously built Shaochang Ancestral Hall and Yifeng Yaji use the same method. Comparing these two buildings, one can see another feature of architecture of that period: a small skylight (tianjing) is made at each corner of the main hall and wing rooms for ventilation and lighting, but in this courtyard the skylights are replaced by two wing rooms. This change may be due to population increase, or may have occurred when the residence was converted into an inn.

The building's envelope has been rebuilt, and small wooden decorations are basically not preserved, but the large wooden frame of the house is relatively well preserved, even including some exquisite carvings. All three-sided corridors use crescent beams (yue liang); the beam brackets under the main hall eaves corridor are carved with coiled dragon patterns, while the wing room eaves corridors use scrolling grass. The sparrow brackets also have different carving themes: the main hall side has openwork carvings of flowers, birds and animals, while the wing rooms have scrolling grass. The scrolling grass pattern on the crescent beam head of the main hall central bay is especially elegant in line and balanced in proportion. Grandma Lu, who has lived here for decades, said: the main hall central bay originally had six exquisitely carved door leaves; the side bays for living each had a set of carved doors and windows; the Taishi Wall in the central bay had doors on both sides leading to the rear courtyard.

The latter two courtyards gradually collapsed after liberation; their traces can only be found from the remaining foundations and platform paving. The second courtyard is a four-sided courtyard, with mingtang width the same as the first courtyard, and depth about halved. The third courtyard is again a three-sided courtyard, with mingtang depth further halved. The positions originally vegetable plots and gardens within the mansion are now scattered with several relatively simple residences. Except for the residence south of the Eight-Foot Road, which was built in the early nineteenth century, the other residences should have been built around the time of "Land Reform," by poor families who received land.

Yifeng Yaji Building Complex — Single-Entry Three-Sided Courtyard Residences of Late Eighteenth Century

Environment

On the west side of Centipede Mountain, between the old street and Fangyan Stream, three courtyard houses stand alone side by side. The west walls of these three courtyards tightly hug Fangyan Stream; crossing the stream is the largest existing rice paddy in the valley. Viewed from afar, the gray bricks and black tiles, slightly crimson after centuries of rain erosion, against the backdrop of green mountains and fields, appear particularly deep and dignified. Among these three courtyard houses, the earliest built is the middle "Yifeng Yaji," followed by the northern "Yifeng Old Shop," and the southern one is the latest, tentatively called "Yifeng South Courtyard"; together they form a building complex of "13 front hall rooms, 9 mother-house rooms, 13 rear hall rooms."

It can be seen that during the construction of these three buildings, a series of modifications were made to the surrounding environment. In plan, the west wall of Yifeng Yaji rotates a few degrees counterclockwise. It can be guessed that this was the course of Fangyan Stream over a hundred years ago. When Yifeng South Courtyard was built, it did not continue along the direction of Yifeng Yaji's west wall, but was built as a square, completely symmetrical courtyard. From this it is believed that the builder of Yifeng South Courtyard pushed the original course of Fangyan Stream westward; this may be why Fangyan Stream makes a nearly ninety-degree sharp turn outside the south wall of Yifeng South Courtyard. In section, like Cheng Lizhong Mansion, these three courtyards all sit steadily on a nearly one-story-high foundation built of giant stones and rammed earth. The reason for this method is that the street backs onto the mountain and the stream runs along the valley; the height of the old street varies with terrain, so in local areas there is a nearly one-story height difference with the valley. This method of raising the courtyard ground level is relatively time-consuming and labor-intensive, so by the early nineteenth century, courtyards here adopted another form, namely "the lower floor is built in the valley, the middle floor faces the street, and the upper floor is the building."

Background

Most people on the old street believe that the builder of Yifeng Yaji was also the fifteenth-generation ancestor Cheng Lizhong. But elderly Cheng Renlong, who lives in Yifeng Yaji, says this courtyard house was built in the second year of Jiaqing (1797); from this calculation, the builder should be a descendant of Cheng Lizhong (1736-1793).

The Cheng clan of Yanxia Old Street was divided into four branches in the early sixteenth century: Fu (Blessing), Lu (Salary), Shou (Longevity), and Bai (Cypress). Among these four branches, the Bai branch had the fewest people; the Fu and Shou branches, although their population was fairly prosperous, were inferior compared to the Lu branch. Zuoxun Gong and his descendants, plus most families who later opened shops on the street, were all under the Lu branch. Several decades after Yifeng Yaji was built, Cheng Leyong (1832-1866) of the Fu branch, i.e. Cheng Renlong's great-grandfather, bought Yifeng Yaji from Cheng Lizhong's descendants. We cannot determine whether Yifeng Old Shop and Yifeng South Courtyard were part of this transaction, or who their builders were. From architectural style, Yifeng Old Shop's architectural form is very simple, with extremely plain carvings, indicating the builder's relatively weak economic situation at the time. Conversely, from the exquisite large wooden structure and small wooden carvings of Yifeng South Shop, the builder's financial resources at the time can be seen. Cheng Leyong was the only son of Cheng Lijin (1778-1862); according to genealogy records, both father and son served as "Zhou Sima" (prefectural military officer). From another perspective, selling houses and land has always been the last choice of feudal families when financially strained. From this it is推测 that Cheng Leyong at that time may have only bought Yifeng Yaji and Yifeng Old Shop, then subsequently added Yifeng South Courtyard for his third son.

The county gazetteer records that Cheng Yifeng Inn opened during the Qing Xianfeng period (1851-1861), founded by Cheng Leyong. Cheng Leyong had three sons: Cheng Zhaogong, Cheng Zhaosuo and Cheng Zhaoming. According to 90-year-old elderly Cheng Chongshun on the old street, these three courtyards were once named after the three brothers' branch names, called from south to north "Feng (Wind), Ya (Elegance), Song (Ode)." After family division, the youngest son Cheng Zhaoming lived in the north courtyard, continued operating Cheng Yifeng Inn and renamed it Yifeng Old Shop; the second son Cheng Zhaosuo lived in the middle, operated Yifeng Yaji using the branch name as shop name; the eldest son Cheng Zhaogong lived in the south courtyard, because his family had four sons and housing was tight, so he did not open a shop.

Architecture

Yifeng Yaji was originally a three-sided courtyard with three-bay main hall and three wing rooms on each side; along the south wall of the courtyard there is a corridor connecting the east and west wing rooms. The courtyard entrance was originally in the center of the south gatehouse; after Yifeng South Courtyard was built, Yifeng Yaji's entrance was moved to the southeast corner of the courtyard, directly connected to the old street. According to elderly Cheng Renlong, the main hall of Yifeng Yaji once hung a plaque reading "Yijin Hall"; it is said this was gifted by others when an ancestor served as an official, so Yifeng Yaji is also called Yijin Hall.

Comparing these three buildings, one can see the development and changes of architecture on the old street within just over half a century. In planar layout, Yifeng Yaji has a rectangular small skylight at each corner of the main hall and wing rooms. Thus in plan, the skylights and mingtang together form a "Pin" (品) character; "Pin"-shaped skylights usually carry the寓意 of "official rank one grade higher." In the other two residences, the skylight positions are each replaced by two wing rooms. The depth of the main halls of the three buildings is basically similar, but because Yifeng Yaji's eaves corridor is wider and there is another corridor between the main hall and back wall, the central bay depth is relatively small, and the interior uses an entire crescent beam spanning the main hall longitudinally. The main hall central bays of Yifeng Yaji and Yifeng South Courtyard are both明显 wider than the side bays; Yifeng Old Shop's practice is the same as most courtyard houses on the old street, i.e. the three main hall bays have only slight width differences. The main hall heights of Yifeng Yaji and Yifeng Old Shop are both about eight meters, while Yifeng South Courtyard is half a meter shorter. Courtyards subsequently built on the old street all have main hall heights of about seven and a half meters; clearly this new height represents a new module and practice for residential architecture. Yifeng Yaji uses sparrow brackets under the eaves corridor, and the second-floor railing style is the same as the contemporaneously built Cheng Lizhong Mansion and Shaochang Ancestral Hall. The other two buildings have neither sparrow brackets under the corridors nor elaborate railings. The mingtang practices of the three courtyards also differ: Yifeng Yaji has drainage ditches outside the platform, with the mingtang paved with stone slabs; Yifeng Old Shop's mingtang is paved with cobblestones, no drainage ditch; Yifeng South Courtyard has a drainage ditch but uses cobblestone paving. Comparing other buildings on the old street, the drainage ditch is an early practice; later buildings all use cobblestones to fully pave the mingtang, with rainwater draining through outlets at the four corners. Another significant difference is reflected in the carvings of wooden components: Yifeng Old Shop's eaves corridor uses neither crescent beams nor elaborate small woodwork, only simple lattice windows; Yifeng Yaji's large wooden carvings and small wood decorations mostly use abstract geometric patterns as decorative motifs, exquisitely carved yet retaining elegance and simplicity; Yifeng South Courtyard's carvings are the most exquisite but slightly affected, with flower windows full of flowers, plants, birds and beasts, and even the small beam brackets under the eaves corridor carved with pavilions and towers on both sides.

The evolution of these architectural details, of course, to some extent objectively reflects the builder's financial situation at the time. But if these changes are compared horizontally, one can see subtle shifts in people's values and aesthetic orientation toward architectural space and the building itself. In Cheng Lizhong's era, the builder's financial resources were reflected in spacious and tall spaces, "Pin"-shaped skylights, two rough yet carved crescent beams in the hall, stone-slab-paved mingtang, and finishing-touch carvings. For late Qing builders, due to population increase, emergence of new economic forms, and changes in people's functional needs for living space, they became more concerned with the practicality and economy of architecture. Conversely, because architectural technology development had relatively stagnated at the time, both builders and craftsmen pursued architectural decoration without restraint.

Cheng Chengchang Inn — Inn-Style Courtyard Residence of Early Twentieth Century

Background

Cheng Chengchang Inn is a typical inn-style courtyard residence, located east of the old street, north of Xiahu Ravine mouth, with the east wall of the courtyard tightly hugging a corner of Lion Mountain. Although its construction date cannot be确定, it can be inferred from the construction times of surrounding courtyards. South of Cheng Chengchang Inn, there are two courtyards belonging to Cheng Zhenxing Inn. The southern courtyard was completed in 1880, the middle one built 19 years later. North of Cheng Chengchang, west of the old street, Cheng Zhenxing Inn acquired its third courtyard in 1924. From this it is inferred that Cheng Chengchang Inn should have been built between 1909 and 1924. The formation process of the old street, generally speaking, was a process of gradual north-south linear development centered on Shang Ravine. Many adjacent buildings on the street were mostly built successively southward or northward along the street. Especially several courtyards belonging to one family, if possible, were all built side by side and spatially interconnected.

The founder of Cheng Chengchang Inn was Cheng Zhaofeng (1855-1928). His second brother Cheng Zhaofu owned the largest inn on the old street, hall name Cheng Zhenchang; his sixth brother Cheng Zhaogong founded Cheng Longchang located at the north end of the old street within Chengli Village; his fourth brother Cheng Zhaolu's Cheng Zhenchang grocery store also switched to inn business after the Cultural Revolution. It can be said that in the early twentieth century, at least one-third of pilgrims coming to Fangyan from afar stayed in inns opened by these four brothers. Cheng Zhaofeng was actually the fifth-generation grandson of Cheng Lizhong; his father was Cheng Lelai, grandfather Cheng Lishu, great-grandfather Cheng Yipeng. As the eldest son of Cheng Yipeng, Cheng Lishu inherited a small courtyard built on the garden within Cheng Lizhong Mansion. Cheng Lishu had no biological heir; Cheng Lelai was adopted by Lishu's third brother Liqi to the elder brother, so Cheng Lelai inherited all his father's property, including this residence. The Lelai family's life should not have been too straitened, so each of his sons, after starting a family, could get some capital and part of daily necessities from his father, move out to live independently and start operating their own small business; and Lelai once used his own residence to operate a small inn.

The existence of "adopted sons" and "only sons" are two very special and meaningful phenomena in Chinese feudal patrilineal society. Brothers adopting sons to each other, of course, has no impact on the clan's population in the short term. But in the long run, the diversity of family backgrounds and living environments greatly increases the possibility of the entire clan's continued reproduction and survival. Browsing the "Shiyuan Gong Genealogy" of the Cheng clan on the old street, it is not difficult to find that this adoption phenomenon is very common. Sometimes the person adopting a son is not without sons, just few; at that time if his brother has more sons, he will also adopt one; sometimes the family giving a son may also only have two sons, but for the benefit of the entire clan, they will忍痛 give the youngest son to the brother without sons; sometimes several brothers, one without heirs, the other brothers each adopt one to him; if biological brothers cannot adopt, occasionally they will choose from paternal cousins. If having more sons is for better continuation of the family line, then "only son" is a very unfavorable situation. But the greatest significance of an "only son" is that he can avoid the pain of family division and smoothly inherit all his father's property. The founders of the inn industry on the old street were basically all nineteenth-generation descendants of the Cheng clan; among the three brother families who did well in this industry, the fathers of two of the brother families were only sons in their families; perhaps there is a certain objective factor in this coincidence.

After Cheng Zhaofeng died, his only son Cheng Xuanni inherited the family business. Among Xuanni's four sons, the eldest died young; the second son moved to a distant place; the youngest son Cheng Zhenyi continued operating Cheng Chengchang Inn, and in 1991 moved to the new street, renaming it "New Cheng Zhenchang"; the third son Cheng Zhenkang's family, as well as some inn clerks, still live in the old house.

Architecture

The planar layout and architectural form of Cheng Chengchang Inn are typical of newly built residences on the old street in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Compared with previously built courtyard houses, the biggest difference of these newly built courtyards is that the builders already considered "operating an inn" as the building's main function, and this change is most directly reflected in the building's plan. Previously, courtyards with residence as the main function — whether Degeng Residence built in the early sixteenth century, Cheng Lizhong Mansion and Yifeng Yaji of the late eighteenth century, or Cheng Zhengwei Ham Shop and its additions built in the mid-late nineteenth century — were either single-entry three-sided courtyards or multi-entry courtyards composed of multiple three-sided courtyards; that is to say, there were no north-facing rooms in the courtyard. North-facing rooms have poor sunlight, cold in winter and hot in summer, unsuitable for living; omitting them is only natural. Another advantage of this practice is that the courtyard facade can become relatively free, undulating, more conducive to highlighting the central gatehouse entrance. But if used as an inn, the more rooms the better. The main courtyards of Cheng Chengchang and Cheng Zhenxing Inn occupy about the same area as Yifeng Yaji, both about 430 square meters, and the mingtang areas are also similar; but Yifeng Yaji has only nine rooms on the ground floor, Yifeng Old Shop and Yifeng South Courtyard (which omitted two small skylights) have no more than thirteen, while these newly built inns have sixteen. The reason, taking Cheng Chengchang Inn as an example, is that the depth of its main hall and wing rooms is each about one meter shorter than Yifeng Yaji; the area thus saved is converted into a row of rooms on the north side of the inner courtyard. Compared with contemporaneous residences in Chengli Village, due to no functional need for operating an inn, all courtyards regardless of orientation do not have this reverse-side row of rooms; locals also俗 call these courtyards "nine-room head," "eleven-room head" etc. according to the number of ground-floor rooms.

Cheng Chengchang Inn generally faces true north-south, with three-bay main hall, five wing rooms on each side, and three-bay reverse-side rooms. Between the main hall and the wing rooms on both sides there is an over-one-meter-wide side passage, with a staircase to the second floor. The central bay of the main hall, here called the West Room, is both the public space of the inn and residence, and the ritual center of this family: the whole family eats here; guests come to rest and drink tea here; festivals and holidays hold ancestor worship here; relatives who pass away are mourned here; even pilgrims who cannot go up Fangyan for various reasons will set up an incense table here, facing Fangyan Mountain to worship Hu Gong. Between the rear gold pillars of the West Room is the Taishi Wall; even in ordinary times, portraits of ancestors hang on the Taishi Wall. Due to functional needs, the West Room can usually be fully opened; if doors are installed, they are removable panel doors; behind the Taishi Wall is a storage room, entered through a side door. The east and west rooms of the West Room are respectively called Upper Great Room and Lower Great Room; east is "upper," slightly higher in status, usually优先分给 the eldest son during family division, and the Lower Great Room to the second son. The east wing rooms from north to south are respectively called Inner Wing, Outer Wing, Small West Room, Yuan Room and Passage Room. The west wing rooms face the street, serving as shop fronts, also called shop halls. The two southern shop halls protrude several meters outward along the street; the northernmost one also forms a small overhanging building on the second floor, spanning the old street. Unfortunately, these two rooms were sold by Cheng Zhaofu; the remaining three from south to north are respectively called Upper Shop Hall, Middle Shop Hall and Lower Shop Hall, among which the Lower Shop Hall bay is the entrance to the courtyard and inn. The three reverse-side rooms from east to west are respectively East Facing Hall, Facing Hall and West Facing Hall. The Facing Hall has smaller depth, so it is the only side in the courtyard, on both first and second floors, without an eaves corridor.

The mingtang is 12 meters wide and about 7.5 meters deep, i.e. the width of three main hall bays and two wing room bays. The mingtang is paved with cobblestones, the ground slightly higher in the middle and lower around, with drainage outlets at the four corners, connected to the drainage ditches on both sides of the street. In the middle of the courtyard there is also an "in-house well" representing wealth and status. The well water is clear and sweet, and至今 is still the main source of drinking water for Cheng Zhenkang's family.

Passing through the passage room at the southeast corner of the courtyard, there is a three-bay-wide storage room and bathroom; exiting the north door of the storage room is the rear courtyard. In the rear courtyard there is a small pond, about half a room in size, formerly used for washing chamber pots, now used for washing farm tools. Against the hillside next to the storage room, there is also a small vegetable plot.

The position north of the courtyard facing the street was originally a large kitchen, because the kitchen not only needed to cook but also brew wine, and raise pigs, chickens, ducks, geese and other livestock. In peak season, Cheng Zhaofu's family plus clerks would also live on the second floor of the kitchen, so as to vacate more rooms for pilgrims. After liberation, part of the kitchen was sold to outsiders; in the 1980s, the remaining kitchen collapsed, so the Small West Room was converted to a kitchen.

Changes

In the early operation of Cheng Chengchang Inn, guest rooms were very simple, mainly receiving pilgrims from Dongyang, Yiwu, Yongkang, Jinhua, Pujiang, Shengxian etc. Their requirements were not high, and they could be satisfied with two people sharing one "bed." The so-called "bed" was a one-meter-plus-wide wooden board supported by two stools, with a thin layer of straw on top. During the August-September incense season, as long as one could sleep on a floor mat under a roof, guests were content. In this situation, upstairs and downstairs could accommodate nearly 300 people. But as Hu Gong's fame grew, guests from big cities such as Shanghai and Shaoxing also increased, and they raised higher requirements for the inn's food and facilities. Cheng Chengchang ultimately could not compete with large inns like Cheng Zhenxing in this regard, so it could only receive "medium" or "lower" grade pilgrims.

In the 1940s, during the years when the Zhejiang Provincial Nationalist Government was stationed at Fangyan, like most other inns, Cheng Chengchang almost ceased operation. Although there were no pilgrims, Cheng Chengchang became busier. Those coming and going were civil servants working in the Civil Affairs Department and their families; the shop hall was also rented out as a printing factory. These civil servants had higher requirements for living conditions; for this Cheng Chengchang also carried out a series of renovations, including laying wooden floors on the ground floor for moisture protection; enlarging the windows on the exterior walls for lighting; and for safety reasons, adding a staircase at the passage room position.

After the Anti-Japanese War ended, Cheng Chengchang resumed business, and the inn business prospered for several more years. From 1949 to 1980, the inn opened and closed several times. During 1958-1960, it also served successively as a nursing home, Zhiying People's Commune Umbrella Factory and Yanxia Brigade Umbrella Factory. Fortunately, because the family had many people, the house was not divided during "Land Reform," which is also an important reason why this courtyard has been well preserved to this day. In August 1980, the inn resumed business again; with the gradual improvement of business, Cheng Zhenyi moved the inn to a modern small building next to the new street in 1991, renaming it "New Cheng Chengchang."

Cheng Renchang Inn, Cheng Zhenxing Inn, Cheng Keng Villa — Chinese-Western Combined Architecture of Mid-Twentieth Century

In the mid-twentieth century, several Chinese-Western combined buildings were successively completed on the old street. Among them, two分别 belong to parts of Cheng Renchang Inn and Cheng Zhenxing Inn, and the other is called Cheng Keng Villa.

This Chinese-Western combined building belonging to Cheng Renchang Inn is located at the west foot of Lion Mountain, west of the old street, outside the north wall of Cheng Renchang Old Shop. This was originally a four-story wooden structure standalone building; its building materials, construction methods and decorative motifs all follow the characteristics of local traditional architecture, and the influence of Western architecture is mainly reflected in spatial layout. According to the recollection of elderly Cheng Zhenlong, a descendant of Cheng Renchang Inn, when building the house, Cheng Zhaoye originally wanted to build a traditional four-sided courtyard, but on the suggestion of Engineer Pan changed it to a standalone mansion. Unlike other courtyard buildings on the old street, this building of Cheng Renchang Inn has its courtyard紧挨着 the old street; the nearly square-plan three-bay building sits on the west side of the courtyard, with a front porch transitioning between rooms and courtyard. The courtyard ground level is the same as the valley; the entrance on the old street is equivalent to second-floor height; after entering, one reaches the first floor through steps on both sides. Another difference in spatial layout is reflected in section. The second floor of courtyard houses on the old street originally did not accommodate people, only for storage, so the second-floor railing practice was just arranging several wooden boards vertically in the frame. Compared with Western architecture, high-rise spaces have always been the main living space, so railings naturally become the focus of decoration. After the rise of the inn industry, second-floor spaces became important living spaces during incense seasons; buildings built after the mid-twentieth century more or less decorated the railings. Each floor of this building has twenty-nine exquisitely carved railing panels. In the mid-1930s, Cheng Zhaoye's eldest son Cheng Xuanhu inherited this building and a small courtyard behind it, renaming the shop Xin Renchang. Cheng Xuanhu had three sons; in early liberation due to poor economic conditions, he was forced to sell the third and fourth floors of the building.

Cheng Keng Villa is located at the entrance of Fangyan Mountain, south of the old street. Cheng Keng (1895-1968), according to genealogy records named Cheng Xuankeng, was the eldest son of Cheng Zhaochun. According to the recollection of elderly Cheng Zhenfeng (born 1939, Chong generation, 21st generation of Cheng), grandson of Cheng Zhaochun, Cheng Zhaochun (born 1864, death year unknown) was the actual builder of this villa; after his death, the villa was jointly owned by the eldest and second sons, and the third son, i.e. his father, inherited the old house. Cheng Keng, as a locally somewhat famous painter in the early twentieth century, left home young to develop in Shanghai, and settled in Yongkang after the "August 13" Incident. Although he may never have lived here and did not own the entire building, people still call this building Cheng Keng Villa because of his fame. Cheng Keng Villa is also a standalone wooden structure building; compared with Cheng Renchang Inn, the influence of Western architecture on spatial layout is more significant here. The entire building sits on a one-meter-plus-high stone platform, facing east, surrounded by courtyard space on all sides. The plan is three bays, composed of six nearly square spaces, with corridors on all four sides. The front and rear central bays are open or semi-open halls; the four north-south rooms are for living, with doors opening to the south and north corridors. One of the greatest advantages of this layout is that each bedroom has windows in two directions, conducive to ventilation; no wonder Cheng Keng's descendants living here emphasize "this house is very cool." Like Cheng Renchang Inn, the second-floor railing of Cheng Keng Villa also has exquisite openwork wood carvings.

Among the many buildings owned by Cheng Zhenxing Inn, there are two connected Western-style buildings. The northern one was built by Cheng Zhaofu in the 1930s; it is a two-story six-bay brick-stone structure building. Its north side connects to the south wall of Cheng Zhaofu Ancestral Hall, and the east wall is紧挨着 the old street. From the outside, almost no trace of local architecture can be seen; replaced by common Western architectural features such as brick pilasters, round small windows and wide bright glass windows. The southern row was built in 1942, commissioned by Cheng Zhaofu's sons Cheng Xuanmei and Cheng Xuanji from a Hangzhou construction factory. This three-story seven-bay Western building is actually still a wooden structure; all rooms face south and are ventilated north-south, with rooms on each floor connected by corridors and open to the south-facing inner courtyard. Western architectural elements are mainly reflected in the detailed treatment of the envelope brick walls, such as brick-arched windows and Western-style gatehouses. In the mid-1940s, Cheng Zhenxing was divided into two; Cheng Xuanmei's son Cheng Chongxue inherited these two buildings, renaming the shop Xin Zhenxing. In early liberation, due to economic reasons, one floor of the second Western building was sold, now only two floors remain.

sections.name: 宗祠
sections.content_zh:
三、宗祠

在农耕社会里，人们无论是盖房、修路，或是开沟渠、整田亩，还是抵抗各种外来的天灾人祸，都不是一个人或是一个家庭可以独立完成的，而是需要许多人的相互扶持和共同努力。在中国几千年的父系社会里，建立在血缘和亲情基础之上的父系家族就很自然地承担起了这个责任。于是，聚族而居和血缘村落就自然而然地成为一种普遍的现象。这种客观现象的存在，以及历代中国社会都尊崇"孝道"的伦理准则，便为宗祠的产生提供了前提条件。纵观中国历史，北方长年战乱并且人口流失严重，相比之下南方相对安定，更易于血缘村落的形成和发展。所以在江浙地区，特别是像岩下老街这样，地处丘陵地带、交通不发达的村落，一般都保留有较强的宗族意识和相对完整的世族体系。

宗祠的基本功能在于，它是一个供奉和祭拜祖先的仪式性场所。这里的祠堂里都供奉着历代先人的牌位；逢年过节和祭祀时，还要挂上本房祖宗的画像。有的宗祠里还设有谱房以便管理宗族人口的派系、行辈、婚姻等问题。祠堂同时也是商议族内大事、调解族人矛盾、旌表功名、办学堂、存放公共器物的场所。在大一点儿的祠堂里还有戏台，在特殊的日子里，宗祠便暂时放下它的神圣地位，而成为全村的文化娱乐中心，甚至还允许族人在这里赌博娱乐。以上这些都体现了宗祠存在的意义和重要性，即通过一系列祖先崇拜的仪式及活动来加强程氏家族的内部凝聚力。"加强宗族的内聚力，就是加强人际合作的社会单元的能量，这是人们生存并发展的最重要依靠，从而促成了祖先崇拜，也便是血缘认同。"

虽然橙麓村和岩下村供奉的是同一始祖程锴，但是老街旁曾先后建造了大大小小至少八座程氏各房派的祠堂。它们在村里都是最重要，通常也是建造最精美的建筑。在江浙地区的多数村落中，祠堂通常会位于村落相对中心的地带，其位置和朝向多少都会影响到村落的布局。但是老街的发展由于受到地形的限制，所以这里的祠堂大多都沿街坐落，并没能对村落的空间序列起到决定性的影响。即便如此，在用地紧张的情况下，祠堂前通常都有水塘或空地，这个空间依旧是村落生活的舞台。

程氏宗祠

程氏宗祠始建于明正德己亥年（1515年），位于橙麓村象鼻岗山脚。它是迁居这里的程氏所建的第一个祠堂，也是岩下老街众多祠堂中唯一被收入县志的，"三十五都程宗祠：始祖闰二闰三"。祠堂坐西朝东，东侧是螺蛳塘山，山上建有三世祖程权之墓。在嘉靖年间，祠堂曾改建为前后两进；在道光丙午年重修成五开间，前后三进院落，并且用石柱代替已经糟朽的木柱。据当地人回忆：整个祠堂宽二十多米，进深近五十米；有牌门一座，享堂五间，寝室九间，还有厢房位于南北两侧。在抗日战争时期，中共浙江省委书记刘英被关在程氏宗祠内，并于1942年5月13日在祠堂内遇害。1992年1月21日，程氏宗祠随着刘英烈士陵园的开工而被拆毁。在当地程氏后人的努力下，部分石柱、柱础和门楣等建筑构件被送到文楼村保存，以便日后重建。居住在橙麓村的程家麟老人还花钱买下了一些柱础，这些柱础现在还依然摆放在他家的院墙外。还有一些柱础上面架上了石条，成了村里人小憩和唠家常的地方。在橙麓村的水塘边和小路旁，还能看到许多似乎曾被用作为台明石的大块石料；水塘里的一块洗衣石上还有两个刚劲的楷体大字"之墓"。老人们已经不记得这块石头的来历，更无法寻找另一半墓碑的下落。这些点点滴滴的痕迹，都记录着那幢曾经矗立在村口长达五百年之久的建筑的辉煌。

世远公祠及作勳公祠

背景

世远公祠，俗称小祠堂，是为纪念程坦（1411—1477年）而建造的。程坦字世远，为永康程氏六世祖。作勳公指的是十三世祖程际烈（1646—1725年）。作勳公祠又叫友恭常祠，友常和恭常分别代表作勳公的两个儿子程伊臣（1691—1765年）和程经臣（1697—1771年）的房派。

村里的老人们已经不记得这两座祠堂具体的建造年代了，但是他们大多都很肯定一点，那就是虽然世远公比作勳公早出生二百多年，但是作勳公祠建在世远公祠之前，并且它们都比不远处的绍常祠堂要早。从两个祠堂的相互关系上看，世远公祠位于作勳公祠前，并挡住了其正门，也从侧面支持了世远公祠建造较晚的说法。现住在作勳公祠里的程茂发（1934年生，崇字辈，程氏21代）老人讲，作勳公祠是程伊臣和程经臣为其父亲共同建造的，所以又叫友恭常祠；而世远公祠是作勳公的孙子建造的。这种说法听起来也不无道理，在时间上也是成立的，即作勳公祠建于十八世纪中叶，世远公祠可能在随后的一二十年后。而曾参加过抗美援朝的程龙兴（1930年生，圣字辈，程氏22代）则振振有词地说，世远公祠是在明嘉靖年间（1522—1566年），由世远公的孙子建造的。家谱中记载，世远公的长孙生活的年代为1494—1568年，所以这在时间上也是可能的。

这两座祠堂的先后建成，标志着岩下村已经从一个杂姓聚居的村落，转变成了一个程氏的血缘村落。之所以人们为作勳公建造祠堂，不仅是因为程际烈家境富足，更是因为他"资雄里闬，每遇岁歉必出粟赈饥，凡有求者缓靡不相济。人皆德之"。不仅如此，程际烈的两个儿子也广受乡亲的尊敬。家谱记载其长子伊臣"文艺精通"，并且独修宗谱；次子经臣"善承家业"。为世远公建造祠堂则意义更为重大，岩下村的程氏一直奉世远公为始祖，村里新修好的家谱就叫《世远公宗谱》。究其原因为，虽然三世祖程权是岩下村的始迁祖，但是他的子孙除程坦外，即世远公，均外迁他乡。自六世祖程坦以后，这支程氏才世代留居在了岩下村。

环境

这两座祠堂位于上坑口外，老街以西。方岩溪在它们的西边，紧贴着世远公祠的后墙绕了一个半圆后，继续向北。这两幢建筑的轴线几乎相互垂直，世远公祠朝东南，作勳公祠朝西南。外墙之间只有一条一米多宽的小道，叫世远巷。紧贴着世远公祠的东墙和部分南墙，有一个长方形的水池，叫源流塘。水塘本身与世远公祠或作勳公祠之间不存在诸如轴线、对称或呼应等空间关系，却像是世远公祠"吃"掉了水塘的一个角。所以世远公祠也不能像其他祠堂一样，把入口冠冕堂皇地设在正中，而是设在了东北角上。即便如此，还是有一部分入口，落在了水塘边界以内。世远公祠的另外一个入口，也是紧贴着水塘，位于侧立面的东南角上。次入口门外不远处，方岩溪缓缓流过，祠堂入口几乎正对着溪上的一座小桥。这是一座两侧有斜撑的平板石桥，叫望屏桥。过桥不远，便是绍常祠堂。

这组祠堂建筑群，没有一般宗祠建筑所具有的那种威严和霸气，反倒是十分生动而亲切。其灵活与不对称的空间构成，不禁让人想起著名的圣马可广场。祠堂建筑和老街之间有一个院落的距离，这样极好地回避了香客们的喧嚣。走在老街上，通过两座院落之间的"世远巷"，也可以隐约看到祠堂和水塘的一角。这两个祠堂，以及源流塘所围合的空间，虽然不大，却是村里重要的公共空间之一。经常可以看到附近的村民来这里浣洗衣物；到了吃饭的时间就会有人坐在水塘边的石板上吃饭；也会有人在水塘和作勳公祠之间不大的空地上晒晒干柴。

世远公祠

按村里的说法，世远公祠是全村人都有份的祠堂。它的平面布局及构造，代表这个地区的一种普遍形式。祠堂长约26米，宽约17米，在横向上有五个开间。中间三个开间纵向全部开敞，直接暴露抬梁式屋架，从前到后分别是前厅，天井，正堂，戏台及左右两个小天井，最后是享堂。侧面是穿斗结构的厢房，并有夹层。除了前厅里面的十根木柱外，其余的柱子均为石柱。三种不同尺寸的柱子与五种规格各异的柱础之间的不同搭配，间接界定了空间的主次。

最重要的空间当然是正堂，正堂位于三个天井之间，有八根圆柱并辅以有覆盆的巨型柱础。正堂的堂号依旧取三世祖程权"终身得耕陇亩足矣"中的"得耕"二字，为"得耕堂"。厢房和享堂内的柱子均为方柱，但是只有正堂两侧的柱子和享堂中间的四根，才配以一种规格较高的方形柱础；余下的只是采用很简单的，大小和柱子截面相当的四面倒锥形柱础。前厅中间面向正堂的两根檐柱采用的是石圆柱，辅以鼓形柱础。前厅内余下的柱子皆为较细的木柱，柱础也采用规格更小的鼓形柱础。

正堂两个前金柱内侧分别写有"六世衍宗祧有典有则，千秋隆孝享是训是行"，后金柱上的对联则在前面，为"后嗣相承祖德与方山并寿，前徽弗替孙谋偕丽水俱长"。"得耕堂"的匾也挂在后金柱之间，略向下倾斜。很显然，这两副对联和横匾共同"指向"的地方，就是程氏子孙在祠堂里双膝碰地的地方。

享堂宽五开间，两侧没有厢房，它的地面比正堂高四十公分。享堂后面原本是按照左昭右穆摆放牌位的地方，虽然这些木构的台面、神龛现已全部缺失，但是从柱子侧面的榫口可以推断出它们的位置和高度。以前老街上如果有程氏男丁过世，家人就要做一个牌位送到世远公祠里来；如果是友恭常下的后人，还要做一个送到作勳公祠；如果又是恭下毅常的，则要做第三个送到绍常祠堂；对于已经结婚的男丁，则要做夫妻牌位。如果当时妻子还在世，则用一块红布把妻子的牌位暂时罩起来；如果妻子先走一步，则要等到丈夫去世后一起进祠堂。

正堂两侧的厢房主要用于储藏一些祭祀用品。二层的夹层则是堆放一些大型的器物，例如每年舞龙灯时用的龙头和龙尾。祠堂南墙外还有一个不规则的小屋，平时是教书先生办公及居住的地方，在过年和清明的时候用做灶堂。

作勳公祠

作勳公祠的建筑规格则小许多，简单地说就是一个三合院。正厅为三开间，抬梁式结构，尺度和世远公祠正堂的尺寸十分接近。东西厢房各三间，为穿斗式结构，靠南的两间有夹层。厢房的首间和正厅围合形成了一个进深约三米的内院。

自从1958年"生产大跃进"后，作勳公的房产由四家人共有。据住在西厢房的程茂发（1934年生，崇字辈，程氏21代）老人讲，他的继父程宣占由于很穷，在1946年便分到了作勳公祠的一部分房产，他和继父，以及生父一家人就住了进来。在这以前由于家里穷没有房，也会到祠堂里租房子住。之后，又有三家人买房。由于居住的需要，作勳公祠如今被划分出了许多小的隔间。但是据程茂发老人讲，以前祠堂里的正房都是开敞的，现在各家用来当作门窗的隔板就是原来正堂里排位前面的门板拆下来的；祠堂里以前有一块写着"贡元"的匾，不幸在"文革"期间被损坏。

绍常祠堂

据说绍常祠堂是程立重（1736—1793年）为报答丈人在"岩脚竖花厅"的赠银之恩，于乾隆五十三年（1788年）建造的。程立重字逢时，号毅庵，为作勳公之孙，程经臣之子。程经臣的四个儿子各以"发"、"强"、"刚"、"毅"为房派，所以程立重的后代又被称为"恭下毅常"。由于程立重排行最小，所以"毅常"又被俗称为"小常"。永康话"小"与"绍"同音，所以得名为绍常祠堂。

环境

绍常祠堂坐北朝南，位于方岩溪以西，背后斜对着方岩山。在建造绍常祠堂以前，这可能只是一片田地。在绍常祠堂建成以后的很长一段时间里，都是孤零零地独自坐落在方岩溪的这一侧。

祠堂前面有一块较大的空场，这里既是秋收后村里人晒谷子的草场，又是正月里迎龙灯的高潮所在。空场的南面还有一幢几十年前建的电影院，如今家家都有了电视，电影院便冷清了。空场的东缘由方岩溪界定，溪水东岸就是程立重丈人出资修建的，有屋里塘、屋里井，有花园、菜地的大宅院。在空场的南、北两端各有一个小桥横跨方岩溪通往宅院。从绍常祠堂向北不远，还可以通过望屏桥走到世远公祠和作勳公祠。

建筑

绍常祠堂的平面布局和世远公祠基本相似，正堂和享堂的尺寸也相当，但是总面积却是世远公祠的两倍。与世远公祠相比，绍常祠堂在平面上的主要区别体现在如下几点：前厅和厢房进深较深，厢房和轴线上的主要空间之间局部有走廊，三个主要天井面积都比较大，在正堂两侧的厢房之间还各有一个有楼梯的小天井。

祠堂的正立面左右两端为高低错落的马头墙，主入口在中间，两边各有一个次入口连接厢房和前厅的走廊。除此之外，在这青砖墙上还高低错落地安插了几个方形和圆形的小窗，主要用来给尽端厢房和前厅次间通风。

前厅明间通高，次间二层的空间与两侧厢房相连。明间用月梁，前后单步梁，中间双步梁上又立童柱，上层采用穿斗结构。穿过前厅是和前厅同宽的明堂，明堂四面有廊，有十二根檐柱环绕。每一根檐柱上方均有一个雕着卷龙、鸟兽或花木的牛腿，牛腿上面还有一组精美的叠斗，用以支撑上面的挑檐枋。叠斗外侧均有镂雕插叶，内侧为盘龙形蟺梁。

正堂三间梁架全部露明，为九檩进深。明间有四柱，采用前后双步梁加中间五架梁；次间用五柱，穿斗与抬梁相结合，柱间有四组双步梁。正堂整个屋顶的重量依次通过檩枋、叠斗、大斗、大斗下的花墩、月梁、梁托，最后传到柱子上。在支撑檩枋的叠斗和柱子之间，还用蟺梁做连接，蟺梁不但有极强的装饰效果，还能起到在纵向上稳定结构的作用。除了蟺梁以外，叠斗、雀替、花墩、梁头和梁托都是绍常祠堂大木结构雕饰的重点。此外，在两根上金檩、前下金檩、檐檩和挑檐枋底面还有精美的镂空浮雕花鸟鱼纹。

正堂后面就是一个平面为方形的戏台，戏台两侧各有一个近方形的天井。从这里开始，厢房的进深变浅，从而使轴线上的主要空间可以拓宽成五开间。

享堂五开间，位于一个两步高的台基上。享堂的梁架结构和正堂大体类似。不同的是前后的双步梁变成了单步梁；后面的单步梁外面又增加了穿枋结构的一个廊，作为摆放神橱的空间；明间前面由于需要和戏台衔接，所以对梁架做了一些变化。享堂中间三开间在金柱间设门，但是可以全部开敞。据老人们讲，门上曾雕有精美的二十四孝，用以教育逢年过节来这里祭拜的程氏子孙。享堂的大木雕饰比正堂的稍简洁，在檩下叠斗之间没有用蟺梁，只是在叠斗两侧饰卷草形插叶。

东西厢房自南向北分别被分隔成大小不同的五个空间。中间三间各自朝向不同的天井开窗采光，尽端的两间则利用外墙开窗通风。厢房与前厅、一进天井、正堂之间均有走廊，在正堂侧壁后面的厢房之间还各有一个小天井，天井一侧各有一个楼梯通往二层。

周氏宗祠

周氏宗祠位于狮子山西麓的一个小山坳里，坐东朝西，紧邻老街。祠堂的位置是这段老街地势最高的部分，它和方岩山之间没有任何建筑物遮挡，有与方岩对视、俯瞰山谷的感觉。

周氏宗祠是老街上唯一一座非程姓的祠堂。据《游川周氏宗谱》记载，这支周氏被称为"草墅周氏"。其始祖时文公（1254—1315年）在元至元十七年至二十八年（1280—1291年）期间任两浙提举，因"奉敕兼管督理台温分司盐课，秩满道经永康，爱其风俗之美"，所以从金华泮塘迁居永康升平乡草墅，由此得名为"草墅周氏"。自此，时文公的子孙便从草墅迁往永康各地。

周氏宗祠建在这里是因为始祖周时文公墓位于它后面不远处，一个叫公道山"狮子撰屙"的洞穴里。据说周姓人家在老街上只居住了很短的时间，并在程氏迁到这里之前就离开了；也有人说周氏从未在这里居住过，只是在清明的前十天会有上百人来这里祭奠周氏始祖。《游川周氏宗谱》中记载这里原来只有"平厅三楹，厅前又有庵屋数间"，用以在清明时给远道来祭祖的子孙提供休息场所。后来由游川、岘川、璋川三宗扩建成现在的规模，现存建筑为光绪三十四年（1908年）重修。在国民党浙江省政府迁驻方岩的时候，这里曾作为浙江省警察大队的办公场所，其中还有一个小型的监狱。

周氏宗祠是一个接近方形的四合院。临街一面两侧是马头墙，白色的墙头上曾绘有彩画，但是如今只能依稀看见斑驳的色彩。正门居中，两旁各有一个偏门通向院内走廊。一进为三开间、七檩进深的拜厅，这是整幢建筑中雕饰最为精美的地方；天井后面，高台之上为五开间、进深略浅的享堂；两侧各有五间厢房供前来祭祀者暂住。不仅如此，"祠外两旁小厅，并楼屋八间，为看守者安身之宅也"。这"小厅"指的是周氏宗祠两边，跨过老街架设的路亭，这两个路亭是老街上为数不多的既能避风雨，又能小憩的地方。"楼屋八间"现在只有三间归周氏所有，守墓人周岩好夫妇及其大嫂现居住在这里。家谱中记载，祠墓应由游川、岘川、璋川三宗轮流派可靠能干的子孙驻守，而"岩好公为游川小四房子孙，自其曾祖起住守始祖公祠墓至今已逾百年"。

其他祠堂

闰二宗祠位于橙麓村东侧，始建于明代。从建筑布局上看，应该和世远公祠类似，即三进正堂、品字形天井布局。基于"土改"时期的政策，闰二宗祠属于五代以上的祠堂，被归为国有。于是它先是作为小学校，又在1988年改作橙麓村老年协会的活动场所。2006年，祠堂内部被修葺一新，地面和部分墙面用混凝土重做，中部的大跨度屋顶也改用钢桁架结构。

程昭夫祠堂位于狮子山西麓，老街西侧。由程昭夫建于1924年，为程振兴旅店的一部分。祠堂形制和世远公祠基本相同，平面尺寸略大。祠堂在香汛时期也做客房使用，中间开敞空间不仅作为旅店的厅堂来招待香客、设摆晚宴，晚上还会请艺人在这里唱戏。浙江省国民政府临时迁驻方岩那段时间，这里还是承办政府会议、各式筵席甚至举办婚礼的场所。

启文公祠位于回龙桥西侧，其建造者为程振兴旅店老板的弟弟程昭纯。程昭纯（1864生，卒年不详），字启文，为程乐涞五子，并于1900年在老街南端开办了程成兴雨伞。据程昭纯孙程振锋（1939年生，崇字辈，程氏21代）老人讲，祠堂布局原本和世远公祠类似。现在可惜只剩下了中间的三开间。

老街上还有一个几乎已经被人们忘记的祠堂，这就是位于下胡坑坑口靠西的禄房祠堂。据程振锋老人回忆，禄房祠堂是其祖父程昭纯主持修建的，并作为祠堂管事。祠堂的规模比世远公祠略小，只有前后两进院落。这样算来，祠堂大约建于二十世纪初。不幸的是在"文革"期间，由于疏于维护，这座祠堂最终毁于白蚁和火灾。目前仅存一些残垣断壁，连基本的平面布局也无法辨认。
