Manichaeism, also called Mingjiao (Bright Religion), was banned during the Tang Huichang period, then转入 secret folk circulation, and through the Five Dynasties to the Song Dynasty still had wide followers in the Fujian-Zhejiang region; therefore this uprising quickly received enthusiastic support and response from the broad peasantry. The Northern Song rulers, when suppressing this religiously-colored peasant uprising, also fully utilized the power of local deities, propagating myths of divine-human assistance. Because this uprising was completely suppressed in just one and a half years, all battles within it could ultimately end with the victory of orthodox deities, thereby killing two birds with one stone by striking at "heretical religion" and "bandits." During this period, the Northern Song Dynasty vigorously rewarded local deities, so "there were no few shrines that manifested spirit to protect official troops during the Fang La Uprising and were reported to the court requesting commendation," such as "Shangyu Yide Temple, Shengxian Xianying Temple, etc." Even in places not harassed by "bandits," local rulers would claim it was because deities secretly assisted.

During the Fang La Uprising, Chen Shisi of Yongkang Fangyan also rose up. They breached Yongkang county seat, forcing Magistrate Zhao Qi to retreat to Fangyan Mountain. Although Zhao Qi ultimately fled Fangyan Mountain in panic, because Chen Shisi's uprising army was soon suppressed, it can be inferred that Magistrate Zhao Qi also followed the emperor's wishes and fabricated a myth of deities assisting the royal army to destroy bandits on Fangyan Mountain. And Hu Ze, a Yongkang native who had "served three dynasties, held ten prefectural seals, six envoy credentials," and was already familiar and beloved by locals, naturally became the protagonist of the divine-assistance myth. Moreover, Hu Ze already had a memorial tablet in the Guangci Temple study hall, so deifying him as the Fangyan Mountain god was most fitting. These myths have many versions; their authenticity and logic are not the focus of this discussion, so we may as well cite the official version recorded in the "Song Gaozong Imperial Edict Granting Heling Temple Plaque": "The people suffered from repeated warfare; the god alone appeared in dreams to the commander, manifesting spirit and secretly assisting. Moreover, the bandit leader dreamed of a giant, in white clothes riding a white horse drinking at the pond; at dawn the water was seen dry, his followers were terrified, and thus suffered a great defeat." In the fourth year of Emperor Huizong's Xuanhe (1122), the year after the Fang La Uprising was fully suppressed, Hu Ze was enfeoffed as "Youshun Marquis" — the first title he received after death. Perhaps because at the same time numerous local deities received titles for similar reasons, "the investigating official Wang at that time requested without proper verification, resulting in the imperial edict not stating the name," and "only used 'Fangyan God' in the report."

Perhaps this canonization was indeed unimportant, failing to attract the attention of Hu's descendants, because the edict for this canonization was not included in the "Kuchuan Hu Clan Genealogy." Guangci Temple, under the prevailing background of promoting Daoism at that time, may have used this canonization to call Hu Ze "Fangyan God Youshun Marquis" and incorporate him into the Buddhist holy land, with "incense offerings made with great reverence." Meanwhile, some areas near Fangyan also began to worship Hu Ze. As a local deity, Hu Ze was "whether flood or drought or plague or epidemic, every request is answered, every prayer is answered." As his fame grew locally, Hu's descendants may have been unsatisfied with this unnamed title, so "the scholars of the entire county petitioned the authorities." In the twenty-first year of Shaoxing (1151), Hu Tingzhi, who was the assistant magistrate of Jian'an County and also Hu Ze's great-grandson, "detailed the whole story to the then Song Gaozong, striving to rectify the name." After verifying with Zhao Shan, registrar of Quzhou, and Zhao Yanlun, registrar of Zhuji County in Shaoxing Prefecture, the Ministry of Rites, following the imperial edict promulgated in the third year of Jianyan (1129) that "divine shrines with spiritual manifestations should first be granted plaques," recommended to the emperor granting "Heling Temple" as the plaque for Hu Ze's shrine. In the second month of the twenty-second year of Shaoxing (1152), Song Gaozong issued the edict "Imperially Granting Heling Temple."

This canonization of Hu Ze was only the beginning of his future series of canonizations. In the Song Dynasty, the canonization system had gradually been perfected, stipulating that for spiritually responsive shrines "those without noble titles should be granted plaques, those already granted plaques should be added noble titles. First enfeoffed as marquis, then as duke, then as king." There were also limits on the number of characters in titles within the same rank, starting with two characters, gradually increasing to a maximum of eight. These specific requirements of the canonization system can be seen from Hu Ze's successive canonizations. In the third year of Song Shaoxi (1192), Hu Ze was granted "Youshun Jiaying Marquis" by Song Guangzong; subsequently in the third year of Jiatai (1203) and the third year of Jiading (1210), he was canonized in two stages by Song Ningzong to "Youshun Jiaying Fuze Xianling Marquis." From the choice of words in these titles, one can see the change in attitude toward commending Hu Ze over time. "Youshun" is an objective recognition from the emperor's perspective; "Jiaying" represents approval and affirmation; "Fuze" is a wholehearted praise from the people's standpoint; finally "Xianling" is a super-objective deification. Meanwhile, Hu Ze was "worshipped in temples between Quzhou and Wuzhou, no fewer than several dozen." By the sixth year of Chunyou (1246), Song Lizong enfeoffed Hu Ze as "Xianying Duke," subsequently "added Zhenghui, in the early Baoyou period further added Zhongyou."

While Hu Ze was being加封 again and again, the study hall on Fangyan Mountain enshrining Hu Ze was "as years passed things changed, the site remained but the hall was ruined." In the third year of Song Jingding (1262), local Wang "could not bear its ruin, and undertook to renew it." In this "Record of Fangyan Study Hall" written by Wu Sui, the author also mentions that after the study hall was rebuilt, he "reverently bowed to the lord's remaining image in this hall." This shows that the Hu Ze statue inside the study hall existed at the latest after the reconstruction. According to former abbot Master Yunming, Hu Gong Temple was formerly located at the study hall site. Thus, the study hall with the Hu Ze statue gradually evolved into the "Youshun Marquis Shrine" mentioned in the Ming Jiajing "Yongkang County Gazetteer" and the "Heling Shrine" referred to in the Qing Daoguang "Yongkang County Gazetteer." Nearly a hundred years later, the "Record on the Back of Hu Shilang Temple Stele" written in the ninth year of Yuan Zhizheng (1349) again mentions that local Hu Ze temples "spread throughout the prefecture, no fewer than several dozen to a hundred districts," and Hu Ze was further evolved into an omnipotent god who "can summon clouds and bring wind and rain."

Continued Development in Ming and Qing Dynasties

After experiencing the Yuan Dynasty which revered Lamaism, the Ming Dynasty was a period when various Buddhist sects gradually recovered and developed. During this period, Guangci Temple's incense also gradually reached its peak; noteworthy is Master Yugu, who served as abbot during the Ming Wanli period (1589-1619), and two events that occurred during his tenure. It is said that Master Yugu bought eight children as disciples, reforming the "descendant school" implemented since the temple's founding, dividing it into eight houses: Qian, Tian, Cheng, Di, Ren, Cai, Bao, Zhi, taking turns managing temple incense and daily affairs. The "descendant school" stipulated that only children under five years old could be received for conversion; young novices lived and ate with their masters from childhood, like father and son, and were buried together after death. Master Yugu's reform both maintained the highly affiliative characteristics of the "descendant school" and enabled temple management to supervise each other, and on this basis developed numerous "subordinate temples." This is also the main reason Guangci Temple could endure various tribulations and stand here as a thousand-year ancient temple.

The other event was a "heavy blow" to Guangci Temple. According to Master Yunming, in the fifth year of Ming Longqing (1571), a nearby Wenlou Village produced a bangyan (second-place imperial examination graduate) named Cheng Zhengyi, who later served as Left Administrative Commissioner of Sichuan. Cheng Zhengyi's father was Cheng Fangfeng (1498-1585), who took a fancy to the precious land of Fangyan Mountain and had his son borrow land from the then abbot Master Yugu for a grave. Master Yugu was initially unwilling, but considering himself a grandson-generation of Cheng Fangfeng, wrote a land deed of "selling ten zhang of land." Some years later, Master Yugu passed away, and Cheng Fangfeng also died; the Cheng descendants changed "selling ten zhang" to "selling a thousand zhang," and began building Cheng Fangfeng Ancestral Hall beside Mother-and-Child Camphor by the front street, giving rise to a lawsuit. The temple monks used the argument that the entire Fangyan Mountain did not even have a thousand zhang to prove "selling a thousand zhang" was false. The trial result was "selling land is true, a thousand zhang is false," and ruled that with Thousand-Man Pit and Changsheng Pond as the boundary, the south belonged to the Cheng family, the north to Guangci Temple. This trial result is also clearly recorded in the Qing Guangxu "Yongkang County Gazetteer": "Mr. Cheng Fangfeng's tomb: on Fangyan, from the flowing water of Thousand-Man Pit as boundary, to the peak gate cliffs all belong to the tomb site. Granted during Wanli (1573-1620)." Sometime after this event, the Cheng family of Wenlou Village saw business opportunities on Fangyan Mountain and began selling incense candles, offerings and other goods on Tianjie.

With half of Fangyan Mountain belonging to others, Guangci Temple's incense and income were more or less affected. In the eleventh year of Qing Shunzhi (1654), Heling Temple underwent a renovation with the help of Hu's descendants. But decades later, the Qing Kangxi "Yongkang County Gazetteer" already recorded that Heling Shrine, due to long neglect, was nearly collapsed; the temple monks then moved Hu Ze's statue into Guangci Temple. Also moved should have been Hu Ze's memorial tablet and the imperially-granted "Heling Temple" plaque, which were together enshrined in the then front hall of Guangci Temple, thereby truly achieving temple-shrine unity. Thereafter, in the over one hundred years from the seventh year of Yongzheng (1729) to the twenty-seventh year of Daoguang (1847), the Kuchuan Hu descendants, who revered Hu Ze as their great-uncle, repeatedly funded the repair or reconstruction of Guangci Temple's front hall and main hall, with six recorded instances. Among them, the reconstruction and expansion of the front hall in the twenty-fourth year of Jiaqing (1819) basically established the final planar layout of Guangci Temple's central axis.

According to Master Yunming's recollection, Guangci Temple's central axis had four halls, connected by corridors between each hall. The first hall was the Guangci Temple front hall, hanging the "Guangci Temple" plaque; the second hall was the front殿, hanging the "Heling Temple" plaque, with the meat-eating "Xinggong" (Traveling Duke) Hu Ze in the center, Skanda behind, and Hu Ze's ten sworn brothers on both sides; the third hall was the Mahavira Hall, with Tathagata Buddha in the center, Hu Ze's statue recast in the third year of Qianlong (1738) in front, Manjushri and Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas beside, and Eighteen Arhats on both sides of the hall; the fourth hall was Pingfeng Pavilion (Screen Wind Pavilion), mainly enshrining the Jade Emperor; east of the Mahavira Hall was also built Guanyin Pavilion. The monk quarters of the eight houses were located around these halls, forming a "Bagua" (Eight Trigrams) pattern in plan. In the second year of Xuantong (1910), in response to criticism of "humans and gods sharing a temple," the temple monks moved the Jade Emperor to the Ksitigarbha Hall on the west side, and separately enshrined the Hu Ze statue in front of the Tathagata in Pingfeng Pavilion, as the vegetarian "Zuogong" (Sitting Duke) Hu Ze. Although Hu Gong was moved out of the Mahavira Hall, according to Master Yunming, even now behind the Hu Gong statue there are still small statues of Tathagata, Manjushri and Samantabhadra.

Decline

Unfortunately, a great fire on the fourth day of the ninth month in the twenty-ninth year of Daoguang (1849) destroyed the entire shrine-temple and monk quarters. Although Guangci Temple was rebuilt over a year later, this had already become the first step toward its decline. According to Master Yunming, in the late Qing Dynasty, local people's lives were very poor. Coupled with the spread of opium, people often went up the mountain to take things from the temple, even demolishing halls to sell wood for a living. Monks therefore became fewer and fewer, and of the eight houses only four remained. "Fangyan Guide" also mentions "during the Qing Guangxu period (1875-1908), temple monks left one after another." In the 20th and 21st years of the Republic, Guangci Temple was even occupied by a Daoist from Houqian Village, and the monks inside were forced to wander to nearby subordinate temples.

Among a series of man-made disasters in the following decades, the Cultural Revolution undoubtedly brought Guangci Temple an unprecedented heavy blow. Almost all buildings of Guangci Temple were demolished in late August 1966, with only Pingfeng Pavilion and one monk quarter surviving. Pingfeng Pavilion was originally assigned to Fangyan Commune for demolition, but out of nearly a thousand years of respect for Hu Ze, people on the old street refused to do so. Thus, Pingfeng Pavilion was preserved, and was successively used as a brigade meeting place, forestry warehouse, post and telecommunications school, and Factory 602. Moreover, the calligraphy, paintings and books inside Guangci Temple were carried down the mountain in ten shoulder loads and burned for a whole day. Although the "Guangci Temple Chronicle" escaped this catastrophe under Master Yunming's protection, it was inexplicably lost among the various files of the Yongkang Municipal Religious Affairs Section.

Recovery after the Cultural Revolution

Two years after the end of the Cultural Revolution, in the early morning of the first day of the eighth lunar month in 1978, initiated by the mother of Yanxia Village villager Huang Pulin, she and three other women carried a newly molded small Hu Gong statue up the mountain. The first post-Cultural Revolution abbot Master Yunming went up the mountain on the third day of the tenth lunar month in 1979, and from memory recast the Hu Ze statue and other statues in Pingfeng Pavilion, including Wenqu Star, God of Wealth, Dragon King and Guan Gong. Because Pingfeng Pavilion still stood, pilgrims came to worship Hu Gong. Master Yunming used donated incense money, during the five years from 1980 to 1984, to buy four ancestral halls to restore Guangci Temple's buildings. The first was a hall in Guzhufan Village bought for over 3,000 yuan in 1980, used to rebuild the Mahavira Hall in front of Pingfeng Pavilion.紧接着 he bought at a relatively cheap price the Zhou Clan Ancestral Hall of Hanxia Zhou Village, which was forced to be demolished due to the construction of Yanghan Reservoir. Subsequently he spent over 4,000 yuan buying the Niuwang (Ox King) Hall of Shanmai Village in Longyou County, used to restore the Heavenly King Hall, Buyun Pavilion, rear mountain pavilions and do some repair work. Finally he bought the Xu Clan Ancestral Hall in Yongkang city, rebuilding the current Guangci Temple Guanyin Pavilion on the original site of the old Guanyin Pavilion.

sections.name: 广慈寺和胡公庙现状
sections.content_zh:
三、广慈寺和胡公庙现状

在二十世纪八十年代中叶，以发展旅游业为目的，胡公庙从广慈寺中被分离出来，作为一个独立的寺院，再次和广慈寺肩并肩地坐落在方岩山顶上。胡公庙在西侧，占据了广慈寺原有中轴线的位置，即以屏风阁为最后一进大殿。在屏风阁前刚刚建好没几年的大雄宝殿再次被拆除，取而代之的是两幢新建的胡公庙前殿和大殿。广慈寺则被迫向东平移，改以重建的观音殿为中轴线，并在后面补建了大雄宝殿。

广慈寺

这里的老人们都说，广慈寺以前的各个殿堂之间也都是有围廊相连的，下雨都不会湿鞋。不仅如此，允明禅师讲，以前从山脚到山顶都是有长廊的，是太平村的一个村民每年来修，用了很多年才建成。现任住持释明修也说，在他去"应聘"广慈寺住持的时候，也曾经见过一张广慈寺的图，上面画着从山下到寺院都有走廊相连。

如今的广慈寺有三进殿堂。一进前厅和二进观音殿为允明禅师于1984年复建；第三进殿堂是在寺、庙分离之后补建的大雄宝殿。观音殿与前厅有侧廊相连，中间围合成一个小的院落。由于是利用祠堂建筑的木料重建，所以无论从大木构件或小木雕饰中都可以看到世俗建筑的影子。一进前厅会让人不禁想起祠堂里的戏台。前厅正中间的神龛里目前供奉着弥勒佛，神龛本身看上去很像戏台上使用的建筑道具。神龛正上方是一个通常只用于祠堂戏台顶上的精致藻井，藻井里的斗拱呈螺旋形层叠上升。边上两间各有一组九格天花，四周还有小斗拱做支撑，天花上绘制的都是《西游记》中的经典场面。壁画颜色以黄、绿色为底，线条精美，退晕渲染也十分讲究。观音殿和两侧围廊中祠堂建筑的痕迹就更加明显。这其中的大木构件不仅用神牛、寿桃、喜鹊做雕饰主题，还可以看到富有张力的月梁，极富装饰效果的"蟺梁"以及活灵活现的狮子舞球。广慈寺的这座建筑是中国建筑构造特点和设计理念的最好体现：一幢建筑不仅能拆了异地重建，而且还能把所有构建重新排列组合，建造成平面和功能都不尽相同的新建筑。

方岩山上另外一幢没有在文化大革命期间被拆毁的建筑就是位于现广慈寺东南角的僧房。这幢仅存的僧房是在清道光二十九年（1849年）的那场大火后重建的。僧房高三层，坡屋顶，平面为异形，中间却围合了一个四四方方的小院，院内正中是一个巨大的"放生池"，池上有小拱桥。说是放生池，其实其主要目的是预防火灾。最值得一提的是，僧房的外立面明显受到西方古典主义建筑的影响：通高的壁柱，三角形山墙，以及山墙中圆形的装饰母题。

胡公庙前殿和大殿

胡公庙的第一进殿是一个三开间的一层木建筑，挂"胡公祠"横匾。虽然我们无法区分建筑的哪些构建来自于拆掉的大雄宝殿，哪些来自于其他建筑，而哪些又是后来新做的，更不用说被允明禅师重建的大雄宝殿本身就是利用拆除后的一幢民居为建筑原料，但是这些都并不重要。乡土建筑的一大魅力就在于它创作中的自由性和追求物尽其用的特点，这种"重新组装"的做法不但延续了原有建筑物的生命，而且这种"再创造"本身就具有非常的意义。

前殿大木雕饰所采用的题材，都明显带有当地祠堂建筑的痕迹。例如，两个中榀檐柱的牛腿上就雕有当地祠堂建筑中通常采用的狮子戏球；牛腿上向各个方向飞扬伸展的叠拱和插叶所采用的卷草图案也和世远公祠里的非常相似。不过，前殿里最有特点的部分还要算天花。这里建筑的梁架通常是露明的，但是前殿的中榀的两个金柱中间却有天花，天花中间还形成一个八面锥体的藻井。藻井正中绘有盘龙，八个面上不但绘有如来佛、弥勒佛、观音、太上老君，还有《西游记》里的四个主要人物；四周的天花上则画满《西游记》中的一些主要故事情节。可以说，在这几米见方的二维画板上，已经完全看不到佛教、道教与世俗尘世之间的任何界限。前殿的屋面应该是新的，但在这里人、神之间的界限也是模糊的。垂脊的末端各有一尊小的雕像，前面分别是哪吒、托塔李天王，后面则是两名天兵天将。

胡公庙大殿是一个用钢筋混凝土做支撑结构的两层高建筑，坐落在一个半米多高的基础上，俨然一副官式建筑的气派。大殿正中有一个两米多高、玉皇大帝扮相的胡公正襟端坐在一个一米多高的须弥座上，他略微低头，审视着跪倒在他面前的虔诚香客。依照惯例，这尊胡公是"吃荤"的，也就是说，三牲之类的供品都会摆放在须弥座前面的香案上。胡公的头顶上也有一个半球形的藻井，上面绘着龙和凤。硕大的一个殿堂，只有一尊塑像在中间，平时显得空荡荡的，但是在庙会期间，据说就会挤得水泄不通。

屏风阁

最后一进殿是屏风阁，现存建筑基本上是清道光二十九年（1849年）那场大火之后重建的。允明禅师说，重建的时候，一些主要构件改用石材以防火灾。可是到清朝末年，寺院变得十分不景气，原本的八房僧人也只剩下了四房，每房的人数也少了许多。于是就有人说是因为"狮子（石子的谐音）吃人"，所以在宣统年间（1909—1911年），屏风阁又改回了木构。

屏风阁也是利用天然岩洞建造的，但是它和罗汉洞或五峰书院有着根本的不同。屏风阁的建筑空间不但延伸到了石洞以外，而且还利用石洞上的巨石作为"楼板"，在上面加建了二层。允明禅师说，二层以前供的是玉皇大帝，直到宣统二年（1910年），才把玉皇大帝移到了现在的地藏殿。屏风阁一、二层之间没有任何垂直的联系，像搬佛像这样大的变故，可能只有在重建或大修的时候才可以进行。把这种可望而不可即的位置留给玉皇大帝本是无可厚非，但是在佛家圣地的正殿里高高供奉道教的"众神之皇"，这不得不归功于中国式"宗教"无与伦比的博大和宽容。

屏风阁和它前面殿堂之间的空间比较小，再加上这里总是烟雾缭绕，所以很难看清它的全貌。屏风阁正面原本有墙，香客通过左右两侧的拱形门洞进出。院墙和凹字形的建筑围合了一个小院，院内靠墙的一侧有香炉。后来因为香客太多，香炉离建筑太近，有火灾隐患，所以拆除了围墙。现在从屏风阁前面的铺地上还可以清楚地看到墙基和门的位置。

屏风阁的大木雕饰奢华精美到了极点。由于一层屋檐有两根挑檐枋承托，所以又多了许多可以用以雕饰的叠斗、穿子、雀替、垂花等构件。抬头审视檐下、柱头的这一圈，眼睛找不到可以小憩的地方：凤凰、牡丹、仙鹤、神仙……又一只凤凰。鎏了金的木雕，在经历了几十年，甚至上百年的烟熏之后，没有了最初的那种浮华亮丽，多了些凝重和斑驳。木雕中最抢眼的就是在两个中榀檐柱上的龙形"牛腿"。一条金龙盘旋在五彩的云海里，头上顶着蜀柱，龙身"穿过"檐柱，又变成一条短梁用以连接后面的蜀柱，短梁和两个梁托也都雕有云海的图案。

屏风阁里面，沿石洞内壁一共排列着大大小小的塑像二十三尊。正中间的一个当然是红面长须、笑容可掬的胡公大帝，他的两个儿子陪坐在两边，后面是他的三个夫人。据说胡则原本只有两个夫人，第三位只是猝死在胡公大帝面前的一位女香客，人们见她如此虔诚，便封她为胡公的第三任夫人。在胡公的右侧依次是关公、龙王和平安菩萨；左边则是文曲星、婚姻美满神和财神。除了婚姻美满神是一对夫妻塑像以外，其他每一个神仙和菩萨两边还配有侍从两人。基本说来，这里可以满足人们生活中的一切所求，不论是求财还是求雨，求前程似锦还是求出入平安，抑或是求家庭美满还是求功名利禄。就算是各路神仙都帮不了忙，还可以求无所不能的胡公大帝。在每组神像前都有一个巨大的蜡烛台，上面插满了高高低低的蜡烛，胡公大帝面前的蜡烛更是多到看不见他的脸。在这黑黢黢的山洞里，扑朔迷离的光影变化加上烟雾缭绕的视觉效果，给诸神平添了些神秘的色彩。

据允明禅师说，自从把胡公从大雄宝殿请到屏风阁之后，他的后面一直有如来、文殊和普贤菩萨的三尊小塑像。如此说来，人们在祭拜胡公大帝的同时，其实是在求助如来佛祖的保佑。在香客眼里，胡公大帝是无所不能的一方神祇；在广慈寺眼里，无所不能的仍旧是胡则后面的如来佛祖，胡则只是能带给寺院旺盛人间香火的护法神。
sections.content_en:
3. Current State of Guangci Temple and Hu Gong Temple

In the mid-1980s, for the purpose of developing tourism, Hu Gong Temple was separated from Guangci Temple, becoming an independent temple, once again standing side by side with Guangci Temple on top of Fangyan Mountain. Hu Gong Temple is on the west side, occupying Guangci Temple's original central axis position, with Pingfeng Pavilion as the final hall. The Mahavira Hall that had just been built in front of Pingfeng Pavilion a few years earlier was again demolished, replaced by two newly built Hu Gong Temple front hall and main hall. Guangci Temple was forced to shift eastward, changing to the rebuilt Guanyin Pavilion as its central axis, and adding a Mahavira Hall behind it.

Guangci Temple

Elders here all say that in the past, the various halls of Guangci Temple were also connected by surrounding corridors, so that one's shoes would not get wet in the rain. Moreover, Master Yunming said that in former times there were long corridors from the foot of the mountain to the top, built by a villager from Taiping Village who came to repair every year, taking many years to complete. Current abbot Shi Mingxiu also said that when he went to "apply" for the position of Guangci Temple abbot, he once saw a drawing of Guangci Temple showing corridors connecting from the foot of the mountain to the temple.

Today's Guangci Temple has three halls. The first hall (front hall) and the second hall (Guanyin Pavilion) were rebuilt by Master Yunming in 1984; the third hall is the Mahavira Hall added after the temple separation. Guanyin Pavilion and the front hall are connected by side corridors, enclosing a small courtyard in the middle. Because they were rebuilt using timber from ancestral hall buildings, traces of secular architecture can be seen in both large wooden components and small wood carvings. The first front hall inevitably reminds one of the stage in an ancestral hall. In the central shrine of the front hall, Maitreya Buddha is currently enshrined; the shrine itself looks much like a theatrical prop used on a stage. Directly above the shrine is an exquisite caisson ceiling usually only used above ancestral hall stages; the dougong (bracket sets) in the caisson rise in spiral layers. The two side rooms each have a set of nine-grid ceilings, supported by small dougong around the perimeter; the ceilings are painted with classic scenes from "Journey to the West." The murals use yellow and green as base colors, with exquisite lines and very refined gradient rendering. The traces of ancestral hall architecture are even more obvious in Guanyin Pavilion and the surrounding corridors. Among them, the large wooden components not only use divine oxen, peaches of longevity, and magpies as carving themes, but also show tension-filled moon beams, highly decorative "shan beams," and vividly lifelike lions playing with balls. This building of Guangci Temple is the best embodiment of Chinese architectural construction characteristics and design concepts: a building can not only be dismantled and rebuilt in a different location, but also all its components can be rearranged and combined to construct new buildings with different plans and functions.

Another building on Fangyan Mountain that was not demolished during the Cultural Revolution is the monk quarter located at the southeast corner of the current Guangci Temple. This only surviving monk quarter was rebuilt after the great fire in the twenty-ninth year of Qing Daoguang (1849). The monk quarter is three stories high, with a pitched roof and an irregular plan, yet enclosing a square courtyard in the middle; in the center of the courtyard is a huge "free-life pond" with a small arched bridge over it. Called a free-life pond, its main purpose is actually fire prevention. Most noteworthy is that the facade of the monk quarter was clearly influenced by Western classical architecture: full-height pilasters, triangular gables, and circular decorative motifs in the gables.

Hu Gong Temple Front Hall and Main Hall

The first hall of Hu Gong Temple is a three-bay single-story wooden building, hanging the horizontal plaque "Hu Gong Shrine." Although we cannot distinguish which components of the building came from the demolished Mahavira Hall, which from other buildings, and which were newly made later — not to mention that the Mahavira Hall rebuilt by Master Yunming itself used a demolished dwelling as building material — none of this is important. One of the great charms of vernacular architecture lies in the freedom of its creation and the pursuit of making the best use of everything; this "reassembly" approach not only extends the life of original buildings, but this "re-creation" itself is of extraordinary significance.

The themes used in the large wood carvings of the front hall clearly bear traces of local ancestral hall architecture. For example, the ox-legs (bracket supports) on the two middle-frame eave columns are carved with lions playing with balls, commonly used in local ancestral hall architecture; the scrolling grass patterns used on the stacked brackets and inserted leaves extending in all directions from the ox-legs are also very similar to those in Shiyuan Gong Hall. However, the most distinctive part of the front hall must be the ceiling. The beam framework here is usually exposed, but between the two gold columns of the middle frame in the front hall there is a ceiling, and in the center of the ceiling an eight-sided pyramidal caisson is formed. In the center of the caisson is painted a coiling dragon; on the eight faces are painted not only Tathagata Buddha, Maitreya Buddha, Guanyin, and the Supreme Lord Lao Zi, but also the four main characters from "Journey to the West"; the surrounding ceilings are filled with major story episodes from "Journey to the West." It can be said that on this few-meter-square two-dimensional canvas, any boundary between Buddhism, Daoism, and the secular world has completely disappeared. The roof of the front hall should be new, but here the boundary between humans and gods is also blurred. At the ends of the vertical ridges are small statues: in front are Nezha and Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King Li, behind are two heavenly soldiers.

The main hall of Hu Gong Temple is a two-story building using reinforced concrete as its supporting structure, sitting on a foundation over half a meter high, with the imposing air of an official-style building. In the center of the main hall, a Hu Gong statue over two meters tall, dressed as the Jade Emperor, sits solemnly on a sumeru pedestal over one meter high; he slightly lowers his head, examining the devout pilgrims kneeling before him. By convention, this Hu Gong "eats meat" — that is, offerings such as the three sacrificial animals are placed on the incense table in front of the sumeru pedestal. Above Hu Gong's head there is also a hemispherical caisson, painted with dragons and phoenixes. The enormous hall has only one statue in the center, appearing empty on ordinary days, but during temple fairs it is said to be packed so tightly that water cannot pass through.

Pingfeng Pavilion (Screen Wind Pavilion)

The final hall is Pingfeng Pavilion; the existing building was basically rebuilt after the great fire in the twenty-ninth year of Qing Daoguang (1849). Master Yunming said that during reconstruction, some main components were changed to stone to prevent fire. But by the late Qing Dynasty, the temple became very不景气; the original eight houses of monks were reduced to four, and the number of people in each house also decreased greatly. So some people said it was because "lion (homophone of stone) eats people," and therefore during the Xuantong period (1909-1911), Pingfeng Pavilion was changed back to wooden structure.

Pingfeng Pavilion was also built using a natural rock cave, but it is fundamentally different from Luohan Cave or Wufeng Academy. The architectural space of Pingfeng Pavilion not only extends beyond the rock cave, but also uses the giant rock above the cave as a "floor slab," adding a second story on top. Master Yunming said the second story formerly enshrined the Jade Emperor, and it was not until the second year of Xuantong (1910) that the Jade Emperor was moved to the current Ksitigarbha Hall. There is no vertical connection between the first and second stories of Pingfeng Pavilion; a major change like moving a Buddha statue could probably only be done during reconstruction or major repair. Leaving this unattainable position to the Jade Emperor is understandable, but enshrining the Daoist "Emperor of All Gods" high in the main hall of a Buddhist holy land must be attributed to the unparalleled broadness and tolerance of Chinese-style "religion."

The space between Pingfeng Pavilion and the hall in front of it is relatively small, and coupled with the constant smoke and incense here, it is difficult to see its full appearance. The front of Pingfeng Pavilion originally had walls, with pilgrims entering and exiting through arched doorways on the left and right sides. The courtyard wall and the U-shaped building enclosed a small courtyard, with an incense burner on the wall side inside. Later, because there were too many pilgrims and the incense burner was too close to the building, posing a fire hazard, the courtyard wall was demolished. Now the wall foundation and door positions can still be clearly seen on the paving in front of Pingfeng Pavilion.

The large wood carvings of Pingfeng Pavilion are luxuriously exquisite to the extreme. Because the first-story eave is supported by two eave-purlins, there are many more components available for carving: stacked brackets, penetrating pieces, sparrow braces, pendant flowers, etc. Looking up at the circle under the eaves and column heads, the eyes find no place to rest: phoenix, peony, red-crowned crane, immortal… another phoenix. The gilded wood carvings, after decades or even a century of smoke exposure, have lost their original flashy brilliance and gained a sense of gravity and mottling. The most eye-catching wood carvings are the dragon-shaped "ox-legs" on the two middle-frame eave columns. A golden dragon coils in a sea of five-colored clouds, with a shu column (short column) on its head; the dragon body "passes through" the eave column and becomes a short beam connecting to the shu column behind; the short beam and two beam brackets are also carved with cloud-sea patterns.

Inside Pingfeng Pavilion, along the inner wall of the rock cave, a total of twenty-three statues of various sizes are arranged. The one in the center is of course the red-faced, long-bearded, smiling Hu Gong the Great; his two sons sit beside him, and behind him are his three wives. It is said Hu Ze originally had only two wives; the third was just a female pilgrim who died suddenly before Hu Gong the Great; seeing her such devotion, people enfeoffed her as Hu Gong's third wife. On Hu Gong's right side are依次 Guan Gong, Dragon King, and Peace Bodhisattva; on the left are Wenqu Star (God of Literature), Marriage Happiness God, and God of Wealth. Except for the Marriage Happiness God which is a couple statue, each other god and bodhisattva has two attendants on both sides. Basically, this place can satisfy all requests in people's lives — whether seeking wealth or rain, seeking a bright future or safe travels, or seeking family happiness or fame and fortune. Even if all the various gods cannot help, one can still seek the omnipotent Hu Gong the Great. In front of each group of statues there is a huge candlestick, filled with candles of various heights; the candles before Hu Gong the Great are so many that his face cannot be seen. In this dark cave, the confusing changes of light and shadow coupled with the visual effect of swirling smoke add a mysterious color to the gods.

According to Master Yunming, ever since Hu Gong was moved from the Mahavira Hall to Pingfeng Pavilion, behind him there have always been three small statues of Tathagata, Manjushri and Samantabhadra. Thus, while people worship Hu Gong the Great, they are actually seeking the protection of Tathagata Buddha. In the eyes of pilgrims, Hu Gong the Great is an omnipotent local deity; in the eyes of Guangci Temple, the omnipotent one remains Tathagata Buddha behind Hu Ze, and Hu Ze is merely a Dharma-protecting god who can bring the temple prosperous worldly incense.

key_terms.en: Hu Gong the Great (deified Hu Ze)

chapters.name: 第六章 五峰坳里的书院

sections.name: 寿山往事
sections.content_zh:
一、寿山往事

书院作为文教建筑的一种，是中国实行科举制度后的产物。科举制度开始于隋大业元年（605年），到清朝光绪三十一年（1905年）举行最后一科进士考试为止，是中国历代皇朝采用的取士制度。尽管科举制度有许多弊端和局限性，但是其最大意义就在于它给广大平民百姓提供了改变自己以至整个家族社会地位的唯一途径。于是乎，在科举制度实行的一千三百年里，中华大地上就出现了无以计数的学子，不计十年寒窗，孜孜苦读。相伴而来的，就是私塾、书院、书斋、文馆、文庙、文昌阁等文教建筑的广泛普及。

唐末至五代期间，战乱频繁导致官学衰败，所以许多读书人就避居山林，以模仿佛教、禅林的讲经制度创立书院。浙江境内始建于唐朝的书院，现知有五处，分别是象山蓬莱书院、诸暨溪山书院、龙游九峰书院、建德青山书院和绍兴丽正书院。这些书院通常是住宅的一部分，建筑形式也十分简朴。

宋代是书院林立的时代。在北宋期间书院多以讲学为主，而随着理学的发展，南宋的书院逐渐成为各学派活动的场所。书院作为一种正式的教育制度，几乎取代官学而成为当时主要的教育机关。浙江地区当时有书院三十余家，数量仅次于江西，居全国第二。

书院制度以及书院建筑在明、清两代又有了进一步的发展，但是已经逐渐从学者云集、自由讲学的私立书院，发展到受统治阶级控制的官学化书院。直至光绪二十七年（1901年），皇帝诏令各省的书院改为大学堂，各府、厅、直隶州的书院改为中学堂，各州县的书院改为小学堂，书院这种教育制度便退出了历史舞台。

在和尚、陈亮、县令、胡氏后人、国民党政府、还有我们这一行人进入寿山坑之前，坑里这五座山峰就已经屹立在那里了。有了这五座山峰，才有了美丽的传说和故事；再然后，才有了接下来所有的事情……

寿山在方岩北三里，有五峰皆石壁平地拔起，周围如城郭，曰固厚、曰瀑布、曰桃花、曰覆釜、曰鸡鸣。固厚之下有大石洞，高敞轩豁，可容千人……

瀑布之上有龙湫，水四时不竭，直下数十丈如练，及霁久水杀，飘飘飏之，溅洒四出若雾雨然，可望而不可即，亦奇观也。

固厚峰，主峰也。悬崖千仞，峭壁如削，较诸峰为淳固深厚，故其名。其下石洞在焉。

瀑布峰，在固厚之右，上有飞泉下注……

覆釜峰，在瀑布之下，巅广而圆，如大釜覆其上。

桃花峰，与覆釜峰相连，专专耸妙，其岩色赤白相间，状类桃花……

鸡鸣峰，……午风微过，嘐然一声，彼唱此应，遂神其说耳……

天蜜，……悬崖直下，天风偶吹，大者如珠，细者如雾，其味甘美故名。

位于五峰之间、石洞之中、瀑布之下的这块世外桃源，终于在南北朝时期的梁普通元年（520年）迎来了它的第一位主人，即吃素念经的和尚们。固厚峰下有两个大石洞，上文中提到的是西边这个，靠东还有一个，叫外洞。这些出家人利用这两个天然的石洞创建了永康县境内的第一座寺院——桃岩寺，并于日后改名为寿山寺。关于寿山寺的具体情况已经无从查证，只知道固厚峰下的这个山洞里曾经有过一个罗汉堂，里面的罗汉还是在明朝为建造五峰书院时撤掉的；外洞"之前有台三层，甚壮伟"，猜想或许是大雄宝殿的位置。据《库川胡氏宗谱》中关于一场官司的记录，"寿山寺自正德以前无论已"，那三层的高台也在"明万历间始圮"。

到了南宋乾道八年（1172年），永康人陈亮（1143—1195年）开始在寿山坑里设帐授学，宣讲他的"商籍农而立，农赖商而行"、"义利双行"和"各务其实"等有悖于传统儒学和经学的新思想。在接下去的两三年中，陈亮的挚友吕祖谦（1137—1181年），即事功学派下金华学派的创始人，也曾来这里讲学。宋淳熙九年（1182年）秋，刚刚上任一年的浙东提举朱熹（1130—1200年）回访陈亮于五峰。这是朱熹与陈亮的第二次会面，第一次是在这年正月，朱熹来婺州赈灾，陈亮赶去相见，并与朱熹畅谈十日。第二次会面的盛况在《五峰书院志》中略有记载，陈亮"请晦翁主讲席，从游者数百人"。相传固厚峰下外洞岩壁上的"兜率台"三个朱砂大字就是朱熹当时题写的。这里的"兜率"二字同"兜率天"，为梵语音译，代表佛教中的第四层天，这层天的内院是弥勒菩萨的净土，外院是天上众生所居之处；"台"应该指的是当时在这里的三层高台。宋绍熙四年（1193年），年已五十一岁的陈亮金榜题名中了状元，却不幸在一年多后死在赴任的途中。在这以后，我们无从查证寿山坑里是否依然回荡有士大夫高亢的辩论；或是仅留下与晨钟暮鼓相伴的木鱼声；还是一切都静了下来，只听得见水激顽石和风吹树叶的声音。
sections.content_en:
1. Past Events of Shoushan

Academies, as a type of cultural-educational architecture, are a product of China's imperial examination system. The imperial examination system began in the first year of Sui Daye (605) and lasted until the last jinshi examination in the thirty-first year of Qing Guangxu (1905), serving as the scholar-selection system adopted by successive Chinese dynasties. Although the imperial examination system had many drawbacks and limitations, its greatest significance was that it provided the broad common people with the only path to change their own and even their entire family's social status. Thus, during the thirteen hundred years of the imperial examination system, countless scholars appeared across China, enduring ten years of hard study without counting the cost. Accompanying this was the widespread普及 of cultural-educational architecture such as private schools, academies, study rooms, literary halls, Confucian temples, and Wenchang pavilions.

During the late Tang to Five Dynasties period, frequent warfare led to the decline of official schools, so many scholars retreated to mountain forests and established academies modeled on Buddhist and Chan forest lecture systems. In Zhejiang, there are currently five known academies founded in the Tang Dynasty: Xiangshan Penglai Academy, Zhuji Xishan Academy, Longyou Jiufeng Academy, Jiande Qingshan Academy, and Shaoxing Lizheng Academy. These academies were usually part of residences, with very simple architectural forms.

The Song Dynasty was an era of numerous academies. During the Northern Song, academies were mainly for lectures; with the development of Neo-Confucianism, Southern Song academies gradually became venues for various schools of thought. As a formal educational system, academies almost replaced official schools as the main educational institutions of the time. Zhejiang region had over thirty academies at that time, second only to Jiangxi, ranking second nationwide.

The academy system and academy architecture further developed in the Ming and Qing dynasties, but gradually evolved from private academies with gathered scholars and free lectures into official-style academies controlled by the ruling class. Until the twenty-seventh year of Guangxu (1901), the emperor ordered provincial academies to be converted into university halls, prefectural and departmental academies into middle school halls, and county academies into primary school halls; the academy educational system then exited the historical stage.

Before the monks, Chen Liang, the county magistrate, Hu descendants, the Nationalist government, and our group entered Shoushan Ravine, the five peaks in the ravine had already stood there. With these five peaks came beautiful legends and stories; and then came everything that followed……

Shoushan is three li north of Fangyan, with five peaks all of stone cliffs rising abruptly from the plain, surrounding like city walls: called Guhou (Solid-Thick), Pubu (Waterfall), Taohua (Peach Blossom), Fufu (Overturned Cauldron), and Jiming (Rooster Crow). Below Guhou is a large stone cave, high and spacious, capable of holding a thousand people……

Above the waterfall is Longqiu (Dragon Pool), its water never exhausted in all four seasons, plunging straight down several dozen zhang like white silk; when the weather clears and the water lessens, it flutters and drifts, splashing in all directions like mist and rain, visible but unreachable — also a wondrous sight.

Guhou Peak is the main peak. With thousand-ren cliffs and sheer walls like cut, compared to the other peaks it is pure, solid and deep, hence its name. Below it is the stone cave.

Pubu Peak, to the right of Guhou, has a flying spring pouring down from above……

Fufu Peak, below the waterfall, has a broad and round summit, like a large cauldron overturned on top.

Taohua Peak, connected to Fufu Peak, stands uniquely graceful; its rock color alternates red and white, resembling peach blossoms……

Jiming Peak, ……when the noon wind passes slightly, with a cry of "jiao," one answers the other, hence the myth……

Tianmi (Heavenly Honey), ……plunging straight down the cliff, occasionally blown by heavenly wind, large as pearls, fine as mist, its taste sweet and delicious hence the name.

This paradise located between the five peaks, within the stone caves, and below the waterfall finally welcomed its first masters in the first year of Liang Putong (520) during the Southern and Northern Dynasties — the vegetarian, scripture-chanting monks. Below Guhou Peak there are two large stone caves; the one mentioned above is the western one, and to the east there is another called the Outer Cave. These monks used these two natural stone caves to found the first Buddhist temple in Yongkang County — Taoyan Temple, later renamed Shoushan Temple. The specific circumstances of Shoushan Temple can no longer be verified; we only know that there was once an Arhat Hall in this cave below Guhou Peak, and the arhats inside were removed when Wufeng Academy was built in the Ming Dynasty; the Outer Cave "previously had a three-tier platform, very grand," conjectured to perhaps be the location of the Mahavira Hall. According to a record of a lawsuit in the "Kuchuan Hu Clan Genealogy," "Shoushan Temple before Zhengde is beyond discussion," and that three-tier high platform also "began to collapse during the Ming Wanli period."

In the eighth year of Southern Song Qiandao (1172), Chen Liang (1143-1195), a native of Yongkang, began setting up tents to teach in Shoushan Ravine, propagating his new ideas such as "merchants depend on farmers to stand, farmers rely on merchants to act," "righteousness and profit both pursued," and "each attends to reality" — ideas contrary to traditional Confucianism and classical studies. In the following two to three years, Chen Liang's close friend Lü Zuqian (1137-1181), founder of the Jinhua School under the School of Practical Statecraft, also came here to lecture. In the autumn of the ninth year of Song Chunxi (1182), Zhu Xi (1130-1200), who had just taken office as Eastern Zhejiang Commissioner for one year, visited Chen Liang at Wufeng. This was the second meeting between Zhu Xi and Chen Liang; the first was in the first month of that year, when Zhu Xi came to Wuzhou for disaster relief and Chen Liang hurried to meet him, talking with Zhu Xi for ten days. The grand occasion of the second meeting is briefly recorded in the "Wufeng Academy Annals": Chen Liang "invited Master Huiweng (Zhu Xi) to give the main lecture, with hundreds of followers." Legend has it that the three large cinnabar characters "Doushuai Terrace" on the rock wall of the Outer Cave below Guhou Peak were inscribed by Zhu Xi at that time. The word "Doushuai" here is the same as "Tusita Heaven," a Sanskrit transliteration representing the fourth heaven in Buddhism; the inner court of this heaven is Maitreya Bodhisattva's pure land, and the outer court is where heavenly beings dwell; "Terrace" should refer to the three-tier high platform that was here at the time. In the fourth year of Song Shaoxi (1193), Chen Liang, already fifty-one years old, passed the examination as zhuangyuan (first-place jinshi), but unfortunately died over a year later on his way to take office. After this, we cannot verify whether Shoushan Ravine still echoed with the impassioned debates of scholar-officials; or whether only the sound of wooden fish accompanied by morning bells and evening drums remained; or whether everything fell silent, with only the sound of water striking stubborn stones and wind blowing leaves.

sections.name: 五峰书院
sections.content_zh:
二、五峰书院

书院历史

再次找到有关于寿山坑的文字记载，已经到明正德年间（1506—1521年）。

尚宝丞应典，周视壁上有龙川书（今遍观壁上，但有时少章记龙川书，或在兜率台上，然无登览矣），志晦翁、东莱行迹，乃即堂东偏之隙建祠，以祀朱、吕、及张南轩、陆象山，而龙川配焉，曰丽泽祠。

丽泽祠，正德间应石门先生建，太守张公钺题此额，嗣守姚公文炤记……

应典字天彝，号石门，浙江永康芝英人，明正德（1506—1521年）九年（1514年）进士，曾任丽泽书院和白鹿书院山长。这也就是说丽泽祠应该建于1514年到1521年之间。这里的朱、吕、张指的是朱熹、吕祖谦和张栻，在宋乾道、淳熙时期（1165—1189年），他们三人被并称为"东南三贤"。除了这三个人之外，还以陆九渊和陈亮配祭。

"丽泽"这个名字，可能取自于位于金华明招山的丽泽书院。丽泽书院原名丽泽堂，为吕祖谦在宋乾道初年（约1165—1166年）创建。书院前有两个湖泊，而"丽泽"的原意为两个沼泽相连，所以恰到好处。更重要的是，《易·兑》中写道，"丽泽，兑。君子以朋友讲习"。由此可见，"丽泽"之意深远，朱熹还曾经做过如下的评价，"两泽相丽，互相滋益，朋友讲习，其象如此"。

十几年之后，丽泽祠东侧又建造了一幢规模稍大的建筑，取名为"桃岩丽泽精舍"。当时的永康知县洪坦写道，"嘉靖癸巳秋，余偕虚谷姚公访石门子于岩，览遗迹名胜，作而叹曰：……朱子欲屋之而未成，盖有所待也，乃命耆老吕瑗购材兴工，因其中岩下为楼数间，以广来学者，犹欲知先人丽泽之义，即名桃岩丽泽精舍"。嘉靖十五年（1536年），桃岩丽泽精舍建成，并改名为"五峰书院"。"五峰书院，嘉靖丙申太守姚公命耆老吕瑗建，原名桃岩丽泽精舍。邑侯洪坦记，嗣守陈公京书。"相比丽泽祠要盖在"堂东偏之隙"，桃岩丽泽精舍的建造则是以"撤去阿罗汉象"为代价的。

明末，永康学者周佑德在丽泽祠西侧又建造了一幢与丽泽祠规模相当，也是三间两层的建筑，取名为"学易斋"。

书院活动

在明朝最后的一百年里，有许多著名的学者都曾在五峰书院讲学，其中包括尚宝丞应典、江西抚州教授周桐、著名学者卢可久、周莹、应玠等人。这其中还有与岩下程氏同祖的三位程氏后人，他们是吏部左侍郎程文德（1497—1559年）、四川左布政程正谊（1531—1610年）和他的父亲程梓（1498—1585年）。来讲学的人大都是王阳明的弟子，讲习内容以倡导"致良知"学说为主，同时也包括"正心诚意"和程朱理学的部分内容。五峰书院在这段时间培养了许多优秀的人才，其中包括三十多位进士。

五峰书院除了"广来学者"和提供讲学场所之外，祭祀活动也是很重要的一个功能。丽泽祠创建之初共祀五人，但是程文德、应延育、周桐以陆九渊和张栻从未到过五峰为缘由，改仅祀朱熹、吕祖谦和陈亮三人。五峰书院则主祀"阳明王文成公；配祀石门应先生，方峰程先生"。学易斋的建造原本就是以纪念婺州学者何基、王柏、金履祥、许谦和章懋为初衷的。除了这五人之外，学易斋里还先后共配祀二十三人，其中不仅包括曾来五峰书院讲学的周桐、周莹等著名学者，还有程銈等当地乡绅。

随着五峰书院的名气越来越大，来赐额题联的名人也越来越多。清康熙二十二年（1683年），永康知县姬肇燕赐额"阐明理学"。乾隆四十五年（1780年），永康太平吕大宗祠和程、应、卢三姓后裔共同出资，重修五峰书院的三幢建筑，并请提督学使彭元瑞赐匾。次年一月彭元瑞亲自书写"丽泽如新"匾额。文楼村的程氏进士们也先后多次题写对联，例如"五峰书院"这幢建筑中就挂有程兆选题写的"学则数言矩矱遥承鹿洞；心传一脉渊源近溯姚江"，还有《五峰书院志》的作者程尚斐题写的"学术启良知，恍示鸢飞鱼跃；讲堂开胜地，何殊鹿洞鹅湖"。

进入清代中后期，讲学的气氛日渐衰退，每年的春秋两会便成了五峰书院最隆重的事情。会期各三天，届时前来讲学、奉祀的地方官绅多达数百人，其盛况不亚于朱熹来这里讲学的日子。关于"春会"的时间，《五峰书院志》里并没有提到，依惯例或许是在清明；秋天则在阴历九月初九，"每岁重阳日，祀朱、吕、陈三子，次日祀阳明王子，三日祀何、王、金、许诸儒"。关于祭祀的费用，则来自于应典、程梓和卢可久三人创置的会田，并由应、程、卢的后人负责料理会田和组织祭祀活动。会田创立之后，陈亮、程文德、王柏和吕祖谦的后人也相继捐出了部分田地。但是由于会田的收入还要支付日常开销，以及建筑修缮的费用，所以依旧入不敷出。清康熙二十年（1681年），五峰书院不得不取消春会，并把秋会祭祀的时间改为阴历九月十二、十三两日。五峰书院"秋会"不仅包括启龛、迎神、读祝文、献礼、献饭等通常意义上的祭祀活动，更是各路学者交流和学习的绝好机会。为此会规里有明确的规定，"十二日早膳后各出质言以相参证，其式正楷大书，登名于尾。凡与会者各带纸笔，午后互相抄录完时，实粘壁上。十三日早膳后，老成者各拈书一章，性理一章。三日内余功，或质疑问难、或阐发格言，言具登载于簿"。五峰书院"秋会"基本每年举行，一直由应、程、卢的后人负责，直到民国时期停办。

书院建筑

五峰书院的三幢建筑均位于固厚峰下能容千人的大石洞内，面南自东向西一字排开，均为三开间两层楼宇。其建筑的最大特点就是"即洞支木为之，不施椽瓦而雨雪霜露自然莫及"。丽泽祠的建造者应典还给这个山洞起名为"朝阳洞"，因为"朝日初出，苍苍凉凉，光射户牖"。

最东边的是"五峰书院"，其平面接近正方形，一层有廊，二层有栏以供凭眺。虽然屡经修缮，但是梁架结构并没有改变，所以仍然可以看到明代建筑的特点，例如梁架采用穿斗式，横梁不加装饰，梁下采用丁头拱，使用有覆盆的鼓形柱础等。建筑东墙外有一间小室，曾作为厨房。

丽泽祠和学易斋规模相当，都是进深较短的长方形平面，只是丽泽祠一层有廊。在门窗的处理上，学易斋和五峰书院较为类似，都是步步锦，丽泽祠则采用较为简单的"满天星"样式。
sections.content_en:
2. Wufeng Academy

Academy History

Finding written records about Shoushan Ravine again brings us to the Ming Zhengde period (1506-1521).

Shangbaocheng (Keeper of the Imperial Seal) Ying Dian, examining the walls, found Longchuan (Chen Liang) calligraphy (now observing the walls everywhere, but sometimes only Zhang's record of Longchuan calligraphy, or on Doushuai Terrace, yet no place to climb and view); recording the traces of Huiweng (Zhu Xi) and Donglai (Lü Zuqian), he then built a shrine in the gap east of the hall, to worship Zhu, Lü, as well as Zhang Nanxuan (Zhang Shi) and Lu Xiangshan (Lu Jiuyuan), with Longchuan (Chen Liang) as accompanying sacrifice — called Lize Shrine.

Lize Shrine, built by Mr. Ying Shimen during the Zhengde period, Prefect Zhang Yue inscribed this plaque, subsequent Prefect Yao Wenzhao wrote a record……

Ying Dian, courtesy name Tianyi, art name Shimen, a native of Zhiying, Yongkang, Zhejiang, became jinshi in the ninth year of Ming Zhengde (1514), and served as head of Lize Academy and White Deer Academy. This means Lize Shrine should have been built between 1514 and 1521. Here Zhu, Lü, and Zhang refer to Zhu Xi, Lü Zuqian, and Zhang Shi; during the Song Qiandao and Chunxi periods (1165-1189), these three were collectively called the "Three Sages of the Southeast." Besides these three, Lu Jiuyuan and Chen Liang were also worshipped as accompanying sacrifices.

The name "Lize" may have been taken from Lize Academy located at Mingzhao Mountain in Jinhua. Lize Academy was originally named Lize Hall, founded by Lü Zuqian in the early years of Song Qiandao (approximately 1165-1166). In front of the academy there were two lakes, and "Lize" originally meant two marshes connected, hence perfectly fitting. More importantly, the "Book of Changes · Dui" states, "Lize, Dui. The superior man uses it for friends to discuss and practice." Thus it can be seen that "Lize" has profound meaning; Zhu Xi once made the following evaluation, "Two marshes adjacent, mutually nourishing and benefiting, friends discussing and practicing — such is its image."

Over a decade later, a slightly larger building was built east of Lize Shrine, named "Taoyan Lize Jingshe" (Taoyan Lize Retreat). The then Yongkang County Magistrate Hong Tan wrote, "In the autumn of Jiajing Guisi (1533), I accompanied Mr. Yao Xugu to visit Shimenzi at the rock, viewing relics and scenic spots, and sighed: ……Master Zhu wanted to build a house but did not complete it, perhaps waiting for something; so he ordered elder Lü Yuan to purchase materials and start construction, building several rooms under the middle rock to welcome coming scholars, still wishing to know the meaning of ancestors' Lize, hence named Taoyan Lize Jingshe." In the fifteenth year of Jiajing (1536), Taoyan Lize Jingshe was completed and renamed "Wufeng Academy." "Wufeng Academy, in Jiajing Bingshen (1536) Prefect Yao ordered elder Lü Yuan to build, originally named Taoyan Lize Jingshe. County Marquis Hong Tan wrote record, subsequent Prefect Chen Jingshu calligraphy." Compared to Lize Shrine which had to be built in "the gap east of the hall," the construction of Taoyan Lize Jingshe came at the cost of "removing the Arhat statues."

In the late Ming, Yongkang scholar Zhou Youde built another building west of Lize Shrine, of similar scale to Lize Shrine, also three bays and two stories, named "Xueyi Zhai" (Study of Changes Studio).

Academy Activities

In the last hundred years of the Ming Dynasty, many famous scholars lectured at Wufeng Academy, including Shangbaocheng Ying Dian, Jiangxi Fuzhou Professor Zhou Tong, famous scholars Lu Kejiu, Zhou Ying, Ying Jie and others. Among them were three Cheng descendants sharing the same ancestor as the Yanxia Cheng family: Cheng Wende (1497-1559), Left Vice Minister of Personnel; Cheng Zhengyi (1531-1610), Left Administrative Commissioner of Sichuan; and his father Cheng Zi (1498-1585). Most of those who came to lecture were disciples of Wang Yangming; the lecture content mainly advocated the doctrine of "innate knowledge" (zhiliangzhi), while also including "rectifying the mind and making intentions sincere" and parts of Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism. During this period, Wufeng Academy cultivated many outstanding talents, including over thirty jinshi.

Besides "welcoming coming scholars" and providing lecture venues, sacrificial activities were also a very important function of Wufeng Academy. Lize Shrine originally worshipped five people at its founding, but Cheng Wende, Ying Yanyu, and Zhou Tong, citing that Lu Jiuyuan and Zhang Shi had never been to Wufeng, changed to worship only Zhu Xi, Lü Zuqian, and Chen Liang. Wufeng Academy mainly worshipped "Wang Wencheng Gong of Yangming (Wang Yangming); accompanying sacrifices: Mr. Ying Shimen, Mr. Cheng Fangfeng." The construction of Xueyi Zhai was originally intended to commemorate Wuzhou scholars He Ji, Wang Bai, Jin Lüxiang, Xu Qian, and Zhang Mao. Besides these five, Xueyi Zhai successively had twenty-three accompanying sacrifices, including not only famous scholars such as Zhou Tong and Zhou Ying who had lectured at Wufeng Academy, but also local gentry such as Cheng Ji.

As Wufeng Academy's fame grew, more and more famous people came to grant plaques and inscribe couplets. In the twenty-second year of Qing Kangxi (1683), Yongkang County Magistrate Ji Zhaoyan granted the plaque "Clarifying Neo-Confucianism." In the forty-fifth year of Qianlong (1780), the Yongkang Taiping Lü Grand Ancestral Hall and descendants of the Cheng, Ying, and Lu families jointly funded the renovation of the three buildings of Wufeng Academy, and requested Education Commissioner Peng Yuanrui to grant a plaque. In January of the following year, Peng Yuanrui personally wrote the plaque "Lize as New." The Cheng jinshi of Wenlou Village also successively inscribed couplets multiple times; for example, the building "Wufeng Academy" hangs a couplet by Cheng Zhaoxuan: "Learning follows few words, standards remotely inherited from Ludong; mind transmits one lineage, origin traced back to Yaojiang"; and another by Cheng Shangfei, author of the "Wufeng Academy Annals": "Learning initiates innate knowledge, vaguely showing kites flying and fish leaping; lecture hall opens at a scenic spot, no different from Ludong and Ehu."

Entering the mid-to-late Qing Dynasty, the atmosphere of lecturing gradually declined, and the annual spring and autumn meetings became the most solemn events of Wufeng Academy. Each meeting lasted three days, with local officials and gentry coming to lecture and worship numbering up to several hundred — the grand occasion no less than when Zhu Xi came here to lecture. Regarding the time of the "Spring Meeting," the "Wufeng Academy Annals" does not mention it; by convention it may have been at Qingming; autumn was on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month, "every year on Double Ninth, worship Zhu, Lü, and Chen three masters; next day worship Prince Yangming (Wang Yangming); third day worship He, Wang, Jin, Xu various Confucians." Regarding sacrificial expenses, they came from the meeting fields established by Ying Dian, Cheng Zi, and Lu Kejiu, and the descendants of Ying, Cheng, and Lu were responsible for managing the meeting fields and organizing sacrificial activities. After the establishment of meeting fields, descendants of Chen Liang, Cheng Wende, Wang Bai, and Lü Zuqian also successively donated part of their fields. But because the income from meeting fields also had to cover daily expenses and building renovation costs, it still fell short of expenditures. In the twentieth year of Qing Kangxi (1681), Wufeng Academy had to cancel the Spring Meeting and change the Autumn Meeting sacrifice time to the twelfth and thirteenth days of the ninth lunar month. Wufeng Academy's "Autumn Meeting" not only included usual sacrificial activities such as opening shrines, welcoming gods, reading congratulatory texts, presenting gifts, and presenting meals, but was also an excellent opportunity for scholars of various schools to exchange and learn. For this, the meeting rules had clear stipulations: "On the twelfth day after breakfast, each presents substantive words for mutual reference and verification, in formal regular script large characters, with name signed at the end. All participants bring paper and pen; after noon, after mutual copying is complete, actually paste on the wall. On the thirteenth day after breakfast, the experienced each select one chapter of a book, one chapter of nature-principle. Within the three days, remaining time may be for questioning and answering difficulties, or elucidating maxims; words are all recorded in the register." Wufeng Academy's "Autumn Meeting" was basically held every year, always managed by descendants of Ying, Cheng, and Lu, until it was discontinued during the Republic period.

Academy Architecture

The three buildings of Wufeng Academy are all located in the large stone cave below Guhou Peak that can hold a thousand people, facing south and arranged in a row from east to west, all three-bay two-story buildings. The greatest feature of their architecture is that they are "built by supporting wood in the cave, without applying rafters or tiles, yet rain, snow, frost and dew naturally cannot reach." Ying Dian, builder of Lize Shrine, also named this cave "Chaoyang Cave" (Morning Sun Cave), because "when the morning sun first emerges, cool and clear, light shines through the windows and doors."

The easternmost is "Wufeng Academy," with a nearly square plan, corridors on the first floor, and railings on the second floor for leaning and viewing. Although repeatedly renovated, the beam framework structure has not changed, so Ming Dynasty architectural features can still be seen, such as the beam framework采用 column-and-tie construction, horizontal beams without decoration, ding-tou brackets under beams, and drum-shaped column bases with overturned basins. Outside the east wall of the building there is a small room that once served as a kitchen.

Lize Shrine and Xueyi Zhai are of similar scale, both rectangular plans with shorter depth, except Lize Shrine has corridors on the first floor. In the treatment of doors and windows, Xueyi Zhai and Wufeng Academy are relatively similar, both using "step-by-step brocade" (bubujin) lattice patterns, while Lize Shrine uses the simpler "sky full of stars" (mantianxing) pattern.

Ludong (White Deer) and Ehu (Goose Lake) academies

sections.name: 胡公家庙
sections.content_zh:
三、胡公家庙

来龙去脉

五峰书院东边不远就是外洞，"此寿山寺旧刹也，今为胡公庙"。据《库川胡氏宗谱》记载，寿山寺在明正德（1506—1521年）以前就已经名存实亡，十多年后为了盖桃岩丽泽精舍又移走了洞里的罗汉像。

到了"嘉靖三十七年（1558年），奉例清查寿山废寺产业，买价入官"，一个叫徐一勤的人用五十一两白银买下了寿山坑里的五十七亩田、二十一亩多的地、十八亩多的山林和近九亩的塘。四年之后，胡氏的后人以寿山为"祖墓所在"，并且"寿山寺虽久废，所存田地山场等业系故祖胡士胜舍助，却被异姓官买"为由，开始了一场长达十八年之久的官司。这块田地山塘在这期间又被转手多次，从徐家转到程家，再从程家转到吕家，最终胡氏在万历八年（1580年）十一月，以一百九十两赎回。

万历三十六年（1608年），库川胡氏后人聚集在寿山坑里，决定利用洞口原有三层高台的基础建造一个"胡公家庙"。或许是广慈寺害怕这个"正宗"的胡公会抢了自己的香火，或许老街上的程氏也担心这个半路"杀"出来的胡公家庙会让老街从此变得萧条，于是一个叫如昌的僧人便把胡氏告上了公堂。从以程氏代管山林的"一审"结果来看，程氏应该也是这场官司的幕后支持或是怂恿者。胡氏当然不服，把官司告上了金华府，"二审"结果虽然保住了胡氏的田地山塘，但是建胡公家庙这件事，还是维持原判。原因是"方岩有像，四方香火供奉……寿山去彼一里许，又安得重建祠宇耶……惟将寿山新建未成者拆毁……"。

经过这次教训之后，远在胡库的胡氏似乎明白了要想在寿山坑站稳脚跟，就要讨好邻山广慈寺的道理，于是在清顺治十一年（1654年），胡氏慷慨资助广慈寺修理前厅。随后，在康熙二十二年（1683年），寿山坑里的胡公家庙就建成了。康熙四十一年（1702年），胡氏又捐田助寺。在这之后的一百多年里，胡氏不仅多次资助广慈寺翻修大殿，双方还协定"方岩祭礼约"。这种友好的关系一直延续到1840年，在程氏的介入下双方再次对簿公堂。虽然胡氏胜诉，但是广慈寺"于道光二十九年（1849年）九月初四合庙并僧房尽皆同禄"，胡氏认为这是天意，决定从此放弃方岩大殿，仅去寿山祭祀。

建筑

民国23年（1934年），胡氏在当时永康罗骏超的建议下开始筹划重建胡公家庙。重建工程自1935年始，至1937年完工，于是就有了今天矗立在固厚峰下的"重楼"。

新建成的胡公家庙坐落在一个用石材垒砌的高大基座上，基座东西两侧的地面高差有一层多高。它的一层有五间，二层、三层原本各三间。三层利用岩壁围合空间，岩壁上"兜率台"三个大字清晰可见。建筑一层和三层进深较浅，二层不但空间高，而且进深为前后二进，一直深入洞中。重楼在结构上采用砖木混合形式，外立面用砖墙做竖向承重结构，辅以木梁和木质门窗，内部做法比较传统，以木构为主。建筑式样上则明显受到"新时代"的影响，东侧入口处为砖砌发券，西洋式小门楼，二层三层栏杆的做法也显然是机器加工的产品。

民国27年（1938年），浙江省政府迁至方岩临时办公，其中财政厅进驻胡公家庙的二层和三层。例如因房间不够，二层两侧便被各增加一间；为解决采光的问题，所有的门窗还被装上了玻璃。国民政府进驻期间，胡公家庙还得匾"春帆楼"，省政府主席黄绍竑还亲自题联"庙貌壮灵岩，历宋元明清，史册相传，会栋宇更新，欣兹后起多才争辉谱谍；官廨邻胜境，仰聪明正直，风微若接，待湖山重整，好与斯邦父母共荐馨香"。
sections.content_en:
3. Hu Gong Family Temple

Origins and Development

Not far east of Wufeng Academy is the Outer Cave, "this was the old site of Shoushan Temple, now it is Hu Gong Temple." According to the "Kuchuan Hu Clan Genealogy," Shoushan Temple had already existed in name only before the Ming Zhengde period (1506-1521); over a decade later, the Arhat statues in the cave were moved away to build Taoyan Lize Jingshe.

By "the thirty-seventh year of Jiajing (1558), following the order to investigate the properties of the abandoned Shoushan Temple, the purchase price was paid into the official treasury," a man named Xu Yiqin bought fifty-seven mu of fields, over twenty-one mu of land, over eighteen mu of mountain forest, and nearly nine mu of ponds in Shoushan Ravine for fifty-one taels of silver. Four years later, the Hu descendants, citing Shoushan as "where ancestral tombs are located" and that "although Shoushan Temple has long been abandoned, the remaining fields, land, mountains and other properties were donated by ancestor Hu Shisheng, but were bought by an outsider through official channels," began a lawsuit lasting eighteen years. During this period, the fields, land, mountains and ponds changed hands multiple times — from the Xu family to the Cheng family, then from the Cheng family to the Lü family — and finally the Hu family redeemed them in the eleventh month of the eighth year of Wanli (1580) for one hundred and ninety taels.

In the thirty-sixth year of Wanli (1608), the Kuchuan Hu descendants gathered in Shoushan Ravine and decided to build a "Hu Gong Family Temple" on the foundation of the original three-tier high platform at the cave entrance. Perhaps Guangci Temple feared this "authentic" Hu Gong would steal its incense, or perhaps the Cheng family on the old street worried that this Hu Gong Family Temple, appearing out of nowhere, would cause the old street to become desolate — so a monk named Ruchang sued the Hu family in court. From the "first trial" result, in which the Cheng family managed the mountain forest on their behalf, it appears the Cheng family was also the behind-the-scenes supporter or instigator of this lawsuit. The Hu family, of course, refused to accept it and appealed to Jinhua Prefecture; although the "second trial" result preserved the Hu family's fields, land, mountains and ponds, the matter of building the Hu Gong Family Temple still upheld the original verdict. The reason was "Fangyan has the statue, with incense offerings from all directions …… Shoushan is about one li from there, how could another shrine be rebuilt …… only the unfinished new building at Shoushan should be demolished ……"

After this lesson, the Hu family, far away in Huku, seemed to understand that to gain a firm foothold in Shoushan Ravine, they must please the neighboring Guangci Temple. So in the eleventh year of Qing Shunzhi (1654), the Hu family generously funded Guangci Temple to repair its front hall. Subsequently, in the twenty-second year of Kangxi (1683), the Hu Gong Family Temple in Shoushan Ravine was completed. In the forty-first year of Kangxi (1702), the Hu family again donated fields to assist the temple. In the following hundred-plus years, the Hu family not only repeatedly funded Guangci Temple to renovate its main hall, but both sides also agreed on the "Fangyan Sacrificial Ritual Pact." This friendly relationship continued until 1840, when with the intervention of the Cheng family, both sides again went to court. Although the Hu family won the lawsuit, Guangci Temple "on the fourth day of the ninth month in the twenty-ninth year of Daoguang (1849), the entire temple together with monk quarters was all destroyed by fire"; the Hu family considered this the will of heaven and decided from then on to abandon the Fangyan main hall, only going to Shoushan for sacrifices.

Architecture

In the 23rd year of the Republic (1934), the Hu family, under the suggestion of Luo Junchao of Yongkang at that time, began planning to rebuild the Hu Gong Family Temple. The reconstruction project began in 1935 and was completed in 1937, resulting in today's "Chonglou" (Multi-Story Tower) standing below Guhou Peak.

The newly built Hu Gong Family Temple sits on a tall stone-masonry base, with a ground level difference of over one story between the east and west sides of the base. Its first floor has five bays; the second and third floors originally had three bays each. The third floor uses the rock wall to enclose space, with the three large characters "Doushuai Terrace" clearly visible on the rock wall. The first and third floors have shallow depths; the second floor not only has high space but also a depth of two front-to-back bays, extending deep into the cave. The Chonglou adopts a mixed brick-wood structural form; the exterior facade uses brick walls as vertical load-bearing structure, supplemented by wooden beams and wooden doors and windows; the interior practice is relatively traditional, mainly wooden construction. The architectural style was clearly influenced by the "new era": the east entrance is a brick arch with a Western-style small gatehouse, and the railings on the second and third floors are obviously machine-made products.

In the 27th year of the Republic (1938), the Zhejiang Provincial Government moved to Fangyan for temporary office work, with the Finance Department stationed on the second and third floors of the Hu Gong Family Temple. For example, due to insufficient rooms, one bay was added to each side of the second floor; to solve lighting problems, all doors and windows were fitted with glass. During the Nationalist Government's occupation, the Hu Gong Family Temple also received the plaque "Chunfan Tower" (Spring Sail Tower), and Provincial Government Chairman Huang Shaohong personally inscribed a couplet: "The temple's appearance strengthens the spiritual rock, through Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing, passed down in history annals; with the hall renewed, rejoice that later talents rise to glorify the genealogy; the government office neighbors the scenic spot, looking up to intelligence and integrity, the subtle influence seems close; when the lakes and mountains are restored, we may together offer fragrance with the parents of this land."

sections.name: 没有了进士的五峰书院
sections.content_zh:
四、没有了进士的五峰书院

没有了科举考试，没有了进士，书院曾经举办的各种活动在民国时期就全部停止了。与胡公家庙一起，五峰书院在民国27年（1938年）到31年（1942年），也曾作为省政府的临时办公场所。或许是因为近千年来，曾经在这里徘徊的进士和学者们都久久不愿离去，所以政府工作人员走后的第一年，五峰书院就作为永康师范学校的校舍，一直到1962年。

如今，学生们也走了。空荡荡的五峰书院变成了展览馆，设有书院历史、书院制度、书院功能、书院与文房四宝、书院与科举制度、五峰书院与永康学派等专题展览，甚至还有祭堂。瀑布下、山洞里、水塘边还设有茶室，倒也颇具些意境。但是不知怎的，没有了进士和学者们穿梭其间，没有了"晦翁主讲席，从游者数百人"的热闹场面，没有了"或质疑问难、或阐发格言"的高声论辩，五峰书院便寂静的可怕。静得连偶尔来参观的游客，都不愿意在这本应该是诗意盎然的茶室里小坐，便毅然转身离去，只留下他们匆匆的脚步声回荡在寿山坑里。
sections.content_en:
4. Wufeng Academy Without Jinshi

Without the imperial examination, without jinshi, the various activities once held by the academy all ceased during the Republic period. Together with the Hu Gong Family Temple, Wufeng Academy also served as a temporary office for the provincial government from the 27th year (1938) to the 31st year (1942) of the Republic. Perhaps because for nearly a thousand years, the jinshi and scholars who once wandered here were reluctant to leave for a long time, in the first year after the government staff left, Wufeng Academy became the school building of Yongkang Normal School, remaining so until 1962.

Today, the students have also left. The empty Wufeng Academy has become an exhibition hall, with thematic exhibitions on academy history, academy system, academy functions, academies and the four treasures of the study, academies and the imperial examination system, Wufeng Academy and the Yongkang School, and even a sacrificial hall. Below the waterfall, in the caves, and by the pond, tea rooms have also been set up, which does have some poetic charm. But somehow, without jinshi and scholars穿梭其间, without the lively scene of "Huiweng (Zhu Xi) giving the main lecture with hundreds of followers," without the loud debates of "questioning and answering difficulties, or elucidating maxims," Wufeng Academy becomes terrifyingly silent. So silent that even occasional visiting tourists are unwilling to sit for a while in this tea room that should be full of poetry, but resolutely turn and leave, leaving only their hurried footsteps echoing in Shoushan Ravine.

chapters.name: 第七章 建筑的雕饰与装修

sections.name: 大木作雕饰
sections.content_zh:
一、大木作雕饰

老街上的建筑装饰，主要以木雕为主，石雕和砖雕的应用并不普遍。彩画虽然曾经被广泛应用在砖墙的檐下，但是能历经风雨保留下来的却很少。祠堂里的大木雕饰使用范围广泛，而且通常都非常精美。但是由于祠堂的主要空间均开敞，所以小木装修仅在厢房上才会使用，多数比较简单。住宅中的精美木雕主要位于门、窗、栏杆等处，部分住宅中的"马腿"、插叶、梁下巴等小型大木构件也雕饰得独具匠心、美轮美奂。

老街上过去由于家家都在忙着做香客的生意，所以没有什么匠人，过去盖房子需要的匠人都要从东阳请。解放后日子困难了，老街上的男孩子们才开始背井离乡出门学手艺，而这其中又以铁匠居多。老街上现在只有一位做大木的木匠，叫程高明（1942年生，第22代，圣字辈）。

马腿

"马腿"即江南民居中通常所说的"牛腿"，它位于檐柱上方，向天井垂直出挑。"马腿"的下半部分固定在马腿垫和檐柱上，用以承托上面的金枋。

金枋一般分为两部分，后面一段雕饰比较简单，通常只沿轮廓做几道线脚，内部辅以花卉题材为主的浅浮雕。但是这里也可以作为精雕细琢的重点，程昭夫祠堂中的部分金枋两侧就雕有生动的人物故事，绍常祠堂的一些金枋上则雕有三维的亭台楼阁。金枋尽端一般都有一个和金枋截面大小相当的一组三维人物或鸟兽，它们通常呈向庭院内伸展或端望的态势。金枋上面是金枋垫，上面承载着平行于立面的叠拱和沿进深方向的插叶。如果叠拱或插叶采用卷草纹造型，则金枋垫下面的这部分金枋垫还会做成花篮形状，使整个构件更为生动统一。

通体透雕的"马腿"可以说是整幢建筑中最精美的一块木雕。这个构件基本上只是对金枋起到一个斜撑的作用，所以它的上半部分，甚至整块木雕都可以和后面的柱子脱离，富于想象的匠人便利用到了这个特点，因地制宜地把部分雕刻内容也"转"到了"马腿"的背面。这样一来整组雕刻便显得更为生动，特别是对于雕有一组人物故事的"马腿"，如此处理后还增加了人物的立体感。这不禁让人想到希腊神庙三角山墙上的人物石雕，这种群雕的最大特点之一就是所有人物的姿态，以及人与人之间的相互关系，都能自然贴合屋顶的斜线，于是每一组山墙上的群雕都成了雕塑构图中的精品。比起希腊神庙三角山墙上的石雕，雕"马腿"的难度就要大多了。不仅所有的雕刻内容要控制在一个厚度单一的倒楔形体内，而且还要照顾到从正面和两侧三个面的视觉效果。由于人的视线较低，所以"马腿"的设计还会利用楔形的这个斜面和下面的观望者产生一种交流。

简单一点的"马腿"会雕"三狮戏球"，类似的母题一般用于祠堂中榀的两个檐柱上。世远公祠里的"马腿"是以一头成年狮子作为木雕的主体，它前腿着地，后腿高抬，守着眼前的绣球；它毛发冲天，略微低头，虎视眈眈地注视着下面的来访者。两只小狮子则在"马腿"整体空间构成的"空隙"中玩耍嬉戏，其实从某种意义上来讲，小狮子的位置和姿态才是设计的难点。

复杂的"马腿"会雕一组人物，并辅以相应的背景。程昭夫祠堂正堂中榀前檐柱上的"马腿"，一边是"王母骑凤"下凡，另一边是"玉皇大帝乘龙"到人间，跟随他们俩的还各有七个和五个辅助人物，分别是侍女、随从、天兵天将等人。王母和玉皇大帝等主要人物均面向中间，并稍适低头；他们身后还各有一个天兵驻守在"马腿"的另一侧，左盼右顾；更让人不禁拍案叫绝的是，在"马腿"的外下角，各有两个侍从，或低头、或坐、或弯腰、或俯身，似乎在暗自体察凡界中的冷暖是非。这些人物造型，个个都精雕细琢，惟妙惟肖；人物和人物之间主次分明，空间层次清楚。更难得的是，整组雕刻不但在立面上形成一个倒楔形，而且全部人物都控制在一个十多厘米的厚度里。

马腿垫上的雕饰一般比较简单，通常沿替木外围勾勒出一些线脚，内部浅雕花卉，或刻上诸如福、禄、寿之类的吉祥字眼，有的则是用几个"马腿"上的替木组成一句四字成语。

随着"马腿"的装饰性越来越大，它的设计也越来越灵活。在很多情况下，马腿垫和"马腿"可以简化为一块木头，只是在靠下的部分做了一个木楔子，插到柱子里。这样做的好处是在设计上可以比较自由，而且又多了一个面可以发挥匠人的创造性。程昭夫祠堂天井角部两个"马腿"的雕刻主题均为"仙人骑鱼"，鱼头向下，做纵身跃起状。"马腿"下原有的垫木在这里演化成了翻滚的浪花，如此一来，"鱼跃龙门"的态势便更加栩栩如生。胡公庙里的"盘龙马腿"则是用统一的图案把金枋、"马腿"和马腿垫连成一体，金枋雕龙头，"马腿"为龙身，马腿垫和后面的短梁化成彩云，整个"马腿"浑然一体，颇具匠心。

梭梁

梭梁的中部微微向上拱起，形如月亮，所以也被称为月梁。梭梁被普遍使用在祠堂的主要开敞空间里，还有部分住宅的檐廊下，甚至是厅堂里。梭梁上的雕饰并不多，基本只是集中在梁头两侧的"寥寥几刀"。但是不得不承认，不论是梭梁两侧弧形的截面，还是它两端卷杀的本身，就已经是绝美的雕刻作品。

梭梁两端卷杀的部分又被称作气堂，这里气堂上的雕饰有几种不同的做法。最简单的就是在梭梁两端雕上三道凹槽，这三条曲线仿佛是有弹性的梭梁在受力时形成的"褶皱"。雕饰讲究的建筑，或是跨度大一点的梭梁，凹槽末端还会衔接上一小束浅浅的阳刻卷草纹饰。这些纹饰紧紧地贴在梭梁尽端，仿佛是从柱子和梭梁的接缝中生长出来的。如果这样还不能尽兴，还可以在梁身上做文章。义丰雅记正堂中的五架梁，不但梭梁尽端的雕饰分外妖娆、极富装饰性，在凹槽的另外一侧又伸出一支更为舒展的卷草纹饰。程立重宅院一进院正堂中榀五架梁梁头的雕饰虽然比较简单，但是气堂内侧的卷草花纹则有半米多长。一些院落的檐下梭梁中部还雕有凤凰、蝙蝠、画卷、扇面等图案。

梭梁两端气堂的做法在不同时期也会略有不同。建造年代较早的建筑，如作勳公祠和世远公祠梭梁气堂中的凹槽较浅，凹槽和梭梁尽端阳刻卷草花纹的衔接也比较自然。相比而言，一百多年后建造的程昭夫祠堂中的梭梁，气堂的凹槽较深，其截面呈三角形，与阳刻卷草花纹的过渡也比较生硬，甚至凹槽本身的曲线也缺乏了那种柔韧之美，变得"硬邦邦"的。

梁下巴

梁下巴，即通常所说的梁托。它的雕刻通常比较程式化：在侧面沿轮廓刻一两道线脚，里面雕上一些简单的花卉，或是阳刻一个吉祥的字，大跨梁架下的梁下巴还可能在曲形底面上浅刻一些纹饰。老街上不论是祠堂还是住宅中的梁下巴大体都如此模式，唯独义丰南院正房檐廊下的四组梁下巴与众不同。这些梁下巴中的雕饰以城市或建筑为主题，并配有花草树木、人物鸟兽。这些建筑本身不但是三维立体的，而且建筑和其他事物之间的空间关系，在视觉上也表现得非常正确。这些梁下巴中所雕刻的建筑类型既有两进的农家小院，又有带长廊的深宅大院；既有小型的亭台楼阁，又有建筑在高台上的城楼殿宇；不仅如此，还有各式的拱桥和渔船若干。其雕刻的精细程度，更是让人叹为观止，三四厘米高的"房子"不但门、窗比例正确，而且可以看到屋面上的瓦线和屋檐下的雀替。就连通常只是一条凹槽的梁下巴轮廓线脚，在这里也变成了几十个紧密排列的"花瓣"。梁下巴的曲形底面上还深雕有精美菊花。

蟺梁

程高明老人说，他不知道"转梁"中的"转"字如何写，只听人说"转"字代表一种动物，由此推断可能是"蟺梁"。蟺梁通常位于梁架结构靠上的部分，一端固定在柱子上，用来在纵向上牵引支撑桁条的叠拱。蟺梁一般只在祠堂建筑中使用，老街上仅有绍常祠堂、程昭夫祠堂和周氏宗祠使用了这用蟺梁。即便如此，这几幢建筑只有在最重要的空间，即正堂的梁架结构中才会使用到蟺梁，由此可见其"级别"之高。在这三幢祠堂建筑中，绍常祠堂中的蟺梁好似盘龙吐水，程昭夫祠堂里的也雕有一个龙头，只有周氏宗祠仅采用抽象的卷纹。

同一幢建筑中的蟺梁造型相似，只是大小会根据桁条和桁条之间的距离做相应的调整。

程高明老人讲，通常如果用"三抽"，即三架梁，就不用蟺梁。绍常祠堂正堂，中榀主要采用抬梁式结构，所以用"三抽"代替正脊下的蟺梁。边榀则为穿斗结构，即采用蟺梁而没有"三抽"。除此之外，每两个桁条或桁枋之间都有蟺梁。每个盘龙形蟺梁都接近一个圆形，龙身高高拱起，视觉上仿佛在支撑着上面的椽子，整个造型极富张力。龙身虽然向屋脊方向盘旋，但是龙头却高高昂起望向檐口，而且有五彩的水花从嘴里喷出。龙身由红、白、蓝、绿等颜色逐层退晕描画，龙身上还有彩绘花饰。

程昭夫祠堂的蟺梁相对抽象，只能通过一双炯炯有神、望向地面的龙眼来确定整条龙的姿态。正堂中榀虽然也用了"三抽"，但是为了造型的统一，在"三抽"上依旧用蟺梁做雕饰。这组蟺梁已经没有结构作用，再加上"三抽"和椽子之间的空间矮小，所以这组蟺梁的尾部向檐口方向旋绕，整体看上去好像"躺"了下来。

周氏宗祠里的蟺梁在外形上与程昭夫祠堂里的蟺梁相似，基本上都呈上大下小的椭圆形，但是它们没有了龙头，梁上的线脚也更为简洁，而且刻槽较浅，使得整个构件造型比较饱满，不乏质朴之美。

米梁、桁条、挑檐枋

米梁是指位于柱子之间的横向结构部件。桁条即檩子，如果截面接近方形也被称作桁枋。这些构件和挑檐枋都是主要的承重结构，一般不做任何雕饰，但是有些时候，这些构件的底面也会成为雕饰的载体。通常来说，这类雕饰只存在于祠堂建筑中，因为这里主要空间的梁架均露明，所以米梁、桁条和挑檐枋抬头可见。周氏宗祠拜厅天井一侧檐柱和金柱之间的米梁上都雕有浅浅的抽象的几何图案。程昭夫祠堂正堂的两个上金桁枋、前下金桁枋和檐枋，还有天井四周的挑檐枋底面都浮雕花草、凤凰、仙鹤、飞鸟、鱼纹和狮子戏球等图案。绍常祠堂在同样的位置也有雕饰：上金桁枋对称雕饰彩色勾连花卉；前下金桁枋和挑檐枋上各透雕一组花卉；檐枋上的透雕鱼纹、花鸟更是精美绝伦。据程高明老人讲，桁条一般都做成圆形，但是为了能在上面做雕饰，所以改成方形。雕饰的部分通常需要额外加上两层、甚至是三层木板，层数越多，越能雕出通透的感觉。

其他

雀替、叠拱、插叶、梁斗、梁斗垫、柱斗等部位也可以成为大木雕饰中的重点。叠拱和插叶是位于米梁、桁条或枋下面一组相互垂直的构件。支撑它们的可以是位于柱子上方的柱斗，也可以是位于梭梁上的梁斗。这些部位采用的雕饰母题多为卷草、花卉或抽象的回纹图案，有时候还会辅以寓意吉祥的字。
