1. Large Timber Carvings and Decorations

Architectural decoration on the old street is mainly wood carving; stone carving and brick carving are not commonly applied. Although painted decorations were once widely used under the eaves of brick walls, very few have survived the wind and rain. Large wood carvings in ancestral halls are widely used and usually very exquisite. However, because the main spaces of ancestral halls are all open, small wood joinery is only used in the wing rooms, mostly relatively simple. Exquisite wood carvings in residences are mainly located at doors, windows, railings and other places; in some residences, small large-timber components such as "horse legs" (corbels), inserted leaves, and beam brackets are also carved with unique ingenuity and beauty.

In the past, because every family on the old street was busy doing business with pilgrims, there were few craftsmen; craftsmen needed for building houses in the past had to be hired from Dongyang. After liberation, when times became hard, boys on the old street began to leave home to learn trades, and among them blacksmiths were the majority. There is now only one carpenter doing large timber work on the old street, named Cheng Gaoming (born 1942, 22nd generation, Sheng character generation).

Horse Legs (Corbels)

"Horse leg" is what is commonly called "ox leg" (niutui) in Jiangnan residences; it is located above the eave column, projecting vertically toward the courtyard. The lower part of the "horse leg" is fixed on the horse-leg pad and eave column, used to support the gold beam (jinfang) above.

The gold beam is generally divided into two parts; the rear section has relatively simple carving, usually only a few moldings along the outline, with shallow relief of floral themes inside. But this can also be the focus of meticulous carving: some gold beams on both sides in Cheng Zhaofu Ancestral Hall are carved with vivid human stories, while some gold beams in Shaochang Ancestral Hall are carved with three-dimensional pavilions and towers. The end of the gold beam generally has a group of three-dimensional figures or birds and beasts of the same size as the gold beam cross-section, usually in a posture extending toward the courtyard or gazing inward. Above the gold beam is the gold-beam pad, carrying stacked brackets parallel to the facade and inserted leaves along the depth direction. If the stacked brackets or inserted leaves use scrolling grass patterns, the part of the gold-beam pad below will also be made into a flower basket shape, making the entire component more vivid and unified.

The fully openwork-carved "horse leg" can be said to be the most exquisite wood carving in the entire building. This component basically only serves as a diagonal brace for the gold beam, so its upper part, even the entire wood carving, can be detached from the column behind; imaginative craftsmen took advantage of this feature, adapting to local conditions by "turning" part of the carving content to the back of the "horse leg." This makes the entire group of carvings more vivid, especially for "horse legs" carved with a group of human stories; this treatment also increases the three-dimensionality of the figures. This inevitably brings to mind the human figure stone carvings on the triangular pediments of Greek temples; one of the greatest features of such group carvings is that the postures of all figures, and the relationships between them, naturally conform to the sloping lines of the roof, so each group of pediment carvings becomes a masterpiece of sculptural composition. Compared with stone carvings on Greek temple triangular pediments, carving "horse legs" is much more difficult. Not only must all carving content be controlled within a single-thickness inverted wedge-shaped body, but also the visual effects from the front and both sides must be considered. Because people's line of sight is low, the design of "horse legs" also uses this wedge-shaped slope to create a kind of communication with the viewers below.

Simpler "horse legs" are carved with "three lions playing with a ball"; similar motifs are generally used on the two eave columns of the middle frame in ancestral halls. The "horse legs" in Shiyuan Gong Hall use an adult lion as the main subject of the wood carving, with its front legs on the ground and hind legs raised high, guarding the embroidered ball before it; its hair bristles upward, head slightly lowered, glaring fiercely at the visitors below. Two lion cubs play and frolic in the "gaps" formed by the overall space of the "horse leg"; in fact, in a sense, the position and posture of the cubs are the difficult part of the design.

Complex "horse legs" are carved with a group of figures, supplemented by corresponding backgrounds. The "horse legs" on the front eave columns of the middle frame of the main hall in Cheng Zhaofu Ancestral Hall have, on one side, the "Queen Mother riding a phoenix" descending to earth, and on the other side, the "Jade Emperor riding a dragon" coming to the human world; following them are seven and five auxiliary figures respectively, namely maids, attendants, heavenly soldiers and generals. The main figures such as the Queen Mother and Jade Emperor all face the center, with heads slightly bowed; behind them each has a heavenly soldier guarding the other side of the "horse leg," looking left and right; even more amazing is that at the outer lower corners of the "horse legs," there are two attendants each, either bowing heads, sitting, bending, or leaning, seemingly secretly observing the warmth and cold, right and wrong of the mortal world. These figure models are all meticulously carved, lifelike; between figures, primary and secondary are distinct, spatial layers clear. What is even rarer is that the entire group of carvings not only forms an inverted wedge on the facade, but all figures are controlled within a thickness of just over ten centimeters.

The carvings on horse-leg pads are generally relatively simple, usually outlining some moldings along the periphery of the substitute wood, with shallow-carved flowers inside, or auspicious characters such as fortune, prosperity, and longevity carved in relief; some use several substitute woods on the "horse legs" to form a four-character idiom.

As the decorative nature of "horse legs" grew, their designs became increasingly flexible. In many cases, the horse-leg pad and "horse leg" can be simplified into a single piece of wood, with only a wooden wedge made in the lower part to insert into the column. The advantage of this is greater design freedom, and one more surface on which to exert the craftsman's creativity. The carving theme of the two "horse legs" at the courtyard corners of Cheng Zhaofu Ancestral Hall is both "immortal riding a fish," with the fish head downward in a leaping posture. The original pad wood below the "horse leg" here evolved into rolling waves, making the "fish leaping through the dragon gate" posture even more lifelike. The "coiled dragon horse leg" in Hu Gong Temple uses a unified pattern to connect the gold beam, "horse leg," and horse-leg pad into one body: the gold beam is carved as a dragon head, the "horse leg" as the dragon body, and the horse-leg pad and short beam behind transform into colorful clouds; the entire "horse leg" is浑然一体, quite ingenious.

Shuttle Beams (Moon Beams)

The middle part of a shuttle beam arches slightly upward, shaped like a moon, hence also called moon beam. Shuttle beams are commonly used in the main open spaces of ancestral halls, under the eaves of some residences, and even in halls. There are not many carvings on shuttle beams, basically concentrated only in the "few strokes" on both sides of the beam head. But it must be admitted that whether it is the curved cross-section on both sides of the shuttle beam or the rolling cuts at both ends itself, it is already a beautiful carving work.

The rolling-cut parts at both ends of the shuttle beam are also called qitang (air hall); there are several different practices for the carvings here. The simplest is to carve three grooves at both ends of the shuttle beam; these three curves seem like "wrinkles" formed when the elastic shuttle beam is under load. In buildings with exquisite carvings, or shuttle beams with larger spans, the ends of the grooves also connect with a small束 of shallow positive-carved scrolling grass patterns. These patterns cling tightly to the ends of the shuttle beam, as if growing out of the joint between the column and shuttle beam. If this is still not enough, one can also work on the beam body. The five-frame beam in the main hall of Yifeng Yaji not only has particularly enchanting and highly decorative carvings at the shuttle beam ends, but also extends a more舒展 scrolling grass pattern on the other side of the groove. Although the carvings at the beam heads of the five-frame beam on the middle frame of the main hall in the first courtyard of Cheng Lizhong Mansion are relatively simple, the scrolling grass pattern on the inner side of the qitang is over half a meter long. The middle parts of shuttle beams under the eaves of some courtyards are also carved with phoenixes, bats, painting scrolls, fans and other patterns.

The practice of qitang at both ends of shuttle beams also varies slightly in different periods. In buildings of earlier construction dates, such as Zuoxun Gong Hall and Shiyuan Gong Hall, the grooves in the shuttle beam qitang are shallower, and the connection between the grooves and the positive-carved scrolling grass pattern at the shuttle beam ends is more natural. In comparison, in the shuttle beams of Cheng Zhaofu Ancestral Hall built over a hundred years later, the qitang grooves are deeper, with triangular cross-sections, and the transition to the positive-carved scrolling grass pattern is more rigid; even the curve of the groove itself lacks that flexible beauty, becoming "stiff."

Beam Chin (Beam Bracket)

Beam chin, commonly known as beam bracket (liangtuo). Its carving is usually quite formulaic: on the side, one or two moldings are carved along the outline, with some simple flowers carved inside, or an auspicious character in positive relief; beam chins under large-span beam frames may also have shallow-carved patterns on the curved bottom surface. Whether in ancestral halls or residences on the old street, beam chins generally follow this pattern, with the sole exception of the four groups of beam chins under the eave corridor of the main house in Yifeng South Courtyard. The carvings in these beam chins take cities or buildings as themes, supplemented by flowers, plants, trees, figures, birds and beasts. These buildings themselves are not only three-dimensional, but the spatial relationships between buildings and other things are also represented very correctly visually. The building types carved in these beam chins include both two-courtyard peasant courtyards and deep mansion compounds with long corridors; both small pavilions and towers, and city gate towers and palace halls built on high platforms; moreover, there are various arched bridges and fishing boats. The fineness of the carving is even more breathtaking: the "houses" only three or four centimeters high not only have correct door and window proportions, but also the tile lines on the roof and the sparrow braces under the eaves can be seen. Even the beam chin outline molding, usually just a single groove, here becomes dozens of closely arranged "petals." The curved bottom surface of the beam chin is also deeply carved with exquisite chrysanthemums.

Shan Beams (Eel Beams)

Elder Cheng Gaoming said he does not know how to write the "zhuan" character in "zhuanliang" (turning beam), only hearing that the character represents an animal, from which he推断 it may be "shanliang" (eel beam). Shan beams are usually located in the upper part of the beam frame structure, with one end fixed on the column, used to longitudinally牵引 and support the stacked brackets of the purlins. Shan beams are generally only used in ancestral hall architecture; on the old street, only Shaochang Ancestral Hall, Cheng Zhaofu Ancestral Hall, and Zhou Clan Ancestral Hall use shan beams. Even so, these buildings only use shan beams in the most important space, namely the beam frame structure of the main hall, which shows how high their "status" is. Among these three ancestral halls, the shan beams in Shaochang Ancestral Hall resemble a coiled dragon spitting water; those in Cheng Zhaofu Ancestral Hall are also carved with a dragon head; only Zhou Clan Ancestral Hall uses abstract scrolling patterns.

Shan beams in the same building have similar shapes, only their sizes are adjusted according to the distance between purlins.

Elder Cheng Gaoming said that usually if "three chou" (three-frame beams) are used, shan beams are not used. In the main hall of Shaochang Ancestral Hall, the middle frame mainly adopts post-and-lintel construction, so "three chou" is used instead of the shan beam under the main ridge. The side frames are column-and-tie construction, i.e. using shan beams without "three chou." In addition, there are shan beams between every two purlins or purlin beams. Each coiled-dragon shan beam is nearly circular, with the dragon body arched high, visually seeming to support the rafters above, the entire shape extremely tense. Although the dragon body coils toward the ridge direction, the dragon head is raised high looking toward the eave, and colorful water sprays from its mouth. The dragon body is painted with layered color gradients of red, white, blue, green and other colors, and there are also painted floral decorations on the dragon body.

The shan beams in Cheng Zhaofu Ancestral Hall are relatively abstract; the posture of the entire dragon can only be determined through a pair of bright eyes looking toward the ground. Although the middle frame of the main hall also uses "three chou," for the sake of造型 unity, shan beams are still used for carving on the "three chou." This group of shan beams no longer has a structural function; coupled with the small space between the "three chou" and the rafters, the tails of this group of shan beams coil toward the eave direction, and the whole looks as if "lying down."

The shan beams in Zhou Clan Ancestral Hall are similar in shape to those in Cheng Zhaofu Ancestral Hall, basically all presenting an ellipse larger at the top and smaller at the bottom, but they lack dragon heads, the moldings on the beams are simpler, and the carved grooves are shallower, making the entire component shape relatively full, not lacking in rustic beauty.

Rice Beams, Purlins, Eave-Protruding Beams

Rice beam refers to the horizontal structural component located between columns. A purlin is a rafter; if its cross-section is nearly square it is also called a purlin beam. These components and eave-protruding beams are all main load-bearing structures, generally without any carvings, but sometimes the bottom surfaces of these components also become carriers for carvings. Generally speaking, this type of carving only exists in ancestral hall architecture, because the beam frames in the main spaces here are all exposed, so rice beams, purlins and eave-protruding beams are visible when looking up. The rice beams between the eave column and gold column on one side of the courtyard in the worship hall of Zhou Clan Ancestral Hall are all carved with shallow abstract geometric patterns. The bottom surfaces of the two upper gold purlin beams, front lower gold purlin beams and eave beams in the main hall of Cheng Zhaofu Ancestral Hall, as well as the eave-protruding beams around the courtyard, are all relief-carved with flowers, phoenixes, red-crowned cranes, flying birds, fish patterns and lions playing with balls. Shaochang Ancestral Hall also has carvings in the same positions: the upper gold purlin beams are symmetrically carved with colored interlocking flowers; the front lower gold purlin beams and eave-protruding beams each have an openwork-carved group of flowers; the openwork-carved fish patterns and flower-and-bird designs on the eave beams are even more exquisite. According to Elder Cheng Gaoming, purlins are generally made round, but to enable carving on them, they are changed to square. The carved part usually requires adding two or even three extra layers of wood boards; the more layers, the more transparent the carving can be.

Others

Sparrow braces, stacked brackets, inserted leaves, beam brackets, beam bracket pads, column brackets and other parts can also become the focus of large wood carvings. Stacked brackets and inserted leaves are a group of mutually perpendicular components located below rice beams, purlins or beams. What supports them can be column brackets above the columns, or beam brackets on shuttle beams. The carving motifs used in these parts are mostly scrolling grass, flowers or abstract meander patterns, sometimes supplemented with auspicious characters.

key_terms.en: Shan beam (eel beam, decorative dragon beam)

sections.name: 小木作装修
sections.content_zh:
二、小木作装修

门、窗

老街上的住宅，正房明间通常有六扇通高并可摘除的门扇，以便在需要的时候，使正堂和明堂在空间上连成一体。除了正房明间以外，余下各间的门窗处理大体相同。每一开间被分为三部分：中间的一扇上面为窗，下面为板；左右两侧上面是高窗，下面为板，其中一侧板的三分之二可以开启为门。整体看起来对比强烈、重点突出，却又疏密有致、匀称均衡。可以说对于老街上大部分的住宅，每间正中的那扇窗就是整幢建筑中最为精美的一件木雕。两侧的高窗一般采用和主窗类似的雕刻主题，但会相对简洁。

以义丰雅记为例，早期住宅的窗子分为上下两屉。下屉窗的位置恰好在视线高度，面积较小，为固定窗。檐廊下常有人走动，做成固定窗，既不会影响房间里的人休息，又不会妨碍檐下的人走路。上屉窗为两扇平推窗，窗下檐高过一般人的头顶。每扇平推窗又会沿水平、垂直、水平方向上依次分格，每次分成比例匀称的小、大、小三部分，并雕以不同的纹饰。整扇窗结构、层次清楚，又重点突出。早期的窗花通常以抽象的几何回纹图案为主，线条匀称、构图大方。类似的回纹构图在附近村落同一时期的住宅里也可以看到。

十九世纪中期以后建造的住宅，上屉平推窗的尺寸在两个方向上都有所减小，三边余下的部分和下屉窗一起组成了一个大的窗套。平推窗本身只沿水平方向做一次划分，窗套的上半部分会再做两次到三次格，成为固定的雕花小窗。从雕饰的题材上来看，含有吉祥寓意的鸟兽、花草、字画，甚至是亭台楼阁等具象图案成为雕刻的主题和重点。这些图案通常位于每个分格的中间部位，四周衬以抽象纹饰。下屉固定窗的面积较大，通常还会嵌上三组这样的图案。用做背景的回纹也变得更为精致、细腻、富有层次，但同时却少了过去的那种朴素之美，略显矫揉造作。

栏板

老街上的早期建筑，可能由于二层原本并不住人，所以二层栏板不做任何雕饰，只是把十多厘米宽的木板竖向排列在栏板的框架之间。清末民初，由于车床的引进，带螺纹的木质栏杆成为一种时尚。对于大户有钱人家，这种千篇一律的机械式加工显然有失水准，所以便出现了手工雕刻的栏板。老街上有两幢中西合璧式木构单体"别墅"，新仁昌旅店和程铿别墅，每一幢都有精美的雕花栏板。这一方面可能是受到了西方建筑装饰的影响，更重要的是这两幢建筑的居住空间都不仅仅局限在一层，所以高层空间也就自然而然地产生了装饰装修的需求。

新仁昌旅店原为四层高单体建筑，现仅剩两层；建筑三开间，雕花栏板位于二层前廊。明间栏板分成三段，每段内有雕花栏板三块，每块约二十五厘米宽、七十厘米高，两块之间的间隔比栏板宽度略小；次间有同样大小的雕花栏板各十块，均匀排列。雕刻的主题大部分以吉祥鸟兽为主，并配以不同的花草，例如狮子、凤凰、仙鹤、鸳鸯、喜鹊、雄鸡等。其中明间正中的一组分别是凤凰、狮子、凤凰，并且两凤凰面面相对。明间栏板的边框处理还和次间略有不同，两侧做竹节状线脚，并且相互间高低错落有致。这二十九块雕花栏板之中，有三块边框的处理手法不同，而且雕的都是姿态相同的白菜，推断是上层的栏板拆下来补缺的。余下的二十六块虽然有的采用相同的主题，但是个个造型独特。

程铿别墅高两层，宽三开间，进深两开间，二层四面有廊。每开间栏板分三组，每组三块；走廊进深这一架也有栏板三块。所有栏板都以回纹为底，镂空雕饰，栏板的宽度根据其所在的位置不同，稍有变化，宽度或位置一样的栏板采用相同的回纹样式。稍宽的栏板在回纹中间嵌雕有宝瓶、仙鹤、月季等图案。
sections.content_en:
2. Small Timber Joinery and Decoration

Doors and Windows

In residences on the old street, the central bay of the main house usually has six full-height removable door leaves, so that when needed, the main hall and the open hall can be spatially integrated. Besides the central bay of the main house, the door and window treatment of the remaining bays is generally the same. Each bay is divided into three parts: the middle one has a window above and a panel below; the left and right sides have high windows above and panels below, with two-thirds of one side panel able to open as a door. Overall it looks strongly contrasting with highlighted focus, yet dense and sparse in harmony, symmetrical and balanced. It can be said that for most residences on the old street, the central window of each bay is the most exquisite wood carving in the entire building. The high windows on both sides generally use similar carving themes as the main window, but relatively simpler.

Taking Yifeng Yaji as an example, the windows of early residences are divided into upper and lower drawers. The lower drawer window is positioned exactly at eye level, with a smaller area, and is a fixed window. People often walk under the eave corridor; making it a fixed window neither affects the rest of people in the room nor hinders people walking under the eaves. The upper drawer window consists of two sliding casement windows, with the lower eave of the window higher than an average person's head. Each sliding casement window is again divided sequentially along horizontal, vertical, and horizontal directions, each time divided into proportionally symmetrical small, large, and small parts, carved with different patterns. The entire window structure has clear layers and highlighted focus. Early window patterns are usually dominated by abstract geometric meander patterns, with symmetrical lines and generous composition. Similar meander compositions can also be seen in residences of the same period in nearby villages.

In residences built after the mid-nineteenth century, the dimensions of the upper sliding casement windows are reduced in both directions, and the remaining parts on three sides together with the lower drawer window form a large window frame. The sliding casement window itself is only divided once along the horizontal direction; the upper part of the window frame is further divided into two to three grids, becoming fixed carved small windows. In terms of carving themes, representational patterns with auspicious meanings such as birds and beasts, flowers and plants, calligraphy and paintings, and even pavilions and towers become the themes and focus of carving. These patterns are usually located in the middle of each grid, surrounded by abstract patterns. The lower drawer fixed window has a larger area, usually embedded with three groups of such patterns. The meander pattern used as the background also becomes more refined, delicate, and layered, but at the same time loses the simple beauty of the past, appearing somewhat contrived.

Railing Panels

In early buildings on the old street, perhaps because the second floor was originally not for living, the second-floor railing panels had no carvings, only vertical arrangement of wooden boards over ten centimeters wide within the railing frame. In the late Qing and early Republican periods, due to the introduction of lathes, threaded wooden railings became fashionable. For wealthy large families, this monotonous mechanical processing was clearly substandard, so hand-carved railing panels appeared. There are two Chinese-Western style single wooden "villas" on the old street, Xinrenchang Inn and Cheng Keng Villa, each with exquisite carved railing panels. On the one hand this may have been influenced by Western architectural decoration; more importantly, the living spaces of both buildings are not limited to the first floor, so the high-level spaces naturally generated a demand for decoration and finishing.

Xinrenchang Inn was originally a four-story single building, now only two stories remain; the building is three bays wide, with carved railing panels on the second-floor front corridor. The central bay railing panel is divided into three sections, each containing three carved railing panels, each about twenty-five centimeters wide and seventy centimeters high, with the gap between two panels slightly smaller than the panel width; the side bays each have ten carved railing panels of the same size, evenly arranged. Most carving themes are auspicious birds and beasts, supplemented with different flowers and plants, such as lions, phoenixes, red-crowned cranes, mandarin ducks, magpies, roosters, etc. Among them, the central group of the middle bay is respectively phoenix, lion, phoenix, with the two phoenixes facing each other. The border treatment of the central bay railing panels is also slightly different from the side bays, with bamboo-joint-shaped moldings on both sides, and mutually staggered heights. Among these twenty-nine carved railing panels, three have different border treatment methods and are all carved with cabbages in the same posture, inferred to be railing panels from the upper floor taken down to fill gaps. The remaining twenty-six panels, although some use the same theme, each has a unique造型.

Cheng Keng Villa is two stories high, three bays wide, two bays deep, with corridors on all four sides of the second floor. Each bay's railing panels are divided into three groups, each group with three panels; the bay along the corridor depth also has three railing panels. All railing panels use meander patterns as the base, with openwork carvings; the width of the railing panels varies slightly according to their location, and panels of the same width or position use the same meander style. Wider railing panels have embedded carvings of treasure vases, red-crowned cranes, Chinese roses and other patterns in the middle of the meander.

sections.name: 砖石雕
sections.content_zh:
三、砖石雕

老街上建筑中的石雕很少，主要用在柱础上。这里的柱础形制比较简单，除了祠堂正堂中间的几个柱础有覆盆之外，其余的皆为鼓形柱础。柱础一般不做雕饰，最多只在上下各做一道线脚。另一处用石雕的地方则在庭院的角落处。以程成昌旅店为例，明堂四角各有一个一尺见方的石板，中间雕成阴阳相间的铜钱纹样，这样雨水就可以从这里流到院落下面的雨水道，再汇入老街两侧的雨水沟，最终流入方岩溪。

砖雕主要应用在马头墙上，还有建筑正立面旁门上，或是小窗上的眉檐。眉檐的做法通常是下面有几排"砖牙子"，然后是仿木构的椽头，上面再加一两皮挑砖，砖上放瓦。"高级"一点的眉檐可以多砌几排"砖牙子"，也可以做两层椽头相叠。程振兴四合院入口上的眉檐，不仅挑了六层"砖牙子"，而且中间还外加收分，整个眉檐还用红、白、黑三色相间描画。

老街上唯一一幢立面上饰有大量砖雕或石雕的建筑是得耕居。得耕居的建造年代较早，采用牌楼式门楼。中间的重檐牌楼为砖砌仿木结构，上面不但用砖堆砌出梁、柱、枋、柱头、柱础、椽头等构件，而且还用砖雕模拟雀替和柱头上的雕饰，甚至是梁枋上的彩画，靠近檐口的部分砖雕还残留有彩绘的印记。砖雕的主题既有一些抽象的花纹，又包括一些精美的鱼纹和鸟兽。最精美的雕饰要属门额上方的"双狮抢球"石雕，门额正中砖刻"得耕居"三字，并在两侧辅以石雕麒麟，下方衬以砖雕花鸟。
sections.content_en:
3. Brick and Stone Carvings

Stone carvings in buildings on the old street are very few, mainly used on column bases. The column bases here are relatively simple in form; except for several column bases in the middle of the ancestral hall main hall which have overturned basins, the rest are all drum-shaped column bases. Column bases generally have no carvings, at most only one molding on the top and bottom each. Another place using stone carvings is at the corners of the courtyard. Taking Cheng Chengchang Inn as an example, each of the four corners of the open hall has a one-chi-square stone slab, with the middle carved into an alternating yin-yang copper coin pattern, so that rainwater can flow from here into the rainwater channel below the courtyard, then into the rainwater ditches on both sides of the old street, and finally into Fangyan Stream.

Brick carvings are mainly applied on horse-head walls, as well as on side doors of building front facades, or on the eyebrow eaves above small windows. The practice of eyebrow eaves is usually several rows of "brick teeth" below, then rafter heads imitating wooden structure, with one or two courses of protruding bricks on top, and tiles placed on the bricks. More "高级" eyebrow eaves can have more rows of "brick teeth" laid, or two layers of overlapping rafter heads. The eyebrow eave above the entrance of Cheng Zhenxing's quadrangle not only protrudes six layers of "brick teeth," but also has additional entasis in the middle, and the entire eyebrow eave is painted with alternating red, white, and black colors.

The only building on the old street whose facade is decorated with a large amount of brick or stone carvings is Degeng Residence. Degeng Residence was built in an earlier period, adopting a paifang-style gatehouse. The central double-eave paifang is a brick-built imitation wooden structure; on it, not only are components such as beams, columns, beams, column heads, column bases, and rafter heads piled up with bricks, but brick carvings are also used to simulate sparrow braces and carvings on column heads, even painted decorations on beams; the brick carvings near the eave still retain traces of colored painting. The themes of brick carvings include both some abstract patterns and some exquisite fish patterns and birds and beasts. The most exquisite carvings are the "double lions grabbing a ball" stone carvings above the door lintel; the center of the door lintel has the three characters "Degeng Residence" carved in brick, flanked by stone-carved qilin on both sides, with brick-carved flowers and birds below.

sections.name: 彩画
sections.content_zh:
四、彩画

彩画通常只位于砖墙上端靠近檐口的位置，并随檐口高低起伏，在青砖墙上形成了一个一尺左右的装饰带。由于风雨的侵蚀，能完整保留至今的彩画很少，老街上保留最完整的彩画要属程振昌旅店里照壁上的挂落式彩画。这套彩画分"三开间"，中间绘有垂莲柱、雀替等建筑构件，每一"开间"分成有韵律一些片段，每段独自为题。彩画的主题包括田园茅舍、鸟兽花草等。色彩以黑白为主，辅以少量的靛青和赭石。
sections.content_en:
4. Painted Decorations

Painted decorations are usually only located at the upper end of brick walls near the eaves, following the ups and downs of the eaves, forming a decorative band of about one chi on the blue brick walls. Due to wind and rain erosion, very few painted decorations have been completely preserved to this day; the most completely preserved painted decoration on the old street is the hanging-falling style painted decoration on the screen wall in Cheng Zhenchang Inn. This set of painted decorations is divided into "three bays," with architectural components such as hanging lotus columns and sparrow braces painted in the middle; each "bay" is divided into rhythmic segments, each segment with its own theme. The themes of the painted decorations include rural thatched cottages, birds, beasts, flowers and plants, etc. The colors are mainly black and white, supplemented by a small amount of indigo and ochre.

chapters.name: 第八章 文化和传统

sections.name: 胡公庙会
sections.content_zh:
一、胡公庙会

历史背景

阴历八九月，刚好是永康一带的农民忙完夏收夏种，而秋收冬种还未开始的农闲季节。恰巧八月十三又是方岩山顶广慈寺护法神胡则的生日。虽然广慈寺里的和尚，还有老街上的许多人都认为胡则的生日是阴历二月二十五，而八月十三这一天仅是胡公"检阅"罗汉班，抑或是被"神化"的日子，但是这个"小小"的分歧并不影响在八九月间方岩山上长达一个多月的胡公庙会。

胡公庙会的重头戏就是"打罗汉"，也称"迎案"或者"胜案"。关于"迎案"和"胜案"的区别，程崇舜老人解释，迎案是指具体的行动，胜案则是对整个过程的统称。"打罗汉"现在演化成以村为单位组织起来的"罗汉班"，以模仿古代军队出征的形式，按旗、棍、刀、叉等顺序排阵游行，并表演各种武术。

关于胡公庙会以及"打罗汉"的来历，允明禅师说，开山祖师正德禅师在的时候就有和尚习武练功，这便是"打罗汉"的由来。胡则在方岩的时候也提倡百姓练武强身。不仅如此，广慈寺最初还出资赞助村里的"打罗汉"活动。当地人则说村里"打罗汉"是从明朝末年开始的。还好这些零碎的信息之间似乎并不矛盾，中间加上一些已知的历史事件做串联，听起来似乎也有理。武举制度经唐朝的初创时期，到宋朝便日趋完善。南宋时期，武举制度更是演变成与进士科举制度相当的一种全国性的系统考试。这种变革进一步激发了民间练武的积极性。婺州地区历史上先后出过两位武状元，其中之一就是在宋光宗绍熙元年（1190年）武科状元东阳人厉仲方。到了明末，浙江地区经常受到倭寇骚扰，再加上当时的军队素质不良，人民深受其害，习武健身便更具有保家卫国的切身目的。老街上的程氏子孙在这期间还出过几个总兵。明末抗倭名将戚继光于嘉靖三十八年（1559年）在义乌成立了以农民和矿工为主的戚家军。这支军队纪律严明，训练精良，屡战屡胜。戚继光独创的"鸳鸯阵"和"打罗汉"还有异曲同工的意味，鸳鸯阵是以十二人为一队，并配以盾、枪、叉、钯、棍、刀等长短兵器，因敌因地变换队形，灵活作战。武举制度的完善，习武健身的传统，再加上保家卫国的需求，到明朝末年，"打罗汉"可能已经成为当地一项普及的民间活动。到了清朝，从县志中可以看出胡公庙会已经颇具规模。

八月十三日，佑顺侯胡公则生辰，各分村落为会，挂大帛为旗，长二三丈，导以鼓乐，从以伞盖，或以纸为马，登方岩。赛神而还。盖一郡香火之盛。未有若此比者。

若方岩香会，旧志不过曰挂帛为长旗，导以鼓乐伞盖而已。今则驾言用胡公卤簿，益以砲械，争道疾驰，各为党伍，其风染于临郡，重茧而至累月不休，其事皆近于兴会豪举。

这寥寥几笔的描写不但生动展示了当时庙会的盛况，而且还揭示了三百多年前胡公庙会的一些重要特点。首先，庙会期间的活动已经发展到以村落为单位。其次，胡公庙会在当时就已经超越了以简单的祭祀或是习武健身为目的的一种形式，而是成为一个集宗教、文化和娱乐为一体的"赛神"会。更重要的是，庙会的影响范围不仅扩大到了相邻的郡县，其过程更是"累月不休"。从康熙三十七年（1698年）《永康县志》中收录的"旧序"中可以知道在这之前的几本县志分别成书于清康熙十一年（1672年）和明万历九年（1581年），也就是说最晚在清初五十年，胡公庙会就已经是一派"挂帛为长旗，导以鼓乐伞盖"的热闹场面了。

作为一种带有宗教色彩的地方文化活动，它的存亡和兴衰既和支撑它的宗教信仰有关，又依赖于承载这个宗教信仰和文化活动的场所，而这三者之间的关系也是相辅相成的。作为建筑和空间的载体，广慈寺并赫灵庙一方面可以依靠与日俱增的香火钱来更好地维护并扩大其自身的建筑和领地；另一方面，修缮一新的大殿和金光灿灿的胡公大帝也能吸引更多远道而来的朝圣者。

据《库川胡氏家谱》记载，从顺治十一年（1654年）到道光二十七年（1847年）的近二百年里，奉胡则为伯祖的库川胡氏后人，先后多次出资帮助广慈寺修理或重建前厅和大殿，有记载的就有七次。库川胡氏不仅会出钱，也会亲自来方岩祭祀他们的伯祖。写于雍正九年（1731年）仲秋望日的《方岩祭说》中提道"八九月间，帜帐蔽道绎如也……他人之事公者且不远数百里，余族至亲且近……于是前辈宗长议以八月诞日拜奠于岩"。在嘉庆十二年（1807年）八月，库川胡氏又与广慈寺签订了《方岩祭礼约》，规定了每年正月、八月在方岩祭祀时的一些细节。在胡公庙会期间的规定包括，"每年八月初一日，住僧到祠请监收油烛，胡宅备酒席如正月初四日例；八月初十日，任事人上岩收油烛，住僧备酒四席仍照旧例；八月十三日秋祭，住僧照例前后迎送"。胡氏家族历来是永康大姓，在地方上也是有钱有势。胡氏家族的介入在客观上进一步扩大了胡公庙会的影响和规模，同时使庙会的性质，在兼有习武健身、宗教、文化和娱乐等功能之后，又加上了祭祖的目的。多种功能的相互交错是胡公庙会不但经久不衰，而且日渐兴旺的重要原因。而兴旺到连年"累月不休"的地步，则必然会形成对住宿、饮食和祭祀用品的需求。当这种需求形成一定规模，就必然会成为促就老街经济模式和发展的必然原因。

准备情况

胡公庙会的准备工作一般从阴历七月就开始了，有的村庄甚至过了正月十五就开始商议筹备。参加筹备的人多是村里德高望重的老人，过去以"族长"或是"祠堂常会"为主。这些人会选一个吉日聚在一起，吃过"拢头酒"后便开始工作。资金的筹集总是第一步。从整个庙会的准备过程到"迎案"当天，前前后后会有不小的花销。在过去，这笔开销主要由村里的祠堂负责，祠堂的收入则主要来自于同族大户人家捐给祠堂的房产、地产和林产。现在这笔开销则要靠"拢头人"挨家挨户筹集。有了钱，就可以请拳师来训练"罗汉班"，除了师傅教的武义外，许多传统的样式多为代代相传。罗汉班通常是一直练到上方岩的前一两天。最后就是准备包括头旗、锣鼓、刀棍、铲子、宝剑、高跷等各式行头道具。由于筹备庙会耗时耗资，所以许多人少力薄的村落并不会年年"迎案"。但是在"迎案"的时间上却有一条不成文的规矩，那就是一旦你选择"迎案"，就要连续迎三年或是三年的倍数。

庙会期间，除了"迎案"之外的另一个重要的内容就是"换香火"。参加庙会的村落，都会有一个用精良木材雕刻的胡公神龛、牌位或龙庭，平时供奉在祠堂或本保庙里。到了农历八月初一就要请出来供奉在祠堂或者罗汉班的练武场，供村民祭拜。练武场一般是因地制宜的利用祠堂前的空场，或晒谷场等。到了约定上方岩的日期，"迎案"的队伍就要背着胡公的牌位上方岩，从胡公殿前的香炉里，掏一把滚烫的香灰放进背着的胡公牌位前的小香炉里，这就叫"换香火"。即使是当年不"迎案"的村子，也会组织一些人抬着胡公的牌位，敲锣打鼓上方岩"换香火"。如果连敲锣打鼓的人都请不起，至少也有大旗和香炉开道。

一些富裕的村落，还会准备几支吹唱班跟随在"迎案"队伍之后。与其说这是"娱神"，不如说这是农民在辛苦了一年之后，一种自娱自乐的表现。正因如此，随着农民生活水平的逐步提高，胡公庙会越办越兴旺。吹唱班表演的曲目多取材于民间故事传说和日常生活，例如十字莲花、十八蝴蝶、十八狐狸、十八罗汉和三十六行等。

庙会过程

胡公庙会正式开始是在八月初一，以胡则出生地胡库村"打罗汉"上方岩作为开端，其他村会在接下来的一个半月里，按照事先约定好的日期陆陆续续上方岩。下文引用了民国乙丑年（1925年）版《方岩指南》中列举的村落"迎案"时间表。

从迎案的时间安排就可以看出，胡公庙会到八月十三日会有一个高潮，而"重阳初八夜"则又是一个小高潮。当地有"八月十三，七十二个胡公上方岩"的说法，意思是说在这天会有七十二个胡公来"换香火"，而这其中绝大多数也是"迎案"的队伍。即使每支队伍平均有一百多人，总共也要七八千人，再加上随行的村民，还有远道而来的香客，总人数至少有两万左右。所以在八月十三日这天，上方岩的山路会拥挤不堪，这就让原本只有一尺多宽的"飞桥"变得更加危险。飞桥后来虽然被屡次加宽到现在的两米多，但是还会被抬着"七十二个胡公"的队伍挤得水泄不通，上下不得。

在各村"迎案"的前几天，村里的罗汉班还要先到附近各村的空场上展示一番，表演拳、刀、棍、叉等各班武义，有的还有叠罗汉和舞狮等，这个沿村表演的过程叫"游案"。"游案"一方面是"迎案"的彩排，同时也向周围的村落展示一下自己的实力。

具体到"迎案"当天的一些细节，村村有异，但大体程序基本相同。在约定好上方岩的前一天晚上，所有参与的人员要沐浴洁身，严格的还要求夫妻不得行房。到了第二天凌晨，要在练武场上向供在这里的小胡公神位举行"祭叉"仪式。全体参与庙会活动的人先用猪、鱼、鸡等供品祭拜胡公；随后便是鞭炮、鼓乐齐鸣，呐喊助威声震耳欲聋；最后罗汉班及吹唱班要在这里先演习一遍。结束以后，大家便回去吃早饭，并带上一些粽子、小麦饼之类的点心准备出发。由于"迎案"的队伍都是当天往返，所以有些路远的村庄在凌晨两三点就上路了。以后塘巷村为例，"迎案"的队伍从前至后依次是举鹅毛旗四人、令字旗一人、抬香案两人、持锣四人、举执事牌四人、挑花烛四人、挑香十人、持开道刀铲两人、举万岁牌一人、背胡公神座一人、掌扇一人、举伞一人及降神童一人，随后才是罗汉班和吹唱班。罗汉班的人数少则四五十人，多则近百，吹唱班也是类似的规模，再加上轮替的人员以及随行的家属和看热闹的人，整个队伍多达几百人。这一队人马浩浩荡荡地来到了方岩山顶上的胡公大殿前。在三响铁铳之后，从村里背上来的胡公神座被放在了大殿前，罗汉们于是在喧闹的锣鼓声中绕大殿顺向跳三圈、再逆向跳三圈，这叫"跳罗汉"。与此同时，降神童会在大殿前的香炉里捧一把香灰放进背来胡公神座前的小香炉里，完成"换香火"的仪式。这些都进行完毕，"迎案"的队伍便原路返回本村，这叫"打回头案"，一直到把村里的胡公神座送回平时存放它的祠堂或本保庙。至此为止，对于这个村庄来讲，胡公庙会才告结束。但是对于岩下老街上的程氏后人，他们在连续一个多月的时间里，每天都会看到几支、甚至几十支这样的队伍从自家的门口经过，不仅如此，他们还要为招待众多来自异乡的香客而忙得不亦乐乎。这或许就是老街上的人从不"打罗汉"的原因吧。

1. Hu Gong Temple Fair

Historical Background

The eighth and ninth lunar months happen to be the slack farming season for farmers in the Yongkang area, after the summer harvest and planting are completed and before the autumn harvest and winter planting begin. Coincidentally, the thirteenth day of the eighth lunar month is also the birthday of Hu Ze, the protective deity of Guangci Temple on the summit of Fangyan Mountain. Although the monks in Guangci Temple and many people on the old street believe that Hu Ze's birthday is the twenty-fifth day of the second lunar month, and that the thirteenth day of the eighth month is merely the day when Hu Gong "reviews" the Luohan troupes or is "deified," this "minor" disagreement does not affect the month-long Hu Gong Temple Fair on Fangyan Mountain during the eighth and ninth months.

The highlight of the Hu Gong Temple Fair is "beating Luohan" (da Luohan), also called "welcoming the case" (ying'an) or "victorious case" (sheng'an). Regarding the difference between "welcoming the case" and "victorious case," Elder Cheng Chongshun explained that "welcoming the case" refers to the specific action, while "victorious case" is the general term for the entire process. "Beating Luohan" has now evolved into "Luohan troupes" organized by village, imitating the form of ancient military expeditions, parading in formation according to the order of flags, staffs, swords, forks, etc., and performing various martial arts.

Regarding the origin of the Hu Gong Temple Fair and "beating Luohan," Master Yunming said that when the founding ancestor Master Zhengde was there, monks already practiced martial arts, which is the origin of "beating Luohan." When Hu Ze was at Fangyan, he also advocated that the people practice martial arts to strengthen their bodies. Moreover, Guangci Temple initially funded and sponsored the village's "beating Luohan" activities. Local people say that village "beating Luohan" began in the late Ming Dynasty. Fortunately, these fragmented pieces of information do not seem contradictory; connecting them with some known historical events in between makes it sound plausible. The military examination system, after its initial establishment in the Tang Dynasty, became increasingly完善 in the Song Dynasty. During the Southern Song period, the military examination system evolved into a nationwide systematic examination equivalent to the civil service examination. This reform further stimulated the enthusiasm of folk martial arts practice. Historically, the Wuzhou area produced two military Zhuangyuan (top scholars), one of whom was Li Zhongfang from Dongyang, the military Zhuangyuan in the first year of Shaoxi of Emperor Guangzong of Song (1190). By the late Ming Dynasty, the Zhejiang area was frequently harassed by Japanese pirates, and coupled with the poor quality of the military at that time, the people suffered greatly; practicing martial arts for fitness thus had a more immediate purpose of defending home and country. The Cheng descendants on the old street produced several commanders-in-chief during this period. The famous late-Ming anti-pirate general Qi Jiguang established the Qi Family Army in Yiwu in the thirty-eighth year of Jiajing (1559), composed mainly of farmers and miners. This army had strict discipline, excellent training, and won every battle. Qi Jiguang's original "Yuanyang Formation" (Mandarin Duck Formation) has similarities with "beating Luohan"; the Yuanyang Formation consists of twelve people per team, equipped with long and short weapons such as shields, spears, forks, tridents, staffs, and swords, changing formations flexibly according to the enemy and terrain. The improvement of the military examination system, the tradition of practicing martial arts for fitness, and the need to defend home and country—by the late Ming Dynasty, "beating Luohan" may have already become a popular folk activity in the area. By the Qing Dynasty, it can be seen from the county annals that the Hu Gong Temple Fair had already reached considerable scale.

On the thirteenth day of the eighth month, the birthday of You Shun Hou Hu Ze, each branch village forms an association, hanging large silk as flags, two to three zhang long, led by drums and music, followed by umbrellas and canopies, or using paper as horses, ascending Fangyan. Competing with the deity and returning. The prosperity of incense in the entire prefecture has never been comparable to this.

As for the Fangyan incense fair, the old annals merely say hanging silk as long flags, led by drums, music, umbrellas and canopies. Now they claim to use Hu Gong's honor guard, adding cannons and weapons, racing on the roads, each forming factions; this custom has spread to neighboring prefectures, people coming with blistered feet for months without rest, all these affairs resemble grand gatherings and heroic displays.

These few lines of description not only vividly show the grand occasion of the temple fair at that time, but also reveal some important characteristics of the Hu Gong Temple Fair over three hundred years ago. First, the activities during the temple fair had already developed to be organized by village. Second, the Hu Gong Temple Fair at that time had already surpassed a form with simple sacrifice or martial arts fitness as its purpose, becoming a "deity-competing" fair integrating religion, culture, and entertainment. More importantly, the influence of the temple fair not only expanded to neighboring counties, but its process was even "months without rest." From the "old preface" included in the Yongkang County Annals of the thirty-seventh year of Kangxi (1698), we can know that the previous county annals were respectively completed in the eleventh year of Kangxi (1672) and the ninth year of Wanli of Ming (1581), meaning that as late as fifty years into the early Qing, the Hu Gong Temple Fair was already a lively scene of "hanging silk as long flags, led by drums, music, umbrellas and canopies."

As a local cultural activity with religious overtones, its survival and rise and fall are related both to the religious belief supporting it and to the place carrying this religious belief and cultural activity, and the relationship among these three is mutually reinforcing. As the carrier of architecture and space, Guangci Temple and Heling Temple can, on the one hand, rely on the ever-increasing incense money to better maintain and expand their own buildings and territory; on the other hand, the newly renovated main hall and the golden Hu Gong Great Emperor can attract more pilgrims coming from afar.

According to the Kuchuan Hu Family Genealogy, in the nearly two hundred years from the eleventh year of Shunzhi (1654) to the twenty-seventh year of Daoguang (1847), the Kuchuan Hu descendants, who regard Hu Ze as their great-uncle ancestor, repeatedly funded the repair or reconstruction of the front hall and main hall of Guangci Temple, with seven recorded instances. The Kuchuan Hu not only contributed money but also personally came to Fangyan to sacrifice to their great-uncle ancestor. The "Fangyan Sacrifice Account" written on the full moon day of the eighth month in the ninth year of Yongzheng (1731) mentions that "in the eighth and ninth months, banners and tents cover the road continuously... others who serve the lord come from hundreds of li away, our clan is close relatives and near... so the elders and clan chiefs agreed to worship at the rock on the August birthday." In the eighth month of the twelfth year of Jiaqing (1807), the Kuchuan Hu again signed the "Fangyan Sacrifice Ritual Agreement" with Guangci Temple, stipulating some details of the annual sacrifices at Fangyan in the first and eighth months. The regulations during the Hu Gong Temple Fair include: "Every year on the first day of the eighth month, the resident monk comes to the ancestral hall to request supervision of oil and candles, and the Hu residence prepares a banquet as on the fourth day of the first month; on the tenth day of the eighth month, the responsible persons go up the rock to collect oil and candles, and the resident monk prepares four tables of wine as usual; on the thirteenth day of the eighth month, the autumn sacrifice, the resident monk greets and sees off as usual." The Hu family has always been a major surname in Yongkang, wealthy and influential locally. The involvement of the Hu family objectively further expanded the influence and scale of the Hu Gong Temple Fair, while adding the purpose of ancestor worship to the temple fair's nature, which already combined martial arts fitness, religion, culture, and entertainment. The interweaving of multiple functions is an important reason why the Hu Gong Temple Fair not only endures but also thrives. And when it prospers to the point of "months without rest" year after year, it inevitably creates demand for accommodation, food, and sacrificial supplies. When this demand reaches a certain scale, it inevitably becomes the inevitable cause promoting the economic model and development of the old street.

Preparation

Preparation for the Hu Gong Temple Fair generally begins in the seventh lunar month; some villages even start discussing preparations after the fifteenth day of the first month. Those participating in preparation are mostly respected elders in the village, in the past mainly "clan chiefs" or "ancestral hall regular meetings." These people choose an auspicious day to gather together, and after drinking the "gathering head wine," they begin work. Fundraising is always the first step. From the entire preparation process to the day of "welcoming the case," there will be considerable expenses before and after. In the past, this expense was mainly borne by the village ancestral hall, whose income mainly came from the real estate, land, and forest products donated to the hall by wealthy families of the same clan. Now this expense relies on the "gathering head person" going door to door to collect. With money, boxing masters can be invited to train the "Luohan troupe"; besides the martial arts taught by the master, many traditional forms are passed down from generation to generation. The Luohan troupe usually practices until a day or two before going up Fangyan. Finally, various props and equipment are prepared, including head flags, gongs and drums, swords and staffs, shovels, treasured swords, stilts, etc. Because preparing for the temple fair is time-consuming and costly, many villages with few people and weak strength do not "welcome the case" every year. But there is an unwritten rule regarding the timing of "welcoming the case": once you choose to "welcome the case," you must do so continuously for three years or a multiple of three.

During the temple fair, another important content besides "welcoming the case" is "changing incense." Villages participating in the temple fair all have a Hu Gong shrine, memorial tablet, or dragon court carved from fine wood, usually enshrined in the ancestral hall or local protection temple. On the first day of the eighth lunar month, it is taken out and enshrined in the ancestral hall or the Luohan troupe's training ground for villagers to worship. The training ground generally makes use of the open space in front of the ancestral hall or a threshing ground according to local conditions. On the agreed date to go up Fangyan, the "welcoming the case" team carries Hu Gong's memorial tablet up Fangyan, and from the incense burner in front of Hu Gong Hall, takes a handful of hot incense ash and puts it into the small incense burner in front of the carried Hu Gong memorial tablet—this is called "changing incense." Even villages that do not "welcome the case" that year will organize some people to carry Hu Gong's memorial tablet, beating gongs and drums, to go up Fangyan to "change incense." If they cannot even afford people to beat gongs and drums, at least there are big flags and incense burners leading the way.

Some wealthy villages also prepare several singing troupes to follow behind the "welcoming the case" team. Rather than saying this is "entertaining the deity," it is better to say it is a form of self-entertainment for farmers after a year of hard work. Precisely because of this, as farmers' living standards gradually improve, the Hu Gong Temple Fair becomes more and more prosperous. The repertoires performed by singing troupes are mostly drawn from folk stories, legends, and daily life, such as Cross Lotus, Eighteen Butterflies, Eighteen Foxes, Eighteen Luohan, and Thirty-six Trades.

Temple Fair Process

The Hu Gong Temple Fair officially begins on the first day of the eighth month, starting with Huku Village (Hu Ze's birthplace) "beating Luohan" going up Fangyan; other villages go up Fangyan one after another over the next month and a half according to pre-agreed dates. The following quotes the village "welcoming the case" schedule listed in the 1925 (Yichou year of the Republic) edition of Fangyan Guide.

From the schedule of welcoming cases, it can be seen that the Hu Gong Temple Fair reaches a climax on the thirteenth day of the eighth month, while "the eighth night of Chongyang" is another minor climax. Locally there is a saying "on the thirteenth of August, seventy-two Hu Gongs go up Fangyan," meaning that on this day seventy-two Hu Gongs come to "change incense," and the vast majority of them are also "welcoming the case" teams. Even if each team averages over a hundred people, the total would be seven to eight thousand; plus accompanying villagers and pilgrims coming from afar, the total number is at least around twenty thousand. So on the thirteenth day of the eighth month, the mountain path up Fangyan becomes extremely crowded, making the originally only one-chi-plus-wide "Flying Bridge" even more dangerous. Although the Flying Bridge was later repeatedly widened to over two meters now, it is still packed solid by teams carrying "seventy-two Hu Gongs," unable to go up or down.

A few days before each village's "welcoming the case," the village's Luohan troupe first goes to the open spaces of nearby villages to perform, demonstrating various martial arts such as boxing, swords, staffs, and forks; some also have human pyramids and lion dances. This process of performing along villages is called "touring the case" (you'an). "Touring the case" is on the one hand a rehearsal for "welcoming the case," and on the other hand demonstrates one's own strength to surrounding villages.

As for the specific details on the day of "welcoming the case," they vary from village to village, but the general procedure is basically the same. On the night before the agreed day to go up Fangyan, all participating personnel must bathe and purify themselves; strict ones also require husbands and wives not to have marital relations. In the early morning of the next day, a "sacrificing forks" ceremony is held at the training ground for the small Hu Gong deity enshrined there. All participants in the temple fair first worship Hu Gong with offerings such as pigs, fish, and chickens; then firecrackers and drums and music sound together, with cheering and shouting deafening; finally the Luohan troupe and singing troupe rehearse once here. After finishing, everyone goes back to eat breakfast and brings some snacks such as zongzi and wheat cakes to prepare for departure. Since "welcoming the case" teams all return the same day, some faraway villages set out at two or three in the morning. Taking Houtangxiang Village as an example, the "welcoming the case" team from front to back is: four people carrying goose-feather flags, one person with a command flag, two people carrying the incense table, four people with gongs, four people carrying ceremonial plates, four people carrying flower candles, ten people carrying incense, two people with path-clearing swords and shovels, one person with a long-life plate, one person carrying Hu Gong's deity seat, one person with a palm fan, one person with an umbrella, and one descending deity child; then come the Luohan troupe and singing troupe. The Luohan troupe numbers from forty to fifty at least to nearly a hundred at most, and the singing troupe is of similar scale; plus rotating personnel, accompanying family members, and onlookers, the entire team numbers several hundred people. This mighty procession arrives at Hu Gong Hall on the summit of Fangyan Mountain. After three volleys of iron cannons, the Hu Gong deity seat carried from the village is placed in front of the main hall, and the Luohan performers then jump three circles clockwise and three circles counterclockwise around the main hall amid the noisy sound of gongs and drums—this is called "jumping Luohan." At the same time, the descending deity child takes a handful of incense ash from the incense burner in front of the main hall and puts it into the small incense burner in front of the carried Hu Gong deity seat, completing the "changing incense" ceremony. After all this is done, the "welcoming the case" team returns to its village by the same route—this is called "beating the returning case"—until the village's Hu Gong deity seat is returned to the ancestral hall or local protection temple where it is normally stored. Up to this point, for this village, the Hu Gong Temple Fair comes to an end. But for the Cheng descendants on Yanxia Old Street, over a continuous period of more than a month, they see several or even dozens of such teams passing by their doors every day; moreover, they are busy entertaining numerous pilgrims from other places. This is perhaps why people on the old street never "beat Luohan."

sections.name: 正月
sections.content_zh:
二、正月

过年

老街上的人家过年，是以"祭灶"揭开序幕的。在江浙地区，关于祭灶的时间有"官三民四船家五"的说法，这也就是为什么在《永康县志》风俗篇里的记载为"十二月二十三日，祭灶"，而当地人却在二十四日"送灶君"。在这天傍晚，家家户户都会在灶台前祭拜灶君，并供上"黏糖"，以保证灶君在玉皇大帝面前只讲好话，不讲坏话，以便带回来年的好运气。

送走了灶王爷，就到了"年头"，又叫"年头禁"。在腊月二十五这一天，"是日不出财。以赤豆和米煮粥，曰蚕花粥云"；不仅如此，还要"洒扫沐浴"。过了二十五以后，每家要选一个好日子来"谢年"，又叫"送年"。谢年是一个以家庭为单位的祭神活动，通常在自家的厅堂里举行，还要准备猪头、鹅、鸡、鱼、豆腐、酒、饭等丰盛的供品。"谢年"由全家的男子参加，在祭拜的同时，大家要相互说一些祝福的话，还要把几天前送走的灶君接回来，请他老人家开始新一年的工作。

除日，即除夕，这天白天要"送年桃，符春帖，蒸饭足新年数日之食"，晚上在团圆饭之后则要全家一起"坐岁"。十二点一过，家家户户都要抢着开门放炮，因为开门最先被视为大吉。新的一年到来之后，老街上的大部分人做的第一件事就是：连夜上方岩山拜胡公、求签。一方面是看看自己在这一年的运气；另一方面也希望无所不能的胡公大帝能保佑自己一家平安，生活美满。

新年这天早上，要吃鸡蛋素面，意味着健康长寿，全家团圆。早上还要有羹，即用青菜、豆腐和米粉等煮成汤；中午要吃粽子，意为"先耕后种"，讨年年有"耕"，年年有"种"的吉利。这小小的细节，再次体现了"得耕"这两个字对老街上程氏后人的深远影响。在早餐过后，就开始一系列的仪式性活动：先是要点香烛，望空而拜，接着就是到祠堂里去"拜太公"，最后是家里人以尊卑长幼为序互拜。自初二开始的四五天里，则是邻里、亲戚互相拜访。

迎龙灯

正月十五是上元节，又称灯节，在这天前后，当地素有"迎花烛"、"迎龙灯"的习俗。这些活动一般以村为单位，临近的几个村则会把时间错开。老街所在的这个小山谷里，按规矩十三日迎花烛，十四日岩下村迎龙灯，十五日橙麓村迎龙灯。

关于迎龙灯的习俗，一些民俗学家把它一直追溯到古越人对水神的一种祭祀活动。他们认为龙灯是龙舟上岸后的一种新的形式，古人通过祭龙娱龙来祈求新一年"风调雨顺，五谷丰登，人丁兴旺"。对于老街上的人，当地话"灯"与"丁"同音，所以"迎龙灯"过程中的许多细节都和"人丁兴旺"、"添丁"的美好希冀密不可分。

老街上迎的龙灯属于"板桥灯"，这种灯的龙头、龙尾各为一节，龙身则是由几十"桥"，甚至一百多"桥"灯首尾相接而成，每桥有两盏"纱灯"。其中龙头和龙尾的做法类似，都是用一块长方形的木板作底，然后用竹篾编成骨架，外裱棉纸；随后上油彩，并辅以龙须、龙珠、龙爪等；最后涂上羊油，这样一方面能显得更为光泽，又能起到防水的作用。支撑龙头用的底板长三四米，宽不到半米，需要四个男青年协力共舞；龙尾则小一些，需要两个人抬。相比起来，龙身的制作则要简单很多。龙身的每一节称作一"桥"，由一个人迎举。所谓的"桥"就是一块一米多长的木板，板上两端各有一个篾扎纸糊，四方八角的彩灯，每盏彩灯上再插上一面写有诸如"五谷丰登"、"风调雨顺"等字样的三角纸糊彩旗。龙头、龙身、龙尾每一桥灯的底板两端都各有一孔，插上"拴灯柱"，就可以把上百桥灯接成长龙。

迎龙灯的准备活动通常从腊月就开始了。负责舞龙头和龙尾通常是一种荣耀，这项工作叫"捻灯"，会优先让给在这一年村里第一个生儿子的人家。由于龙头和龙尾的骨架是要被重复使用的，所以平日就存放在世远公祠厢房的二层。正月初六这天，负责舞龙头和龙尾的人家就要开始着手准备了。他们先要把龙头和龙尾拿到固厚峰东面的"深塘"里去清洗；随后要到方岩山上去砍毛竹，回来请师傅修理破损的骨架；最后重新糊纸、上色、装点龙珠等。仅仅这些工作还不够，这家人还要负责请人舞龙头、举迎牌、作领灯、司敲锣打鼓等工作，外加准备迎龙灯当天的食物、烟酒，开销可是不菲。所以，即便是件荣耀喜庆的事，也不是每个家庭都能负担得起的。如果这个家庭选择不做，就会轮到村里这一年第二个生儿子的人家，以此类推，直到有一家决定承担这项工作为止。对于轮到又选择不做的人家，就要负责出十桥灯；如果做这个也有负担，则要做一些麻酥分给当天舞灯的人吃。对于村里其他的人家，几乎每家每户都要出至少一桥灯，或者准备些点心。

正月十四日早上七点开始，负责捻灯的人家会找两个人，敲着大锣，走遍老街的每一个角落，这叫"催灯"。催灯一般上午要三四次，下午又要三四次。下午三点的时候，在得耕居内会有为晚上舞灯的人准备好的饭菜。晚饭后夜幕降临，各家各户开始放鞭炮，并举行点灯仪式。这里的规矩是"红灯出，红灯入"，家家户户点好的一桥桥的龙灯，从老街上的各个角落出发，纷纷向得耕居前的空场上聚集，开始"接灯"。得耕居前爆竹声震耳欲聋，陆陆续续到达的部分桥灯依次和龙头接好，在"接灯"的同时，龙灯已经在空场上转上了三小圈。随即龙灯在举迎牌的、吹喇叭的、敲锣的和领灯人的引导下，走向蜥蜴山前山头上的朱公位。朱公位后有一棵大柏树，龙灯会绕着朱公位和大柏树转几圈，并向朱公磕头。下山的时候还会在八世祖程濂，即松门公墓前拜一下。后两圈比较小，基本上就是绕着空场和澈月塘转。龙灯每次回到得耕居前，就会有更多的桥灯顺次接上，到第三圈结束的时候，龙尾才会最终出现。于是，接好的龙灯在众人的簇拥下和震耳的锣号声中开始游街。由于整个游街过程长达十多个小时，所以每个舞灯手都要有另一个人随行以备轮换。这些人，再加上围观的乡亲，组成了一支几百人浩浩荡荡的队伍。

龙灯首先沿老街向北行进，沿街的家家户户都会在门前挂纱灯，放鞭炮，摆好香烛、猪肉、鸡肉等供品迎接龙灯，龙头也会进到家里去磕头"讨彩"。讨来的钱会归总到一起，再统一发给参与迎龙灯的人家。当龙灯行进到位于下胡坑坑口的经堂前，不能进去打扰菩萨，但是会在外面"跳灯"，所谓跳灯就是龙头要往前走，龙尾却偏要往后拉，这样来来去去要反复几次，直到大家都精疲力竭了才罢休。随后龙灯会沿着老街一直走到橙麓村北，象鼻岗山脚的程氏总祠。这时龙头会被抬进祠堂摆放在大厅中间，由领香的人代为上香，祭拜程氏先祖。迎龙灯的队伍在祠堂前稍事休息后会向西进入寿山坑，并沿方岩山北面的山路上山。上山的时候，已经是深夜了，几百桥龙灯蜿蜒近一里，纱灯里的烛火可以照亮整个方岩山。走到天门的时候，广慈寺的住持已经身着袈裟、手持法杖，带领众僧在这里迎候。龙灯被迎到寺院里，这里早就备好茶点、糖果以招待舞灯的人，寺里的和尚还会把没有烧完的蜡烛分给大家。休息片刻，龙灯便再次起程，从前山下山。下山的路十分难走，最陡峭的一段是飞桥，还不到一米宽，所以在下山以后，迎龙灯的队伍要在山门处吃茶点、小憩。随后龙灯再次进村，并分别到世远公祠和绍常祠堂里拜祭，最后龙灯来到绍常祠堂前的空场上。这时天色已经微明，舞灯的人们在这里再做最后一次休息后，以备迎龙灯活动的高潮，即"盘龙灯"，也称"团龙灯"。盘龙灯一开始，龙头便以圆形路线向内盘旋，直到龙头被几圈桥灯团团围在中间。这时，龙头要设法逃出重围，而龙尾又要带领几百桥龙身尽力阻拦，这叫"翻龙灯"。"翻龙灯"会反反复复进行许多次，这期间舞灯者还会轮换休息，直到大家都筋疲力尽。这时绍常祠堂的管事会出来"讲好话"，在管事的好言劝说下，龙尾终于让龙头翻出重围。

当龙灯再次回到得耕居前的时候，天已经大亮了。龙灯被一桥桥的拆开，换上新的蜡烛之后，桥灯便在鞭炮声中被村民们纷纷迎回了家。最后，龙头上的"珠灯"要取下来，送给村里的新婚夫妇，或是想要儿子的人家，这叫"送灯"。由于"送灯"暗含着"送丁"的吉祥祝福，所以收到珠灯的人家要准备好红包。每年龙头上会有多少珠灯也是要提前计算好的，以保证每个想要儿子的人家都能得到祝福。到此为止，长达十几个小时的迎龙灯活动在正月十五日的早上终于结束了。人们在吉祥和喜庆的氛围下，新一年的各项工作便陆陆续续开始了。正如老街上的俗话，"灯过年过，牛归牛栏，马归马舍"。
sections.content_en:
2. First Lunar Month

New Year

Families on the old street begin the New Year with "sacrificing to the stove god." In the Jiangsu-Zhejiang region, regarding the time of stove god sacrifice, there is a saying "officials on the third, commoners on the fourth, boatmen on the fifth," which is why the Yongkang County Annals customs chapter records "on the twenty-third day of the twelfth month, sacrifice to the stove," while local people "send off the stove god" on the twenty-fourth. On this evening, every family worships the stove god in front of the stove, offering "sticky candy" to ensure that the stove god only speaks good words and not bad words before the Jade Emperor, so as to bring back good luck for the coming year.

After sending off the stove god, comes the "year head," also called "year head prohibition." On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, "on this day no wealth is spent. Red beans and rice are cooked into porridge, called silkworm flower porridge"; moreover, one must "sweep and bathe." After the twenty-fifth, each family chooses an auspicious day to "thank the year," also called "sending the year." Thanking the year is a family-based deity sacrifice activity, usually held in one's own hall, with abundant offerings such as pig head, goose, chicken, fish, tofu, wine, and rice prepared. "Thanking the year" is attended by all the men of the family; while worshipping, everyone says some blessing words to each other, and also brings back the stove god sent away a few days ago, asking the old gentleman to begin a new year of work.

On New Year's Eve, during the day one must "send New Year peaches, paste spring couplets, steam enough rice for several days of the New Year"; in the evening after the reunion dinner, the whole family must "sit through the year" together. After twelve o'clock, every family rushes to open the door and set off firecrackers, because opening the door first is considered great fortune. After the new year arrives, the first thing most people on the old street do is: go up Fangyan Mountain overnight to worship Hu Gong and draw divination sticks. On the one hand, to see their luck for this year; on the other hand, they hope the omnipotent Hu Gong Great Emperor will bless their family with peace and a happy life.

On New Year's morning, one eats egg plain noodles, meaning health, longevity, and family reunion. In the morning there is also soup, made from green vegetables, tofu, and rice flour; at noon one eats zongzi, meaning "first plow then plant," seeking the auspiciousness of having "plowing" and "planting" every year. This small detail once again reflects the profound influence of the two characters "Degeng" (obtaining plowing) on the Cheng descendants on the old street. After breakfast, a series of ritual activities begins: first lighting incense and candles, bowing toward the sky, then going to the ancestral hall to "worship the great ancestor," and finally family members bowing to each other in order of seniority. From the second day for four or five days, neighbors and relatives visit each other.

Welcoming the Dragon Lantern

The fifteenth day of the first lunar month is the Shangyuan Festival, also called the Lantern Festival. Around this day, locally there are customs of "welcoming flower candles" and "welcoming the dragon lantern." These activities are generally organized by village, with nearby villages staggering their times. In the small valley where the old street is located, by custom the thirteenth day welcomes flower candles, the fourteenth day Yanxia Village welcomes the dragon lantern, and the fifteenth day Chenglu Village welcomes the dragon lantern.

Regarding the custom of welcoming the dragon lantern, some folklorists trace it all the way back to a sacrificial activity of the ancient Yue people to the water deity. They believe the dragon lantern is a new form after the dragon boat comes ashore; ancient people sacrificed to and entertained the dragon to pray for "favorable weather, abundant harvests, and prosperous population" in the new year. For people on the old street, in the local dialect "lantern" (deng) and "male child" (ding) are homophones, so many details in the process of "welcoming the dragon lantern" are inseparable from the beautiful hopes of "prosperous population" and "adding a male child."

The dragon lantern welcomed on the old street belongs to the "board bridge lantern" type; the dragon head and dragon tail of this lantern are each one section, while the dragon body is formed by dozens or even over a hundred "bridge" lanterns connected end to end, each bridge having two "gauze lanterns." The dragon head and dragon tail are made similarly: both use a rectangular wooden board as the base, then bamboo strips are woven into a skeleton, pasted with cotton paper on the outside; then painted with oil colors, supplemented with dragon whiskers, dragon pearls, dragon claws, etc.; finally coated with sheep oil, which on the one hand makes it more glossy and on the other hand serves as waterproofing. The base board supporting the dragon head is three to four meters long and less than half a meter wide, requiring four young men to dance together; the dragon tail is smaller, requiring two people to carry. In comparison, the making of the dragon body is much simpler. Each section of the dragon body is called a "bridge," held up by one person. The so-called "bridge" is a wooden board over one meter long, with a bamboo-framed paper-pasted square octagonal colored lantern at each end of the board; each colored lantern has a triangular paper-pasted colorful flag inserted on top, with inscriptions such as "abundant harvests" and "favorable weather." The base boards of each bridge lantern of the dragon head, body, and tail each have a hole at both ends; inserting "lantern-connecting posts" allows hundreds of bridge lanterns to be connected into a long dragon.

Preparation for welcoming the dragon lantern usually begins in the twelfth lunar month. Being responsible for dancing the dragon head and tail is usually an honor; this work is called "niandeng" (twisting the lantern), and is优先 given to the family that had the first son born in the village that year. Since the skeletons of the dragon head and tail are to be reused, they are normally stored on the second floor of the wing room of Shiyuan Gong Hall. On the sixth day of the first lunar month, the family responsible for dancing the dragon head and tail begins preparations. They first take the dragon head and tail to the "Deep Pond" east of Guhou Peak for cleaning; then go to Fangyan Mountain to cut moso bamboo, and upon return ask a master to repair the damaged skeleton; finally re-paste paper, color, and decorate with dragon pearls etc. This work alone is not enough; the family must also be responsible for hiring people to dance the dragon head, hold welcome plaques, serve as lead lantern, beat gongs and drums, plus prepare food, tobacco and alcohol for the day of welcoming the dragon lantern—the expenses are considerable. So even though it is an honorous and festive matter, not every family can afford it. If this family chooses not to do it, it passes to the family that had the second son born in the village that year, and so on, until one family decides to undertake the work. For families whose turn it is but choose not to do it, they must be responsible for providing ten bridge lanterns; if even this is a burden, they must make some sesame cakes to distribute to the people dancing lanterns that day. For other families in the village, almost every household must provide at least one bridge lantern or prepare some snacks.

Starting at seven in the morning on the fourteenth day of the first lunar month, the family responsible for niandeng finds two people to beat a large gong and walk through every corner of the old street—this is called "urging the lantern." Urging the lantern generally happens three or four times in the morning and three or four times in the afternoon. At three in the afternoon, meals prepared for the evening lantern dancers are served inside Degeng Residence. After dinner as night falls, every household sets off firecrackers and holds a lantern-lighting ceremony. The rule here is "red lantern out, red lantern in"; the bridge-by-bridge dragon lanterns lit by every household set out from various corners of the old street, gathering one after another at the open space in front of Degeng Residence to begin "connecting lanterns." The sound of firecrackers in front of Degeng Residence is deafening; the bridge lanterns arriving one after another are connected to the dragon head in sequence, and while "connecting lanterns," the dragon lantern has already made three small circles in the open space. Then the dragon lantern, guided by those holding welcome plaques, blowing trumpets, beating gongs, and the lead lantern person, heads toward Zhu Gong's position on the front hilltop of Lizard Mountain. Behind Zhu Gong's position is a large cypress tree; the dragon lantern circles around Zhu Gong's position and the large cypress tree several times, and kowtows to Zhu Gong. When going down the mountain, it also pays respects at the tomb of the eighth-generation ancestor Cheng Lian, i.e. Songmen Gong. The latter two circles are smaller, basically circling around the open space and Cheyue Pond. Each time the dragon lantern returns to in front of Degeng Residence, more bridge lanterns are connected in sequence; by the end of the third circle, the dragon tail finally appears. Then the connected dragon lantern, surrounded by the crowd and amid deafening gongs and trumpets, begins parading through the streets. Since the entire parade process lasts over ten hours, each lantern dancer must have another person accompanying for rotation. These people, plus the watching villagers, form a mighty team of several hundred people.

The dragon lantern first travels north along the old street; every household along the street hangs gauze lanterns in front of their doors, sets off firecrackers, and arranges offerings such as incense, candles, pork, and chicken to welcome the dragon lantern; the dragon head also enters homes to kowtow and "seek fortune." The money sought is collected together and then distributed uniformly to families participating in welcoming the dragon lantern. When the dragon lantern reaches the front of the Jingtang (scripture hall) at the mouth of Xiahu Pit, it cannot enter to disturb the Bodhisattva, but will "jump lantern" outside; so-called jumping lantern means the dragon head wants to go forward while the dragon tail insists on pulling backward, going back and forth repeatedly several times until everyone is exhausted. Then the dragon lantern travels along the old street all the way to the Cheng Clan General Ancestral Hall north of Chenglu Village, at the foot of Xiangbi Hill. At this time the dragon head is carried into the ancestral hall and placed in the middle of the main hall, with the lead-incense person burning incense on its behalf to worship the Cheng ancestors. After a brief rest in front of the ancestral hall, the dragon lantern welcoming team heads west into Shoushan Pit and climbs the mountain along the path on the north side of Fangyan Mountain. By the time of climbing, it is already deep night; hundreds of bridge dragon lanterns wind for nearly one li, and the candle flames in the gauze lanterns can illuminate the entire Fangyan Mountain. When reaching the Heavenly Gate, the abbot of Guangci Temple, already in kasaya robe and holding a staff, leads the monks to welcome here. The dragon lantern is welcomed into the temple, where tea, snacks, and candies have long been prepared to entertain the lantern dancers; the monks in the temple also distribute unburned candles to everyone. After a brief rest, the dragon lantern sets off again, descending from the front mountain. The descent path is very difficult; the steepest section is the Flying Bridge, less than one meter wide, so after descending, the dragon lantern team has tea and snacks and a brief rest at the mountain gate. Then the dragon lantern enters the village again, and respectively goes to Shiyuan Gong Hall and Shaochang Ancestral Hall to worship; finally the dragon lantern comes to the open space in front of Shaochang Ancestral Hall. By this time the sky is already faintly bright; the lantern dancers take one final rest here, preparing for the climax of the dragon lantern welcoming activity, namely "coiling the dragon lantern," also called "grouping the dragon lantern." At the start of coiling the dragon lantern, the dragon head spirals inward in a circular path until the dragon head is surrounded by several circles of bridge lanterns. At this point, the dragon head tries to escape the encirclement, while the dragon tail leads hundreds of bridge dragon bodies to尽力 block—this is called "flipping the dragon lantern." "Flipping the dragon lantern" is repeated many times, during which lantern dancers rotate to rest until everyone is exhausted. At this time the steward of Shaochang Ancestral Hall comes out to "speak good words"; under the steward's kind persuasion, the dragon tail finally lets the dragon head flip out of the encirclement.

When the dragon lantern returns to in front of Degeng Residence again, it is already broad daylight. The dragon lantern is disassembled bridge by bridge; after replacing with new candles, the bridge lanterns are welcomed back home by villagers amid the sound of firecrackers. Finally, the "pearl lanterns" on the dragon head are taken down and given to newlywed couples in the village, or families wanting a son—this is called "sending lanterns." Since "sending lanterns" implicitly contains the auspicious blessing of "sending a male child," families receiving pearl lanterns must prepare red envelopes. How many pearl lanterns will be on the dragon head each year is also calculated in advance to ensure that every family wanting a son can receive the blessing. Up to this point, the over-ten-hour dragon lantern welcoming activity finally ends on the morning of the fifteenth day of the first lunar month. Amid an atmosphere of auspiciousness and festivity, the various tasks of the new year begin one after another. As the saying on the old street goes, "when the lantern festival passes, the ox returns to the ox pen, the horse returns to the horse stable."
