sections.name: 祭祖
sections.content_zh:
三、祭祖

对祖先的祭祀活动一直是中国民众社会生活的重要组成部分，同时也是一种最淳朴的宗教意识的体现。人们通过一系列的丧葬仪式来安抚死者的灵魂，使他们能够顺利地进入另一个世界，并在那里安逸舒适的"生活"。仅仅这样还不够，人们还要借助定期供奉食物、送钱、送衣物的形式和祖先保持联系，祈求祖先保佑整个家族人丁兴旺，财源茂盛，五谷丰登。在一年中众多的节日里，有三个节日被认为是"阴间的节日"。在这三天里，村里都有或大或小的祭祖活动。

清明

祭祖仪式最隆重的要属清明，即每年的四月初。在清明的前三天、后四天，村里的人要到各房的祖坟上去祭扫，添土和"标青"，"标青"即是在坟前挂白纸。祭祀用的食物通常包括猪头、鹅、豆腐、糕、大麦面、金团和清明果等，其中以清明果最有特色。清明果有红、白、青三种，它是用糯米做皮，红糖或白糖做馅的点心。磨好的糯米直接用的话就可以做出白色的清明果；如果加入野菜汁（野蒿），就可以做成青色的；红色的则是加入了食用颜料。和其他地方不同的是，当地的清明果是借用馃印压制成的。金团类似于清明果，只是用豆腐、粉丝、青菜和猪肉做馅。

祭祀的过程是由在场的辈分最大的人主持，主持人通过高喊"通"和"引"来指挥其余的人。"通"是让大家准备好一起做事，而"引"则是让某个人前去祭拜。整个祭祀的程序大致包括拈香、点烛、跪拜、奠酒、进汤、献饭、读祝文和焚祝文，其中在焚祝文的同时还会打锣、吹号和放鞭炮。祭祀结束之后所有的人会在一起席地围坐吃午餐，又名"散清"。

岩下老街的程姓人中，如今多数是十五世毅庵公的后人。据民国33年（1944年）《程氏天房谱》记载，毅庵"葬四十二都小墟塘龟山墳前墈下"，距岩下村35里，现属舟山镇。因为距离远，坐轿子单程要走三四个小时，再加上开销大（雇轿子的费用由个人出一半，祖上出一半），所以每年去的人不多，一般也只有四五十人左右。能去的人多来自地位较高和家境较好的人家，而且妇女和外姓人也可以去。已经年过古稀的程镇康老先生回忆说，他小时候随父亲去过舟山两次祭祖。让他印象最深的就是：经过的村庄都会觉得这四五十顶轿子组成的队伍很是威风。这在客观上也是对岩下程氏的一种宣传，使邻村的姑娘都愿意嫁到这样的望族。这或许也是岩下程氏在近二三百年来人丁兴旺，并且能够一直保持这样一个单姓血缘村落的原因。程毅庵的夫人被子孙们尊称为"太婆"。因为她葬在较近的金龙江，每年清明去的人就较多。

村里的一部分人还会到下胡坑里作勳公的坟地去"拜天官"。作勳公是岩下程氏第十三世上的人，岩上村的作勳公祠也是以他命名的。他之所以受到如此尊敬，是因为他"性情敦朴，节俭持躬，铢积寸累以成家业。而资雄里闬，每遇岁歉必出粟赈饥，凡有求者缓急靡不相济。人皆德之"。

在清明那天，村里的几个祠堂会打开祠堂门，挂起祖宗像，摆上猪头、鹅、豆腐等供品，等待子孙们的祭拜。比起那些有钱有地位的人，村里那些穷苦的程氏后人就只能在清明那天到祠堂里去拜拜祖宗，期待着可以分到的那点供品。现住在作勳公祠里，74岁的程茂发老人讲：他在十六岁以后就可以去祠堂祭祖，并且他有三个祠堂可以去。他可以从村里人人都有份的世远公祠和一部分人有份的作勳公祠里各领到一斤饭、两片肉和两片豆腐；他还能从本房的，一个在几家人中轮换管理的"祠堂"里领到一点钱。

1995年，永康程氏第一到第四世祖的墓被统一移到了离村子三里的北政岭。自此，遍布永康地区十七个村的程氏后人开始在清明期间进行联合祭祖。祭祖的活动由十七个村庄的程氏轮流主持，通常情况下是由村里老年协会的主席带头组织。

冬至

冬至是另外一个祭祀祖先的重要时间。不同于清明时期的宗族集体祭祖，冬至主要是以家庭为单位进行小型的祭祖活动，祭拜的对象通常也仅限于自家前四代的祖宗。在清光绪编《永康县志》中提道"旧家大族四时祭于祖庙，而冬至祭最重"。或许是因为"冬至祭最重"，所以住在岩下老街的程氏后人在"四时"之中只保留了冬至祭祖的习俗。当地人称冬至为"下世人过年"。在岩下老街和橙麓村里，关于冬至祭祖的时间有两种说法：一种说法是在冬至的当天祭祖；另一种说法则认为要在冬至的前三天或后四天中的一天中祭祖。但是他们祭祖的形式都是相似的。每一家都要做"羹饭"，在厅堂里摆供品以招待先祖。据程崇舜老人讲，冬至祭祖的"羹饭"要比其他日子里的多一些点心。

祭祀过程多在午饭之前，有的人家还会放鞭炮。岩下街79号的程镇康家每年都在冬至这天祭祖，2008年冬至这天他家的供桌上摆了猪肉、煎豆腐、鸡蛋、自家种的橘子和用糯米做皮，豆腐、粉丝、猪肉和青菜做馅的团子。这些供品放在桌子中间，旁边整整齐齐的摆放了九副碗筷和酒杯。在靠近明堂一侧的桌子上有两个烛台和两束各三支的香。在一切都准备好以后，程家的女主人，即程镇康的夫人，拿着一束香到院门口拜三拜请祖宗们回家。如果这时外面正好有人的话，大家都会自觉地让开门口。等祖宗们"落座"之后，程家的儿子要给每个祖宗敬三次酒，酒是用自家酿的上好黄酒。随后，家里的人开始在院子里一起给祖宗烧些纸钱和纸银锭。最后，程家的女主人要拿着另一束香，走到门口再拜三拜送祖宗们回去，然后关上院门。在整个祭祀过程结束之后，供桌上的部分美味就成了当日午餐的一部分。

中元

第三个祭祖的日子是在阴历七月十五的中元节，也称鬼节。在这一天里，家家户户也要做"羹饭"来盛筵祖先。但是不同于另外两个节日的是，在这一天，短命的和没有后代的孤魂野鬼也可以享受到祭祀。正如县志里说："中元，荐祖考、祀孤"。所以这里有些善良的人家会在祭祖之后，用篮子带上一些供品，到村庄外的路口或者空地上进行野祭，俗称"路头羹饭"。更有富裕的人家会结队去寺院或是祠堂去"拜星"，以超度饿鬼和死囚。这一切都是为了能让自己的祖先安心地享受儿孙们孝敬的香烛、食物和钱财，而不会被那些受不到祭祀的孤魂野鬼骚扰。
sections.content_en:
3. Ancestor Worship

Ancestor worship activities have always been an important part of Chinese people's social life, and at the same time a manifestation of the simplest religious consciousness. Through a series of funeral rituals, people appease the souls of the dead, enabling them to smoothly enter another world and live comfortably there. This alone is not enough; people also maintain contact with ancestors through regular offerings of food, money, and clothing, praying that ancestors will bless the entire family with prosperous population, flourishing wealth, and abundant harvests. Among the many festivals in a year, three are considered "festivals of the underworld." On these three days, there are ancestor worship activities of varying sizes in the village.

Qingming (Pure Brightness)

The most solemn ancestor worship ceremony is Qingming, at the beginning of April each year. Three days before and four days after Qingming, villagers go to the ancestral graves of each branch to sweep, add soil, and "mark green" (biaoqing), which means hanging white paper in front of the grave. Food for sacrifice usually includes pig head, goose, tofu, cakes, barley flour, golden dumplings, and Qingming fruit, among which Qingming fruit is the most distinctive. Qingming fruit comes in red, white, and green; it is a pastry made with glutinous rice as the skin and brown or white sugar as the filling. Directly using ground glutinous rice makes white Qingming fruit; adding wild vegetable juice (wild mugwort) makes green; red is made by adding food coloring. Unlike other places, local Qingming fruit is pressed using a guo (cake) mold. Golden dumplings are similar to Qingming fruit, but filled with tofu, vermicelli, green vegetables, and pork.

The sacrifice process is presided over by the person of the highest generation present; the presider commands the others by shouting "tong" (connect) and "yin" (guide). "Tong" means everyone prepares to do things together, while "yin" means a certain person goes forward to worship. The entire sacrifice procedure roughly includes lighting incense, lighting candles, kneeling and bowing, pouring libation wine, offering soup, offering rice, reading the prayer text, and burning the prayer text; during the burning of the prayer text, gongs are beaten, horns blown, and firecrackers set off. After the sacrifice, all people sit together on the ground in a circle for lunch, also called "sanqing" (scattering Qingming).

Among the Cheng surnamed people on Yanxia Old Street, most today are descendants of the fifteenth-generation Yi'an Gong. According to the Cheng Family Tian Branch Genealogy of the 33rd year of the Republic (1944), Yi'an "was buried at the front slope of Turtle Mountain, Xiaoxu Pond, Forty-second Du," 35 li from Yanxia Village, now belonging to Zhoushan Town. Because of the distance, taking a sedan chair takes three to four hours one way, plus high expenses (sedan chair costs are borne half by the individual and half by the ancestors), so not many people go each year, generally only about forty to fifty. Those who can go mostly come from families of higher status and better circumstances, and women and people of other surnames can also go. The over-seventy-year-old Elder Cheng Zhenkang recalled that when he was young he went to Zhoushan twice with his father for ancestor worship. What impressed him most was that villages passed by would find the procession of forty to fifty sedan chairs very imposing. Objectively this was also a kind of publicity for the Yanxia Cheng, making girls from neighboring villages willing to marry into such a prominent clan. This is perhaps why the Yanxia Cheng have had a prosperous population for the past two to three hundred years and have been able to maintain such a single-surname blood-relation village. Cheng Yi'an's wife is respectfully called "Grandma" by descendants. Because she was buried in the closer Jinlong River, more people go there each Qingming.

Some people in the village also go to Zuoxun Gong's grave in Xiahu Pit to "worship the heavenly official." Zuoxun Gong was a person of the thirteenth generation of the Yanxia Cheng; the Zuoxun Gong Hall in Yanshang Village is also named after him. The reason he is so respected is because he "was simple and honest in disposition, thrifty in personal conduct, accumulating bit by bit to establish his family. With wealth prominent in the neighborhood, every year of famine he would certainly give grain to relieve hunger, and anyone seeking help in urgency was never refused. All people praised his virtue."

On Qingming day, several ancestral halls in the village open their doors, hang ancestor portraits, and arrange offerings such as pig head, goose, and tofu, waiting for descendants to worship. Compared with those wealthy and prestigious people, the poor Cheng descendants in the village can only go to the ancestral hall on Qingming day to worship their ancestors, hoping for a share of the offerings. Elder Cheng Maofa, 74, who now lives in Zuoxun Gong Hall, said: after he turned sixteen he could go to the ancestral hall for ancestor worship, and he had three ancestral halls to go to. He could each receive one jin of rice, two slices of meat, and two slices of tofu from Shiyuan Gong Hall (which everyone in the village has a share in) and Zuoxun Gong Hall (which some people have a share in); he could also receive a little money from his own branch's "ancestral hall," which is managed in rotation among several families.

In 1995, the graves of the first to fourth-generation ancestors of the Yongkang Cheng were uniformly moved to Beizheng Ridge, three li from the village. Since then, Cheng descendants spread across seventeen villages in the Yongkang area have begun joint ancestor worship during Qingming. The ancestor worship activity is hosted in rotation by the Cheng of the seventeen villages, usually organized under the leadership of the village elderly association chairman.

Winter Solstice

Winter Solstice is another important time for ancestor worship. Unlike the clan collective ancestor worship of Qingming, Winter Solstice mainly involves small-scale ancestor worship activities by family unit, and the objects of worship are usually limited to the previous four generations of one's own ancestors. The Qing Guangxu edition of Yongkang County Annals mentions that "old prominent families sacrifice at the ancestral temple in all four seasons, but the Winter Solstice sacrifice is the most important." Perhaps because "the Winter Solstice sacrifice is the most important," the Cheng descendants living on Yanxia Old Street have only retained the Winter Solstice ancestor worship custom among the "four seasons." Locals call Winter Solstice "the lower world people's New Year." In Yanxia Old Street and Chenglu Village, there are two说法 about the timing of Winter Solstice ancestor worship: one says to worship on the day of Winter Solstice; the other says to worship on one of the three days before or four days after Winter Solstice. But their forms of ancestor worship are similar. Every family makes "soup rice" (gengfan), arranging offerings in the hall to entertain ancestors. According to Elder Cheng Chongshun, the "soup rice" for Winter Solstice ancestor worship has more pastries than on other days.

The sacrifice process mostly takes place before lunch, and some families also set off firecrackers. The Cheng Zhenkang family at No. 79 Yanxia Street worships ancestors every Winter Solstice; on Winter Solstice 2008, their offering table had pork, fried tofu, eggs, homegrown oranges, and dumplings made with glutinous rice skin and tofu, vermicelli, pork, and green vegetable filling. These offerings were placed in the middle of the table, with nine sets of bowls, chopsticks, and wine cups neatly arranged beside. On the side of the table near the open hall were two candlesticks and two bundles of three incense sticks each. After everything was prepared, the mistress of the Cheng family, Cheng Zhenkang's wife, took a bundle of incense and bowed three times at the courtyard gate to invite the ancestors home. If there happened to be people outside at this time, everyone would voluntarily step aside from the doorway. After the ancestors "took their seats," the Cheng son poured wine three times for each ancestor, using fine homemade yellow rice wine. Then the family members burned paper money and paper silver ingots for the ancestors together in the courtyard. Finally, the mistress took another bundle of incense, went to the door and bowed three times to send the ancestors back, then closed the courtyard gate. After the entire sacrifice process ended, part of the delicacies on the offering table became part of that day's lunch.

Zhongyuan (Ghost Festival)

The third ancestor worship day is the Zhongyuan Festival on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month, also called Ghost Festival. On this day, every family also makes "soup rice" to feast ancestors. But unlike the other two festivals, on this day, short-lived and descendantless wandering ghosts can also enjoy sacrifice. As the county annals say: "Zhongyuan, offer to ancestors, sacrifice to the lonely." So some kind families here, after ancestor worship, take some offerings in a basket to the crossroads or open spaces outside the village for wild sacrifice, commonly called "roadhead soup rice." Wealthier families go in groups to temples or ancestral halls to "worship stars," to超度 hungry ghosts and condemned prisoners. All this is to enable one's own ancestors to peacefully enjoy the incense, candles, food, and money offered by descendants, without being harassed by those wandering ghosts who receive no sacrifice.

sections.name: 分家
sections.content_zh:
四、分家

分家主要有两种方法，一种是当家里的长辈年迈或去世后，儿子们相互分家，有时也可能是长孙和叔叔们分家。在这种情况下，分家的主持人一般由家族中有威望的人来担当，更重要的是要请娘舅和姑父来作证，找会写字的人来执笔写分家契。分家的第一步是要把属于大家庭的家产和财务情况做登记。对于一般的人家，分家主要只涉及房产和地产。在分房产的时候，如果全家只有一个宅院，院里的厅堂或称西间，会留作公用，用以举行红白喜事。在西间东侧的叫上大房，会分给长子；西间西侧的叫下大房，会分给次子；余下房间的分法并无特定的模式。对于一些大户人家来讲，分家时家具和器物也都要逐一登记，并力图平均分配。例如，1945年老街上最大的旅店程振兴被一分为二。据说，因为东西和钱财太多，分家前前后后用去了三个多月的时间。一般来说，长子和有长孙的儿子，在分家时会得到较好的一份。如果当时家里还有未成家的男子，也会得到相应的照顾。这种照顾多局限在钱财或器物上，例如，母亲可能把自己的私房钱分给未婚的儿子。在分家后，如果父母还在世，一般会跟长子一起生活；有些人家，父母也会轮流到几个儿子家居住，享受子女的照顾。

另外一种分家的方法是每当一个儿子结婚以后，父母就会拿出一些钱财和器物，让小两口单过。据程镇康老人讲，其太公程乐涞就是这样给他的七个儿子分家的。当程乐涞帮长子程昭斌成亲后，就给了他两千铜钱、一条扁担、两个布袋、一个锅、几个盆和碗，让他们出去租房单过。别看这几样再普通不过的东西，里面却饱含老人的一片苦心。扁担和布袋是给他到杭州和金华去做茶叶生意；两千铜钱当然就是起家和做生意的本钱；有了锅、盆和碗，就可以起灶做饭，填饱肚子。老人没给被褥之类的东西，是因为这些都来自于随嫁的嫁妆。对于接下来的五个儿子，老人都是如此：帮他们娶亲，给他们一些本钱和生活的必需品，让他们出去单过。区别只是当家境好的时候，一条扁担可能变成了两条扁担；家境不好的时候，两千铜钱或许变成了五百铜钱；等到最小的儿子程昭祥成家的时候，老人把他留在了身边，帮助料理，并最终继承了家里的小旅店。有趣的是，这六个被"扫地出门"的儿子，日后都成了颇有成就的大商人，远比备受照顾的小儿子家境好。其中有三个在老街上做起了旅店生意，而且都是赫赫有名的大旅店；另外三个分别经营着茶叶生意、南货店和雨伞店。
sections.content_en:
4. Family Division

Family division mainly has two methods. One is when the elders of the family are elderly or deceased, the sons divide the family among themselves; sometimes it may also be the eldest grandsons and uncles dividing the family. In this case, the presider of family division is generally a person of prestige in the clan; more importantly, maternal uncles and paternal uncles by marriage are invited to testify, and a literate person is found to write the family division contract. The first step of family division is to register the family property and financial situation belonging to the large family. For ordinary families, family division mainly only involves real estate and land. When dividing real estate, if the whole family has only one courtyard, the hall in the courtyard, also called the west room, is kept for common use, for holding weddings and funerals. The one east of the west room is called the upper great room, assigned to the eldest son; the one west of the west room is called the lower great room, assigned to the second son; the division of the remaining rooms has no specific pattern. For some large families, furniture and utensils must also be registered one by one during family division, and an effort is made to distribute them equally. For example, in 1945, the largest inn on the old street, Cheng Zhenxing, was split in two. It is said that because there were too many things and money, the family division took over three months from start to finish. Generally speaking, the eldest son and the son who has an eldest grandson receive a better share during family division. If there were still unmarried men in the family at that time, they would also receive corresponding care. This care is mostly limited to money or utensils; for example, a mother might distribute her private savings to unmarried sons. After family division, if parents are still alive, they generally live with the eldest son; in some families, parents also take turns living with several sons, enjoying the care of their children.

Another method of family division is that whenever a son marries, the parents give some money and utensils to let the young couple live separately. According to Elder Cheng Zhenkang, his great-grandfather Cheng Lelai divided the family this way for his seven sons. After Cheng Lelai helped his eldest son Cheng Zhaobin marry, he gave him two thousand copper coins, one carrying pole, two cloth bags, one pot, several basins and bowls, letting them go out to rent a house and live separately. Don't underestimate these most ordinary things; they contain the old man's painstaking care. The carrying pole and cloth bags were for him to do tea business in Hangzhou and Jinhua; the two thousand copper coins were of course the capital for starting up and doing business; with the pot, basins, and bowls, they could start a stove to cook and fill their stomachs. The old man did not give things like bedding because these came from the dowry. For the next five sons, the old man did the same: helped them marry, gave them some capital and daily necessities, and let them go out to live separately. The difference was only that when the family circumstances were good, one carrying pole might become two; when circumstances were bad, two thousand copper coins might become five hundred; when the youngest son Cheng Zhaoxiang married, the old man kept him by his side to help manage, and he eventually inherited the family's small inn. Interestingly, these six sons who were "swept out the door" all became quite accomplished big merchants later, with far better family circumstances than the much-cared-for youngest son. Three of them started inn businesses on the old street, all famous large inns; the other three respectively operated tea business, a southern goods store, and an umbrella shop.

sections.name: 附录A 浙江省政府各厅处机关在方岩的办公场所
sections.content_zh:
附录A 浙江省政府各厅处、机关、附属机构在方岩的办公场所

浙江省政府迁至方岩办公后，其各厅处位置：

浙江省政府，位于五峰书院，主席黄绍竑。纪念周及省政府会议均在山洞中进行。

浙江省政府秘书处，位于五峰书院，秘书长初为张梁任，后为李立民。

浙江省民政厅，初位于岩下街新隆兴旅店，民国29年（1940年），迁至绍常祠堂。厅长初为王先强，后为阮毅成。

浙江省财政厅及省营贸易局，位于五峰书院旁重楼，又大部分在老仁昌旅店办公。厅长初为程远帆，后为黄祖培。

浙江省教育厅，位于程振兴旅店，厅长许绍棣。

浙江省政府会计处，位于新仁昌旅店，会计长陈宝麟。

浙江省动员委员会，位于五峰路。

浙江省建设厅、浙江省政府社会处、浙江省粮食管理局、浙江省赈济会，位于永康境内其他地区。

浙江省保安处、军官区司令部、浙江省抗日自卫队总司令部，留在金华。

同时迁到方岩的省政府平行机关：

中国国民党浙江省执行委员会，位于五峰旁的空地上，一座由胡库人新建的木构二层楼房内。

浙江省高等法院，位于岩下街南端回龙桥边程氏宗祠（又说程铿别墅），院长郑文礼。

浙江省高等法院检察处，位于岩下街南端，一周姓人家院内，首席检察长王秉彝。

位于岩下街和寿山坑内的浙江省各厅处附属机构：

浙江省地政局、土地测量总队，在民政厅内，即新隆兴旅店，后迁至绍常祠堂。

浙江省警察大队，位于周氏宗祠。

浙江省民政厅公馀进修会，位于岩下街。

浙江省电报局、邮政局及电话局，位于五峰路，租用程中财家3间半民房。

浙江省民政厅卫生处、医疗防疫大队、省会卫生事务所及卫生试验所，位于五峰路及世雅。其中抗战医院位电报、电话局对面，租用四间半民房。

浙江省立建国小学（政府工作人员子弟学校），位于五峰书院内。

浙江省立方岩小学，位于岩下街北端民房内。

浙江省史料征集委员会，位于鸡鸣峰南麓的万成庙内。

浙江省国民通讯社，位于程振兴旅店。

浙江省天赋管理处，位于岩下街北端金标祠堂。

民族夜校，位于岩下街北端，橙麓村民房内，后为程元昌旅店。

省政府主席黄绍竑公馆，位于寿山坑北面山腰，即现在五峰宾馆所在地。

民政厅厅长阮毅成公馆，位于鸡鸣峰南麓，万成庙前。

抗战阵亡将士纪念碑，1939年7月7日建于桃花峰北。
sections.content_en:
Appendix A: Office Locations of Zhejiang Provincial Government Departments, Agencies, and Affiliated Institutions at Fangyan

After the Zhejiang Provincial Government moved to Fangyan for office, the locations of its various departments:

Zhejiang Provincial Government, located at Wufeng Academy, Chairman Huang Shaohong. Memorial weeks and provincial government meetings were all held in caves.

Zhejiang Provincial Government Secretariat, located at Wufeng Academy, Secretary-General initially Zhang Liangren, later Li Limin.

Zhejiang Provincial Department of Civil Affairs, initially located at Xinlongxing Inn on Yanxia Street; in the 29th year of the Republic (1940), moved to Shaochang Ancestral Hall. Department Head initially Wang Xianqiang, later Ruan Yicheng.

Zhejiang Provincial Department of Finance and Provincial Trade Bureau, located at the multi-story building beside Wufeng Academy, with most offices at Laorenchang Inn. Department Head initially Cheng Yuanfan, later Huang Zupei.

Zhejiang Provincial Department of Education, located at Cheng Zhenxing Inn, Department Head Xu Shaodi.

Zhejiang Provincial Government Accounting Office, located at Xinrenchang Inn, Accounting Chief Chen Baolin.

Zhejiang Provincial Mobilization Committee, located at Wufeng Road.

Zhejiang Provincial Department of Construction, Zhejiang Provincial Government Social Affairs Office, Zhejiang Provincial Grain Management Bureau, Zhejiang Provincial Relief Committee, located in other areas within Yongkang.

Zhejiang Provincial Security Office, Military District Command, Zhejiang Provincial Anti-Japanese Self-Defense Force General Command, remained in Jinhua.

Provincial government parallel agencies simultaneously moved to Fangyan:

Chinese Kuomintang Zhejiang Provincial Executive Committee, located on the open ground beside Wufeng, in a newly built two-story wooden building by people from Huku.

Zhejiang Provincial High Court, located at Cheng Clan Ancestral Hall by Huilong Bridge at the southern end of Yanxia Street (also said to be Cheng Keng Villa), President Zheng Wenli.

Zhejiang Provincial High Court Prosecutor's Office, located at the southern end of Yanxia Street, in the courtyard of a Zhou family home, Chief Prosecutor Wang Bingyi.

Affiliated institutions of Zhejiang provincial departments located in Yanxia Street and Shoushan Pit:

Zhejiang Provincial Land Bureau, Land Survey Corps, within the Department of Civil Affairs, i.e. Xinlongxing Inn, later moved to Shaochang Ancestral Hall.

Zhejiang Provincial Police Brigade, located at Zhou Clan Ancestral Hall.

Zhejiang Provincial Department of Civil Affairs Spare-time Further Education Association, located on Yanxia Street.

Zhejiang Provincial Telegraph Bureau, Post Office and Telephone Bureau, located at Wufeng Road, renting three and a half civilian houses from the Cheng Zhongcai family.

Zhejiang Provincial Department of Civil Affairs Health Office, Medical Epidemic Prevention Brigade, Provincial Capital Health Affairs Office and Health Laboratory, located at Wufeng Road and Shiya. Among them, the Anti-Japanese War Hospital was opposite the telegraph and telephone bureau, renting four and a half civilian houses.

Zhejiang Provincial Jianguo Primary School (school for children of government workers), located within Wufeng Academy.

Zhejiang Provincial Fangyan Primary School, located in civilian houses at the northern end of Yanxia Street.

Zhejiang Provincial Historical Materials Collection Committee, located at Wancheng Temple on the southern foot of Jiming Peak.

Zhejiang Provincial National News Agency, located at Cheng Zhenxing Inn.

Zhejiang Provincial Natural Endowment Management Office, located at Jinbiao Ancestral Hall at the northern end of Yanxia Street.

Ethnic Night School, located at the northern end of Yanxia Street, in civilian houses in Chenglu Village, later became Cheng Yuanchang Inn.

Provincial Government Chairman Huang Shaohong's Residence, located on the northern mountainside of Shoushan Pit, i.e. the current location of Wufeng Hotel.

Civil Affairs Department Head Ruan Yicheng's Residence, located on the southern foot of Jiming Peak, in front of Wancheng Temple.

Anti-Japanese War Fallen Soldiers Memorial Monument, built on July 7, 1939, north of Taohua Peak.

sections.name: 附录B 胡公庙会吹唱班部分曲目
sections.content_zh:
附录B 胡公庙会吹唱班部分曲目

十八狐狸

"十八狐狸"又名"大面姑娘"，它是方岩庙会中不可或缺的，而且是最受欢迎的节目。此舞蹈根据民间故事改编，相传唐朝有位官员原有4子18孙。后因门庭败落，17个孙子相继夭亡，撇下17个寡妇。不得已，最小的孙子迫使17位嫂嫂加上其妻共18个人开妓院、卖唱。这一舞蹈由20名男演员组成。18人男扮女装，头戴各种表情的女性面具，上穿蓝色花边大襟衣，下系黑色百褶裙，脚穿绣鞋，一手拿纸扇，一手拿绸帕。一人扮演妓院老板娘，戴羊角髻大面具，穿红色花边大襟衣，系彩带，穿彩裤，着绣鞋，一手捧水烟筒，一手执麦秸扇。另一人扮嫖客，头戴瓜皮帽面具，身穿咖啡色长衫、紫黑色马褂，脚穿黑布鞋，手握长烟管。表演时，嫖客游弋于狐狸中间，丑态百出地进行挑逗调情，狐狸有的斥责反抗，有的卖弄风骚；妓院老板娘则前窜后跳，对嫖客巴结逢迎，对狐狸软哄硬压。在《望乡台》的打击乐伴奏下，只演不唱。

十八蝴蝶

"十八蝴蝶"由18人饰"蝴蝶"，2～4人饰"花神"。蝴蝶"翅膀"用竹篾扎成骨架，覆以纱布或丝绸，上绘各种花纹图案，"翅膀"固定在肩背上，可以自由扇动。"花神"为婺剧花旦打扮，上穿红色对襟水袖衫，下着百褶长裙，手曳披肩长飘带。音乐采用现成的民间小调，如《孟姜女》、《姑娘相思》等，乐队多由四人组成，两人拉二胡，一人敲钹，一人打鼓，演员只舞不唱。

十八鲤鱼

"十八鲤鱼"是由18名女青年扮演的大道具舞蹈。演员身背可以用双手控制自由开合的红色鲤鱼壳。鲤鱼壳的骨架用竹篾扎制，糊上彩纸或纱绸，绘上鱼身。表演时用打击乐，如大小锣、大小钹、小鼓等伴奏。

讨饭莲花

"讨饭莲花"又名永康莲花，一般由18～36个男演员扮演。一人扮演"讨饭头"，其重彩丑脸，赤膊赤脚，头戴"红缨帽"或"草辫箍"，身穿破白裙。身穿破烂衣衫的"讨饭帮"随后，他们每人手执一副莲花竹板，唱《永康莲花》调。通常由"讨饭头"领唱一句，"讨饭帮"跟一句腔，唱词一般有"顺十字"、"倒十字"，或即兴随编。

三十六行

"三十六行"是由38名男性扮演的舞蹈。其中36人扮演36个行业的特征，他们手拿各行各业的典型工具，摆出各自的架势。另有2个男演员各人头戴"草辫箍"，脸施重彩，衣衫不整，腰系稻草绳，赤脚，各打一面大锣，领头开路。
sections.content_en:
Appendix B: Selected Repertoires of the Singing Troupes at the Hu Gong Temple Fair

Eighteen Foxes

"Eighteen Foxes," also known as "Big-Face Girl," is an indispensable and most popular program at the Fangyan temple fair. This dance is adapted from a folk story: legend has it that an official in the Tang Dynasty originally had 4 sons and 18 grandsons. Later, due to the decline of the family, 17 grandsons died one after another, leaving 17 widows. Out of necessity, the youngest grandson forced the 17 sisters-in-law plus his wife, totaling 18 people, to open a brothel and sing for a living. This dance consists of 20 male actors. Eighteen men dress as women, wearing female masks of various expressions, blue lace-front robes, black pleated skirts, and embroidered shoes, holding paper fans in one hand and silk handkerchiefs in the other. One person plays the brothel madam, wearing a large ram's-horn bun mask, red lace-front robe, colored ribbons, colored pants, and embroidered shoes, holding a water pipe in one hand and a wheat-straw fan in the other. Another person plays a client, wearing a melon-rind cap mask, brown long gown, purple-black mandarin jacket, black cloth shoes, and holding a long pipe. During performance, the client roams among the foxes, making a fool of himself with flirting and teasing; some foxes scold and resist, some show off their charms; the brothel madam dashes back and forth, fawning over the client and coaxing or coercing the foxes. Accompanied by percussion music of "Wangxiangtai," it is danced only, not sung.

Eighteen Butterflies

"Eighteen Butterflies" has 18 people playing "butterflies" and 2-4 people playing "flower gods." The butterfly "wings" are framed with bamboo strips, covered with gauze or silk, painted with various floral patterns; the "wings" are fixed on the shoulders and back and can flap freely. The "flower gods" are dressed as Wuju opera female leads, wearing red front-opening water-sleeve tops, long pleated skirts, and holding long shawl ribbons. The music uses existing folk tunes such as "Meng Jiangnu" and "Girl's Longing"; the band usually consists of four people: two playing erhu, one playing cymbals, one playing drums; actors only dance, not sing.

Eighteen Carp

"Eighteen Carp" is a large-prop dance performed by 18 young women. Actors carry on their backs red carp shells that can be freely opened and closed with both hands. The carp shell skeleton is made of bamboo strips, pasted with colored paper or gauze silk, and painted with fish bodies. During performance, it is accompanied by percussion instruments such as large and small gongs, large and small cymbals, and small drums.

Begging Lotus

"Begging Lotus," also known as Yongkang Lotus, is generally performed by 18-36 male actors. One person plays the "begging head," with heavily made-up clown face, bare-chested and barefoot, wearing a "red-tassel hat" or "straw-braid band," and a tattered white skirt. The "begging gang" in tattered clothes follows, each holding a pair of lotus bamboo clappers, singing the "Yongkang Lotus" tune. Usually the "begging head" leads one line, and the "begging gang" follows with a refrain; lyrics generally include "forward ten characters," "reverse ten characters," or improvised verses.

Thirty-Six Trades

"Thirty-Six Trades" is a dance performed by 38 males. Among them, 36 people portray the characteristics of 36 trades, holding typical tools of each trade and striking their respective poses. Another 2 male actors each wear a "straw-braid band," heavy face paint, disheveled clothes, straw rope around the waist, barefoot, each beating a large gong, leading the way.

sections.name: 附录C 方岩旅店情况统计
sections.content_zh:
附录C 方岩旅店情况统计（仅限于新中国成立之前）

本统计表综合了《永康县志》（1991）、《永康名店名厂》（1995）、《方岩指南》（1925）、方岩明清街示意图（应业湘提供）及村民访谈等来源。房间数目可能会随家庭成员人数的增减而稍有变化。表中"分拍"之意即开分店。

清道光末年至咸丰年间（1821-1861）开业的早期旅店：

程隆兴，创建人程岳标（后传程昭卿、程昭亨），清道光末年（1821-1850年），据程岳标曾孙程里鹏回忆，两层高合院建筑（已坍塌），位于上坑口北侧，老街西侧。

马大和，创建人程茂发的曾祖父，姓马，来自东阳，清咸丰年间（1851-1861年），合院建筑（已烧毁），位于老街南端转弯处，1925年之前被烧毁。

程义丰，创建人程乐镛（1832-1866年），后传三子程昭明，清咸丰年间（1851-1861年），房间数10间，两层高三合院，位于蜈蚣山西麓，老街西侧。

高永兴，清咸丰年间（1851-1861年），仅在《永康县志》被提到，《方岩指南》中未提及，在老街上的位置不详。

清光绪年间（1875-1908）开业的旅店：

新隆兴，创建人程昭相、程昭业（程岳标长子和三子），清光绪初年（1875-1882年），房间数14间，三层高合院建筑（近年烧毁），位于下胡坑坑口，老街西侧。

程振兴，创建人程昭夫（1857-1939年），1939年程乐涞三子，清光绪六年（1880年），两层高四合院两幢（1880，1909年），祠堂一座（1924年），两层高洋楼（1924-1942年之间），三层高洋楼（1942年），位于下胡坑坑口以北，老街两侧。

程仁昌，创建人程昭业（程岳标三子），清光绪八年（1882年），三层高合院，三层高小三合院（1887年），沿街两层高建筑（1920年），四层高洋楼（20世纪30年代初），位于狮子山西麓，老街中段西侧。

程义丰雅记，创建人程昭俊（程乐镛二子），两层高三合院，位于蜈蚣山西麓，老街西侧。

民国初年（1925年以前）开业的旅店：

程成昌，创建人程昭丰（1855-1928年，程乐涞二子），民国初年（1925年以前），房间数15间，两层高四合院，位于下胡坑坑口，老街东侧。

程隆昌，创建人程昭贡（程乐涞六子），民国初年（1925年以前），房间数10间，两层高四合院，位于橙麓村，老街西侧。

程洪昌，创建人程宜成，民国初年（1925年以前），房间数10间，两层高四合院，位于橙麓村，老街西侧。

程乾昌，创建人程德喜，民国初年（1925年以前），房间数4间，两层高四合院，位于橙麓村，老街西侧。

程宝昌，创建人程扬荀，民国初年（1925年以前），房间数5间，两层高三合院，位于松门桥以南，老街西侧。

程大昌，创建人程金方，民国初年（1925年以前），房间数10间，三层高四合院，位于三间头，老街西侧。

程顺兴，民国初年（1925年以前），沿街两层高建筑，位于三间头，老街西侧。

程永成溯记，创建人程烂章，民国初年（1925年以前），房间数10间，沿街两层高建筑，位于上坑口以南，老街西侧。

程美义，创建人烂头恕，民国初年（1925年以前），房间数6间，沿街两层高异型合院建筑，位于上坑口以南，老街东侧。

程同昌，民国初年（1925年以前），沿街两层高建筑，位于橙麓村，老街北端西侧。

程顺昌信记、程信昌、程宝元孝记、程宝元仁记、程永全：民国初年（1925年以前），仅在《方岩指南》中被提到，位置及其他情况不详。

民国年间（1925年以后）开业的旅店：

程沅沅，创建人程宜灿，民国年间（1925年以后），房间数6间，两层高三合院建筑沿街一侧，位于蜥蜴山西麓，老街西侧。

程义兴，创建人程方吐，1934年，房间数3间，在老街上的位置不详。

老仁昌，创建人程宜洁，1935年由程仁昌分拍，房间数22间，三层高四合院，位于狮子山西麓，老街中段西侧。

新仁昌，创建人程宜祜，1935年由程仁昌分拍，房间数22间，四层洋楼，三层高小三合院，位于狮子山西麓，老街中段西侧。

程仁兴，创建人程方斗，1937年，房间数4间，仅在《永康名店名厂》中被提到，位置不详。

某某良记，创建人程宜贤，1937年，房间数4间，仅在《永康名店名厂》中被提到，名称和位置不详。

新顺兴，创建人程崇祯，1942年，房间数5间，推测由程顺兴分拍，位于三间头，老街西侧。

程新民，创建人程宣科、程昭亨二子、程岳标孙，1944年，房间数6间，两层高三合院，位于松门桥以西，老街西侧。

程安利，创建人程宣秋，1945年，房间数6间，沿街两层高建筑，位于松门桥以西，老街东侧，程新民对面。

龙山，创建人仙姜，1945年，房间数5间，仅在《永康名店名厂》中被提到，位置不详。

老振兴，创建人程宣吉，1945年由程振兴分拍，房间数51间，两层高四合院一幢，程昭夫祠堂，位于下胡坑口以北，老街两侧。

sections.name: 后记
sections.content_zh:
后记

北京奥运会前的那个夏天，当我正在清华东门外租的板楼里埋头写作的时候，收到了来自美国爱荷华州立大学（Iowa State University）建筑系的邀请信，聘请我去做讲师。兴奋之余，不免有许多忧虑。由于美国大学开学早，况且我还要顾及找房子、买家具等事宜，我需要在七月底离开北京，这比我原定完成书稿的计划至少早了两个月。我向李秋香、陈志华老师解释了情况，并表明我希望能在美国继续完成书稿的意愿，他们表示非常理解和支持。李老师依旧用她一向和善的口气说，"要注意身体，工作也要抓紧"。陈老师只是在电话里语重心长地嘱咐，"想把工作完成是好，但是不要拖"。就这样，在数以万计的各国运动员、记者以及游客纷纷降落在崭新的T3航站楼的那个星期，我匆匆地离开了。

在美国教书的工作远远要比我想象得辛苦，也极具挑战性。整个秋季学期，我觉得自己每天都如同打仗一般。晚上一到家，赖在沙发上就什么都不想做了。由于周末经常还要给十几个学生改论文，所以很少能拿出时间来继续我在清华乡土组未完成的工作。惭愧地说，我辜负了李老师和陈老师的嘱托，把这件事拖了下来。去年年底之前，李老师来了一封信，客气地问工作进展如何。我无言以对，于是下定决心无论如何要把这件事尽快做完、做好，也好给无数信任我的人一个交代。转眼间，春季学期几近尾声，虽然外面时常还会下雪，但是至少我心中的这块石头逐渐落了下来，可以翘首企盼姗姗来迟的春天了。

回想在清华的那些日日夜夜，包括去方岩测绘调研、回来整理以及日后写作的整个过程，心中依旧会感慨万千。这其中我得到了许许多多来自各个层面的帮助，而这项工作也只有在整个研究团队的共同努力和协作下，才能最终完成。在这个过程中，我不但收获颇丰，而且受益匪浅。

在方岩的日子里，当地村民对我们的工作给予了极大的支持和关照，让我深刻感受到了人与人之间以心换心的历程。当那些朴实的村民看到我和我的同事们不论刮风下雨、一趟一趟地从老街上走过，当我一边专心聆听、一边认真记笔记，当我一次又一次的登门拜访，当我把冲洗好的照片送到他们手里的时候，他们对我的信任也随之增加。于是他们会把压在箱子底的"宝贝"翻出来给我们看，他们会把刚刚出锅的、准备孝敬祖宗的"金团"拿给我们吃，他们会把自家院里结的橘子塞到我们的包里，他们会讲更多的故事给我们听。

写到这里，不免要说一些"题外话"。印度著名建筑师查尔斯·柯里亚（Charles Correa）曾经说，"如果我们留意一下人道主义者和环境主义者当前所关心的主要问题，例如生态系统的平衡，垃圾的回收和再利用，公众的参与，适宜的生活模式，本土技术的应用等，我们发现亚洲人民已经开始这样做了"。我想他这里指的是亚洲人民以及他们所居住的没有建筑师的建筑。在我从事研究和写作工作的这两年间，世界性的气候变化以及经济危机无疑给世界各国决策者、各种经济实体乃至每一个人前所未有的挑战，同时也迫使世界各地的建筑师们更加关注如何用新的建筑材料及建筑技术来缓解环境与能源的问题。由此，我想借柯里亚的话说下去：乡土建筑留给我们的不仅仅是悠久的历史和灿烂的文化，更应该超越雕梁画栋与户牖之美，乡土建筑中的许多原则和做法足以给二十一世纪的建筑师们解决环境、能源以及资金问题一些启示，甚至是设计的灵感。

虽然终于写到了结尾，但是我想这本书、这件事，乃至这项工作对我来说仅仅是个开始。陈志华老师曾经感慨：

——乡土文化是中华民族文化中还没有充分开发的宝藏，没有乡土文化的中国文化是残缺不全的，不研究乡土文化就不能真正了解我们这个民族。

——乡土建筑是乡土生活的舞台和物质环境，它是乡土文化最普遍存在的、信息含量最大的组成部分……乡土建筑研究是乡土文化系统研究的基础。

——没有乡土建筑的中国建筑史也是残缺不全的。

我没有陈老师那令人钦佩的远见卓识，更没有资深的阅历来讲出这样深刻的话给别人听；我有的，只是我点点滴滴的真实感受。余秋雨先生曾经感慨，"我居留的大城市里有很多贮存古籍的图书馆，讲授古文化的大学，而中国文化的真实步履却落在这山重水复、莽莽苍苍的大地上"。所以，我很庆幸，我能有机会把自己融入乡土文化这"莽莽苍苍的大地上"；能连续一个星期工作在黄河岸边，感受它的伟大；能坐在有几百年历史的塘边屋前，听年过古稀的老人讲他小时候的故事；能爬进大屋顶，给近人高的斗拱掸掸灰，和它合个影；能怀揣手炉，喝着略带甜涩的井水沏的新茶，翻看着手抄的家谱……

我想，方岩我会再去。我要在"重阳初八夜"那晚和成百上千的人一起上方岩祭拜"胡公大帝"；我也要在正月十四那天和老街上的程氏后人一起迎龙灯；我还要争取参与更多类似的研究工作，让更多的人、特别是年轻人重视和参与到乡土研究工作中来；我更要把我的经历和研究成果写成英文，把中国的乡土建筑推向全世界！

曾经给我们提供帮助的人很多，在此感谢永康市博物馆陈景馆长给予的各方面支持与帮助；方岩镇政府提供的大力协助；永康市的胡春鸿与方岩镇的程伯敦两位学者，以及王岳阳摄影家向我提供了一些他们收集的地方资料；广慈寺前任住持僧允明与现任住持释明修给我讲述了许多广慈寺的重要历史。还要感谢那些住在老街上的程氏后人，程崇舜、程镇康、程茂发、程振锋、程高明、程明星、程圣言、程人龙、程水保、倒插门到程家的应业湘、嫁到老街上的白珑珑和骆巧燕，还有许许多多没来得及记下名字的热心人。

陈志华为岩下老街研究课题总策划，李秋香为项目负责人及测绘主持人，赵巍撰写文字，由陈志华、李秋香指导修改。方岩老街的研究是一项集体共同完成的研究项目，研究组于2007年9月和12月先后两次到方岩进行测绘和调研，参与测绘及调研的人有：李秋香、赵巍、毛葛、孙娜，及建筑学院五年级的林永明、陈华。测绘图主要由赵巍、孙娜、毛葛、林永明和陈华完成，陈金花参加了部分测绘图的绘制修改。随后赵巍又先后两次前往方岩老街，进行调研资料的核实及补充收集。书中手绘插图由赵巍绘制，没有另外注明拍摄者的照片均由赵巍拍摄。

赵巍
2009年4月
艾姆斯（Ames），爱荷华（Iowa）
美国
sections.content_en:
Afterword

In the summer before the Beijing Olympics, while I was buried in writing in a rented apartment building outside the east gate of Tsinghua University, I received an invitation letter from the Department of Architecture at Iowa State University in the United States, hiring me as a lecturer. Beyond excitement, there was inevitably much anxiety. Since American universities start early, and I also had to take care of finding housing, buying furniture, and other matters, I needed to leave Beijing by the end of July, which was at least two months earlier than my original plan to complete the manuscript. I explained the situation to Professors Li Qiuxiang and Chen Zhihua, and expressed my wish to continue completing the manuscript in the United States; they expressed great understanding and support. Professor Li, as always in her gentle tone, said, "Take care of your health, and keep up the work." Professor Chen only earnestly instructed over the phone, "It's good to want to finish the work, but don't delay it." Thus, in the week when tens of thousands of athletes, journalists, and tourists from various countries landed at the brand-new Terminal 3, I left in a hurry.

Teaching in the United States was far more arduous and challenging than I had imagined. Throughout the fall semester, I felt like I was fighting a battle every day. Once home in the evening, I would collapse on the sofa and not want to do anything. Since weekends often still involved grading papers for over a dozen students, I rarely found time to continue the unfinished work of the Tsinghua Vernacular Architecture Group. Ashamed to say, I failed to live up to the trust of Professors Li and Chen, and let this matter drag on. Before the end of last year, Professor Li sent a letter, politely asking about the progress of the work. I had nothing to say in reply, so I made up my mind to finish this matter as soon as possible and do it well, to give an account to the countless people who trusted me. In the blink of an eye, the spring semester is nearly over; although it still snows outside from time to time, at least the stone in my heart has gradually lifted, and I can look forward to the long-awaited spring.

Looking back on those days and nights at Tsinghua, including the entire process of going to Fangyan for surveying and research, returning to organize, and later writing, my heart still fills with countless emotions. During this process, I received help from many levels, and this work could only be finally completed through the joint efforts and collaboration of the entire research team. In this process, I not only gained much but also benefited greatly.

During my days in Fangyan, local villagers gave tremendous support and care to our work, letting me deeply experience the process of heart-to-heart exchange between people. When those simple villagers saw my colleagues and me walking through the old street time and again regardless of wind or rain, when I listened attentively while taking careful notes, when I visited door to door again and again, when I delivered developed photos into their hands, their trust in me grew accordingly. So they would dig out the "treasures" pressed at the bottom of their boxes to show us, they would bring us the freshly cooked "golden dumplings" prepared to honor their ancestors, they would stuff oranges from their own courtyards into our bags, and they would tell us more stories.

Writing to this point, I cannot help but say some "digressions." The famous Indian architect Charles Correa once said, "If we look at all the major concerns of humanists and environmentalists today: balanced eco-systems, recycling of products, people's participation, appropriate life-styles, indigenous technology, etc, we find the people of Asia already have it all." I think what he refers to here is the Asian people and the architect-less architecture they inhabit. During the two years I engaged in research and writing, global climate change and the economic crisis undoubtedly presented unprecedented challenges to policymakers, economic entities, and every individual around the world, while also forcing architects everywhere to pay more attention to how to use new building materials and technologies to alleviate environmental and energy problems. Thus, I would like to continue in Correa's words: what vernacular architecture leaves us is not only long history and splendid culture, but should also transcend the beauty of carved beams and painted rafters and doors and windows; many principles and practices in vernacular architecture are sufficient to give twenty-first-century architects some inspiration, even design inspiration, for solving environmental, energy, and funding problems.

Although I have finally reached the end, I think this book, this matter, and even this work are only a beginning for me. Professor Chen Zhihua once lamented:

— Vernacular culture is a treasure in Chinese national culture that has not been fully developed; Chinese culture without vernacular culture is incomplete, and without studying vernacular culture one cannot truly understand our nation.

— Vernacular architecture is the stage and material environment of vernacular life; it is the most ubiquitous and information-rich component of vernacular culture... Research on vernacular architecture is the foundation of systematic research on vernacular culture.

— The history of Chinese architecture without vernacular architecture is also incomplete.

I do not have Professor Chen's admirable foresight, let alone the senior experience to speak such profound words to others; what I have is only my bit-by-bit true feelings. Mr. Yu Qiuyu once lamented, "In the big cities where I reside, there are many libraries storing ancient books and universities teaching ancient culture, but the true footsteps of Chinese culture fall on this land of mountains upon mountains and vast, boundless wilderness." So I am very fortunate to have had the opportunity to immerse myself in this "vast, boundless wilderness" of vernacular culture; to work for a week straight on the banks of the Yellow River, feeling its greatness; to sit in front of a centuries-old house by a pond, listening to an over-seventy elder tell stories of his childhood; to climb into a large roof, dust off a nearly human-height dougong bracket set, and take a photo with it; to hold a hand warmer, drinking slightly sweet-bitter new tea brewed with well water, while flipping through hand-copied genealogy...

I think I will go to Fangyan again. I want to go up Fangyan with hundreds or thousands of people on the "eighth night of Chongyang" to worship the "Hu Gong Great Emperor"; I also want to welcome the dragon lantern with the Cheng descendants on the old street on the fourteenth day of the first lunar month; I will strive to participate in more similar research work, letting more people, especially young people, value and participate in vernacular research; I will even write my experiences and research results in English, pushing Chinese vernacular architecture to the whole world!

Many people have provided us with help. Here I thank Curator Chen Jing of Yongkang City Museum for all-round support and assistance; the great assistance provided by Fangyan Town Government; scholars Hu Chunhong from Yongkang City and Cheng Bodun from Fangyan Town, as well as photographer Wang Yueyang, for providing some local materials they collected; former abbot Monk Yunming and current abbot Shi Mingxiu of Guangci Temple, for recounting much important history of Guangci Temple. I also thank the Cheng descendants living on the old street: Cheng Chongshun, Cheng Zhenkang, Cheng Maofa, Cheng Zhenfeng, Cheng Gaoming, Cheng Mingxing, Cheng Shengyan, Cheng Renlong, Cheng Shuibao, Ying Yexiang who married into the Cheng family, Bai Longlong and Luo Qiaoyan who married into the old street, and countless warm-hearted people whose names I did not have time to record.
